Preparativi.2.full: Complete the standard setup for {0} players as shown in the rulebook, with the three exceptions below. *Note that the {icon:AngryMob_Icon} track and starting player will be set by the Storybook in the coming pages.*

Preparativi.3.full: Before shuffling the decks, **set aside**, face up next to the board:

Preparativi.4.full: • the **Love Potion** Masterwork Experiment, before dealing the Masterworks;

Preparativi.5.full: • the Compulsion **"The power to change and transform…"** (*Must complete a Chemistry Type Experiment*);

Preparativi.8.full: This unofficial scenario uses some components from the **Fear of the Unknown** Scenario Box. Keep it close at hand, but **do not open it**: the Storybook will tell you which components to take, and when. Everything else must stay in the box, unseen.

SalePrologo.4.full: If you are reading this, I am dead, and someone has respected my last wishes: I am surprised, and I thank you. This file was begun by my father, Silas Pell, your family's notary for forty years, and I kept it for another thirty. Inside are letters, police reports, cuttings from the gazette, a will and a handwriting expert's report: everything two honest notaries could gather about a man who, according to the register of births, was never born.
SalePrologo.4.easy: If you are reading this, I am dead, and someone has respected my last wishes. I am surprised, and I thank you. My father, Silas Pell, began this file. He was your family's notary for forty years. I kept it for another thirty. Inside are letters, police reports, newspaper cuttings, a will and a report by a handwriting expert. It is everything two honest notaries could gather about a man who, according to the records, was never born.
SalePrologo.4.short: If you are reading this, I am dead. Two notaries kept this file, my father Silas and I: letters, reports, a will and an expert's study of a man who, on paper, was never born.

SalePrologo.5.full: Read the documents in the order I have put them, and skip none. And forgive my hand in the last pages: for some years now I have written badly, and some mornings I hardly recognise my own handwriting.
SalePrologo.5.easy: Read the documents in the order I have put them, and do not skip any. And forgive my writing in the last pages: for some years now I have written badly, and some mornings I can hardly recognise my own handwriting.
SalePrologo.5.short: Read the documents in order, skipping none. And forgive my handwriting in the last pages: some mornings I do not recognise it.

SalePrologo.6.full: **Record of the burial – Silas Pell, notary, *March 1861.***

SalePrologo.7.full: At ten in the morning, in the village cemetery, in the presence of the heirs, the parish priest and the undersigned, the remains of the deceased were laid to rest, closed in the coffin the evening before by the carpenter and not reopened since, by his express wish. Overcast sky. Some twenty people present, nearly all out of curiosity.
SalePrologo.7.easy: At ten in the morning, in the village cemetery, the dead man was buried. The heirs, the priest and the writer of this report were present. The carpenter had closed the coffin the evening before, and no one opened it again, because that was the dead man's wish. The sky was grey. About twenty people came, nearly all of them out of curiosity.
SalePrologo.7.short: At ten the deceased was buried, in a coffin closed the night before and never reopened, as he wished. Some twenty onlookers.

SalePrologo.8.full: It is noted, for thoroughness, that at the far end of the cemetery, by the gate, stood a man whom none of those present could name: short of stature, in a black coat too large for him. During the blessing the man was laughing. When the undersigned approached to ask for his particulars, the gate was open and he was gone.
SalePrologo.8.easy: For thoroughness, I note one thing. At the far end of the cemetery, near the gate, stood a man nobody knew. He was short, and wore a black coat too large for him. During the blessing he was laughing. When I went over to ask his name, the gate was open and he was gone.
SalePrologo.8.short: At the back of the cemetery stood a short stranger in a black coat too large for him. During the blessing he laughed. Then he was gone.

PreparaFolla.1.full: Place the Suspicion Marker on space **{0}** and the {icon:AngryMob_Icon} marker one space to its left. Give the {icon:StartPlayerToken} marker to **{1}**.

Traguardi.2.full: The first time a player reaches space 3 of the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track this Generation,

Traguardi.5.full: The first time a player reaches space 3 of the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track this Generation,

Traguardi.8.full: The first time a player reaches Level 2 of the Chemistry Journal Track this Generation,

Traguardi.11.full: The first time a player reaches 15VP this Generation,

PosaTraguardi.2.full: Place one on **space 3** of the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track, one on **space 3** of the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track and one on **space 15** of the Victory Point track. The fourth goes at the top of the **Level 2 column of the Chemistry Journal Track**: it counts for every player.

PosaTraguardi.3.full: When a player's marker reaches one of these tokens, that player clicks the matching entry in the Storybook and reads a message. Then the token returns to the supply.

TkCreepy.2.full: People are talking about you. At the market, conversations stop when you pass and start again, lower, as soon as you have turned the corner. The washerwoman swears she saw a little man dressed in black come out of your alley at dawn, and heard him whistling your favourite tune.
TkCreepy.2.easy: People are talking about you. At the market they stop talking when you pass, and start again more quietly as soon as you turn the corner. The washerwoman swears she saw a little man dressed in black come out of your alley at dawn. She says he was whistling your favourite tune.
TkCreepy.2.short: People talk about you. The washerwoman swears a little man in black left your alley at dawn, whistling your tune.

TkCreepy.3.full: People are talking about you, and now they are writing about it too. In the Gazette's gossip column, under the heading *Who Goes Out at Night?*, there is a riddle in verse about an heir "of good family and bad habits". It does not name you. It does not need to: every rhyme is on your surname.
TkCreepy.3.easy: People are talking about you, and now they are writing about it too. The Gazette's gossip page has a heading: *Who Goes Out at Night?* Under it is a rhyming riddle about an heir "of good family and bad habits". It does not say your name. It does not need to: every rhyme is on your surname.
TkCreepy.3.short: The Gazette prints a rhyming riddle: *Who Goes Out at Night?* It does not name you, but every rhyme is on your surname.

TkCreepy.4.full: People are talking about you, and it is the children who do it. In the street they skip rope to a new rhyme: *Umber, Umber, who is he? Papa's face is what you'll see.* When you pass they stop singing, look at you, and start again, louder.
TkCreepy.4.easy: People are talking about you, and the children too. In the street they skip rope and sing a new rhyme: *Umber, Umber, who is he? Papa's face is what you'll see.* When you pass they stop singing and look at you. Then they start again, louder.
TkCreepy.4.short: The children sing: *Umber, Umber, who is he? Papa's face is what you'll see.* When you pass they stare, and sing louder.

TkCreepy.6.full: You feed the rumour: a little fear comes in handy.

TkCreepy.7.full: You deny it, out loud, where it matters.

TkCreepy.8.full: You deny nothing. Rather, when people ask, you answer with half a smile and let them draw their own conclusions. In the weeks that follow suppliers deliver promptly, creditors wait, and the undertakers give you a discount.
TkCreepy.8.easy: You do not say it is untrue. In fact, when someone asks, you answer with half a smile and let people think what they like. In the weeks after, suppliers deliver quickly, creditors wait, and the undertakers give you a discount.
TkCreepy.8.short: You deny nothing: you smile and let them talk. Suppliers hurry, creditors wait, undertakers give you a discount.

TkCreepy.9.full: Gain 1 {icon:Bodies_Icon}. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkCreepy.10.full: You speak to the priest, to the bank manager, to the ladies of the charity committee: the rumours are slander, and your family suffers for them. They listen with great understanding. Someone, perhaps, believes you.
TkCreepy.10.easy: You talk to the priest, to the bank manager, to the ladies who do charity work. You say the rumours are lies, and that your family is hurt by them. They listen very kindly. Perhaps someone believes you.
TkCreepy.10.short: You tell the priest, the banker and the charity ladies it is all slander. Perhaps someone believes you.

TkCreepy.11.full: Move back 1 space on the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkInsanity.2.full: You are washing your face when the mirror, for an instant, gives you back another face: younger, smaller, with a smile you have never smiled. When you look again you are yourself again; but that smile stays on you all morning, and you cannot take it off.
TkInsanity.2.easy: You are washing your face when, for a moment, you see another face in the mirror. It is younger, smaller, and it smiles a smile you have never smiled. You look again, and it is you again. But that smile stays on you all morning, and you cannot get rid of it.
TkInsanity.2.short: For a moment the mirror shows another face, with a smile that is not yours. It stays on you all morning.

TkInsanity.3.full: In a shop window, while you wait for the carriage, your reflection turns a moment before you do. Only a moment: the time of a glance. Then it is back in its place, polite, precise, copying you in everything. Almost everything: it is not holding its hat in its hand.
TkInsanity.3.easy: You are waiting for the carriage in front of a shop window. Your reflection turns a moment before you do. Only a moment, the time of a glance. Then it goes back to its place, polite and precise, and copies you in everything. Almost everything: it is not holding its hat.
TkInsanity.3.short: In the window your reflection turns a moment before you. Then it copies you in everything. Almost: it is not holding its hat.

TkInsanity.4.full: In the family photograph just collected from the photographer's studio, everyone is looking at the lens. Everyone but you: in the photograph you are looking sideways, towards the door, and smiling. The photographer swears he retouched nothing. You swear you have never smiled like that.
TkInsanity.4.easy: You collect the family photograph from the photographer. Everyone is looking at the camera. Everyone except you: in the photo you are looking to the side, towards the door, and smiling. The photographer swears he changed nothing. You swear you have never smiled like that.
TkInsanity.4.short: In the family photo everyone looks at the lens. You look at the door, smiling as you never have.

TkInsanity.8.full: You break the glass with the palm of your hand, without thinking. The pain does you good: it is yours, and no one else's. You bind your hand with a handkerchief and for a while, in the evenings, you avoid shiny surfaces.
TkInsanity.8.easy: You break the glass with the palm of your hand, without thinking. The pain does you good: it is yours, and nobody else's. You wrap your hand in a handkerchief. For a while, in the evenings, you avoid anything that shines.
TkInsanity.8.short: You smash the mirror with your hand. The pain is yours alone. For a while you avoid reflections.

TkInsanity.9.full: Move back 1 space on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track and pay $1. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkInsanity.10.full: You look a while longer. The other face does not show itself again, but it leaves you something: an idea, sharp and complete, as if someone had whispered it in your ear while you were not paying attention.
TkInsanity.10.easy: You look for longer. The other face does not come back, but it leaves you something: a clear, complete idea. It is as if someone had whispered it in your ear while you were thinking of something else.
TkInsanity.10.short: The other face does not return, but leaves you an idea, clear and whole, as if whispered.

TkInsanity.11.full: Draw an Experiment from the deck of your choice. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkChemistry.2.full: In your Journal, below last night's notes, there is a page you do not remember writing. It is a formula, and it is right: more elegant than anything you have ever found. The ink is from your inkwell. The handwriting slants backwards.
TkChemistry.2.easy: In your Journal, under last night's notes, there is a page you do not remember writing. It is a formula, and it is right: more beautiful than anything you have ever found. The ink is from your inkwell. But the writing slants backwards.
TkChemistry.2.short: In your Journal is a formula you do not remember writing. It is right, and beautiful. The handwriting slants backwards.

TkChemistry.3.full: A letter with no sender, posted in town: inside, on the estate's own paper, the solution to the problem that has tormented you for months, written with a confidence you have never had. The postmark is from last night. Last night, as far as you remember, you were asleep.
TkChemistry.3.easy: A letter arrives with no sender, posted in town. Inside, on the estate's own paper, is the answer to the problem that has troubled you for months. It is written with a confidence you have never had. The postmark is from last night. Last night, as far as you remember, you were asleep.
TkChemistry.3.short: An unsigned letter, on estate paper, solves your problem. Postmarked last night. Last night you were asleep.

TkChemistry.4.full: You wake at the laboratory desk with a pen in your hand and a stiff neck. In front of you, three pages thick with calculations: all of them right, all of them new. The first lines are in your handwriting. The last ones, ever smaller and quicker, slant backwards.
TkChemistry.4.easy: You wake at the laboratory desk, pen in hand and neck stiff. In front of you are three pages full of calculations: all correct, all new. The first lines are in your handwriting. The last ones, smaller and faster, slant backwards.
TkChemistry.4.short: You wake at the desk before three pages of correct sums. The last lines slant backwards.

TkChemistry.8.full: The formula works, of course. It works so well that for a whole day you feel a genius, and for a whole night you are afraid to fall asleep.
TkChemistry.8.easy: The formula works, of course. It works so well that for a whole day you feel like a genius, and for a whole night you are afraid to fall asleep.
TkChemistry.8.short: The formula works. By day you feel a genius; by night you dare not sleep.

TkChemistry.9.full: Gain 1 {icon:Chemical_Icon} and 1 Chemistry Knowledge. Move up 1 space on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkChemistry.10.full: You burn it in the laboratory stove, sheet by sheet, and watch the paper blacken until nothing is left. What you find without help is less beautiful. But it is yours.
TkChemistry.10.easy: You burn the formula in the laboratory stove, one sheet at a time, and watch the paper turn black until nothing is left. What you find by yourself is less beautiful. But it is yours.
TkChemistry.10.short: You burn it, sheet by sheet. What you find yourself is less beautiful. But it is yours.

TkChemistry.11.full: Gain 1VP. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkVP.2.full: An invitation arrives on heavy paper: dinner with decent people, with the bank manager and two ladies who fund charitable works. All evening no one at the table mentions Umber. When you take your leave, your host shakes your hand longer than necessary and puts an envelope in it: "For your research. Science needs respectable people."
TkVP.2.easy: An invitation arrives on heavy paper: dinner with respectable people, with the bank manager and two ladies who do charity work. All evening nobody mentions Umber. When you leave, your host shakes your hand for longer than usual and gives you an envelope: "For your research. Science needs respectable people."
TkVP.2.short: At a respectable dinner no one mentions Umber. As you leave, your host hands you an envelope: "Science needs respectable people."

TkVP.3.full: The town club, the one with the leather armchairs and the portrait of the sovereign, puts your name forward as a member. They welcome you with a toast and a speech on progress. Later, in the library, the chairman takes you aside: some members would gladly fund your research, provided the estate's name stays out of the papers.
TkVP.3.easy: The town club, the one with leather armchairs and a portrait of the king, invites you to become a member. They welcome you with a toast and a speech about progress. Later, in the library, the chairman takes you aside. Some members would happily pay for your research, as long as the estate's name stays out of the newspapers.
TkVP.3.short: The club makes you a member. The chairman offers money for your research, if the estate stays out of the papers.

TkVP.4.full: The university in the capital invites you to give a lecture. The hall is full: professors, students, journalists, and in the back row veiled ladies taking notes. At the end an elderly academic stands up and offers you a research grant. Then he adds, with a smile, that of course nobody believes the stories about the salt.
TkVP.4.easy: The university in the capital invites you to give a lecture. The hall is full: professors, students, journalists, and at the back some veiled ladies taking notes. At the end an old professor stands up and offers you a grant. Then he adds, with a smile, that of course nobody believes the stories about the salt.
TkVP.4.short: Your lecture at the university is packed. An old professor offers you a grant, adding that no one believes the salt stories.

TkVP.6.full: You accept the money, and keep quiet.

TkVP.7.full: You refuse, and speak about Umber in front of everyone.

TkVP.8.full: You accept, thank them, and say not a word too many. The money is good, the company is good, the silence is excellent. On the way home you notice you have been whistling the whole way, and that you do not know the tune.
TkVP.8.easy: You accept, say thank you, and say not one word too many. The money is good, the company is good, and the silence is perfect. On the way home you notice you have been whistling the whole way. And you do not know the tune.
TkVP.8.short: You accept and keep quiet. On the way home you whistle a tune you do not know.

TkVP.9.full: Gain $2. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkVP.10.full: You refuse, politely, and tell them about Umber: the cheques, the nights, your family. The silence that follows is very long. Then someone applauds, and others follow, uncertain. You have told the truth in a place where it is not done, and someone, strangely, liked it.
TkVP.10.easy: You refuse, politely, and talk about Umber: the cheques, the nights, your family. A very long silence follows. Then someone claps, and others join in, a little unsure. You have told the truth in a place where people do not, and strangely, someone liked it.
TkVP.10.short: You refuse and speak of Umber. After a long silence, someone claps. The truth, strangely, went down well.

Bevi.1.full: **This page is secret: do not show it to the others.**

Bevi.3.full: The phial comes from the chemist's, like all the others: white salt, perfectly pure, with the new label. In the water the colour begins to change, but not as it should. It turns red, and stops there, like a wound that will not close.
Bevi.3.easy: The phial comes from the chemist, like all the others: white salt, very pure, with the new label. In the water the colour starts to change, but not as it should. It turns red and stops there, like a wound that will not close.
Bevi.3.short: The new salt turns the water red, and stops there, like a wound that will not close.

Bevi.4.full: You open the laboratory drawer: the phials are empty. Only the smell is left, bitter, at the bottom of the glass. You breathe it in for a long time before putting them back.
Bevi.4.easy: You open the laboratory drawer: the phials are empty. At the bottom of the glass there is only the smell, bitter. You breathe it in for a long time before you put them back.
Bevi.4.short: The phials are empty. Only the bitter smell is left.

Bevi.6.full: The zinc box is still under the loose board by the stove, where your parents found it. There are **{0}** phials left. In twenty-five years the salt has taken on a warmer colour, almost ivory, and a faint smell of bitter almond. In the glass, though, it still does what it should: red, violet, green. Whoever drank it before you died in their bed. More or less.
Bevi.6.easy: The zinc box is still under the loose board by the stove, where your parents found it. There are **{0}** phials left. In twenty-five years the salt has turned almost ivory, and smells faintly of bitter almond. But in the glass it still does what it should: red, violet, green. Whoever drank it before you died in their bed. More or less.
Bevi.6.short: **{0}** phials are left. The salt has turned ivory, but in the glass it still goes red, violet, green.

Bevi.7.full: The white powder falls into the glass of water, and the colour begins to change: red, then deep violet, then the green of a pond. Your hand trembles a little. One sip is enough.
Bevi.7.easy: The white powder falls into the glass of water, and the colour starts to change: first red, then dark violet, then green like a pond. Your hand shakes a little. One sip is enough.
Bevi.7.short: In the glass: red, violet, green. Your hand shakes. One sip is enough.

Bevi.10.full: The new salt works, but the wrong way round. The other one goes out as always, quick and merry; but in the morning, when you try to come back, part of you stays outside the door, and will not come in.
Bevi.10.easy: The new salt works, but the wrong way round. The other one goes out as always, quick and cheerful. But in the morning, when you try to come back, part of you stays outside the door, and will not come in again.
Bevi.10.short: The new salt works backwards: in the morning part of you stays outside, and will not come back in.

Bevi.11.full: Gain 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon} and 1 {icon:Creepy_Icon}. You gain no resources.

Bevi.12.full: The pain lasts a minute, as the Journal said: the bones, the heart, the floor. Then you go out into the city of stone, in the other's small, quick body, and the city is yours. You run across wet roofs, look at yourself in shuttered shop windows, light a cigar from a gas lamp and blow the lamp out. You laugh, and the fog laughs behind you.
Bevi.12.easy: The pain lasts a minute, as the Journal said: the bones, the heart, the floor. Then you go out into the city of stone, in the other's small, fast body, and the city belongs to you. You run over wet roofs, look at yourself in closed shop windows, light a cigar at a gas lamp and blow the lamp out. You laugh, and the fog laughs with you.
Bevi.12.short: A minute of pain, then you go out in the other's small, quick body. You run on the roofs and laugh, and the fog laughs too.

Bevi.13.full: In the morning you wake in your bed, your shoes black with soot. In your pocket is a cheque signed with your name, and a ticket for a theatre you have never set foot in.
Bevi.13.easy: In the morning you wake in your bed, your shoes black with soot. In your pocket is a cheque signed with your name, and a ticket for a theatre you have never been to.
Bevi.13.short: Morning: sooty shoes, a cheque in your name and a ticket to an unknown theatre.

Bevi.14.full: The pain lasts a minute: the grinding bones, the leaping heart, the floor coming closer. Then comes a new lightness: a small, quick body, without a single regret in the world, going out by the servants' door.
Bevi.14.easy: The pain lasts a minute: the bones creaking, the heart jumping, the floor coming closer. Then comes a new lightness: a small, fast body, with no regrets at all, going out through the servants' door.
Bevi.14.short: A minute of pain. Then a small, quick body, without regret, slips out by the servants' door.

Bevi.15.full: In the morning you wake in your bed, your shoes caked with mud. In your pocket is a cheque signed with your name, in a handwriting that slants backwards.
Bevi.15.easy: In the morning you wake in your bed, your shoes covered in mud. In your pocket is a cheque signed with your name, but the writing slants backwards.
Bevi.15.short: Morning: muddy shoes and a cheque in your name, in a backward-slanting hand.

Bevi.16.full: Immediately gain one resource of your choice ({icon:Bodies_Icon}, {icon:Chemical_Icon}, {icon:Gears_Icon} or {icon:Animal_Icon}) and 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}.

Bevi.17.full: You tip the glass into the sink and watch the red go down the drain, slowly, as if it did not want to. No one will know what you chose. Not even the other one, perhaps.
Bevi.17.easy: You pour the glass into the sink and watch the red go down the drain, slowly, as if it did not want to. No one will know what you chose. Perhaps not even the other one.
Bevi.17.short: You empty the glass into the sink. No one will know what you chose. Perhaps not even the other one.

Bevi.18.full: You put the phial back in the drawer and turn the key twice. Your hands are still shaking when you go back to the others. No one will know what you chose.
Bevi.18.easy: You put the phial back in the drawer and lock it twice. When you go back to the others your hands are still shaking. No one will know what you chose.
Bevi.18.short: You put the phial back. No one will know what you chose.

BeviEffetti.3.full: You are the first to drink the salt: take the **Love Potion** Masterwork that was set aside and put it in place of your Masterwork, which goes back in the box. Also take the Compulsion that was set aside.

BeviEffetti.4.full: It is your first time drinking it: draw two **Obsession cards** from the box, keep one and put the other back.

BeviEffetti.5.full: It is your third time: take the **Addict** Maladjustment that was set aside.

BeviEffetti.12.full: Place a **Sighting** {icon:S2_HuntTokenFRONT} face down on a Location chosen by whoever drank.

SaleG1Intro.1.full: **GENERATION I: The Door on the Alley**

SaleG1Intro.2.full: **Record of the reading of the will – Silas Pell, notary, *March 1861.***

SaleG1Intro.3.full: The heirs gathered in the estate library the day after the burial, at five in the afternoon. The curtains were drawn, as always in that house; the fire was out, and no one asked for it to be lit. The undersigned broke the seals in the presence of all and read the document aloud, written in the deceased's own hand two years ago.
SaleG1Intro.3.easy: The heirs met in the estate library the day after the funeral, at five in the afternoon. The curtains were closed, as always in that house. The fire was out, and no one asked for it to be lit. I broke the seals in front of everyone and read the document, which the dead man had written by hand two years before.
SaleG1Intro.3.short: The day after the funeral, in the library, curtains drawn and fire out, I read the will to the heirs.

SaleG1Intro.4.full: The estate, with the laboratory, the instruments, the animals and the debts, goes in equal shares to the children. The Journal goes to whoever can read it. So far, nothing strange.
SaleG1Intro.4.easy: The estate, with the laboratory, the instruments, the animals and the debts, goes to the children, in equal shares. The Journal goes to whoever can read it. So far, nothing strange.
SaleG1Intro.4.short: The estate goes to the children, the Journal to whoever can read it. Nothing strange.

SaleG1Intro.5.full: There follows a clause, which the undersigned had to read twice at the request of those present: *"Should I disappear without explanation, or die in circumstances my notary judges doubtful, all the rest of my property, the money in the bank, the shares and the key to the study on the alley, shall go to my friend Mr. Umber, who will know how to put it to good use."*
SaleG1Intro.5.easy: Then there is a clause. I had to read it twice, because those present asked me to: *"Should I disappear without explanation, or die in circumstances my notary judges doubtful, all the rest of my property, the money in the bank, the shares and the key to the study on the alley, shall go to my friend Mr. Umber, who will know how to put it to good use."*
SaleG1Intro.5.short: Then the clause: *"Should I disappear, or die in doubtful circumstances, all the rest, with the key to the study on the alley, shall go to my friend Mr. Umber."*

SaleG1Intro.6.full: None of those present knows a Mr. Umber. No one knew the deceased had a friend. No one, to tell the truth, knew the estate had a study on the alley.
SaleG1Intro.6.easy: None of those present knows any Mr. Umber. No one knew the dead man had a friend. And no one, to tell the truth, knew the estate had a study on the alley.
SaleG1Intro.6.short: No one knows Mr. Umber. No one knew of a study on the alley.

SaleG1Intro.7.full: The undersigned notes that the deceased died in his bed, of a fever, attended by the village doctor: the circumstances are not doubtful. The undersigned will nonetheless hand nothing over to anyone until this Mr. Umber presents himself at his office, in person and in broad daylight.
SaleG1Intro.7.easy: I note that the dead man died in his bed, of a fever, with the village doctor beside him. The circumstances are not doubtful. But I will give nothing to anyone until this Mr. Umber comes to my office, in person and by day.
SaleG1Intro.7.short: He died of a fever, in his bed. But Mr. Umber gets nothing until he comes to me, in person and by day.

SaleG1Intro.8.full: Before taking his leave, the undersigned gave each of the heirs a page of the Journal, torn out and sealed, with their name written on it by the deceased. They too were in the will.
SaleG1Intro.8.easy: Before I left I gave each heir a page of the Journal, torn out and sealed, with their name written on it by the dead man. These pages were in the will too.
SaleG1Intro.8.short: I gave each heir a sealed page of the Journal, with their name on it in the dead man's hand.

G1JournalA.3.full: **With your name on it, in your father's hand.**

G1JournalA.4.full: *Lomax's salt, the first batch, and no other. Dissolved in a glass of well water: red, then violet, then green. A single sip, on an empty stomach.*
G1JournalA.4.easy: *Lomax's salt, the first batch, and no other. Dissolved in a glass of well water: red, then violet, then green. Only one sip, on an empty stomach.*
G1JournalA.4.short: *Lomax's salt, the first batch, and no other. One sip, on an empty stomach.*

G1JournalA.5.full: *I have tried the salt of other chemists, and nothing happens. I have tried a second batch from Lomax, and nothing happens. There must have been something in that first batch that was not written in the order.*
G1JournalA.5.easy: *I have tried salt from other chemists, and nothing happens. I have tried a second batch from Lomax, and nothing happens. There must have been something in that first batch that was not written in the order.*
G1JournalA.5.short: *Other salts fail, even a second batch from Lomax. The first held something unwritten.*

G1JournalA.6.full: *It is not I who goes out at night. I swear it on all I hold dear. And yet in the morning I have his keys in my pocket, and he has mine; I have his shoes on my feet, and they are my size.*
G1JournalA.6.easy: *It is not I who go out at night. I swear it on everything I love. And yet in the morning I have his keys in my pocket, and he has mine. I have his shoes on my feet, and they are my size.*
G1JournalA.6.short: *It is not I who go out at night. Yet in the morning I have his keys, and his shoes are my size.*

G1JournalA.7.full: Halfway along the next line the writing changes: it becomes smaller, quicker, and slants backwards, as if the hand were pulling the other way. *Stop writing about me.*
G1JournalA.7.easy: Halfway through the next line the writing changes: it gets smaller, faster, and slants backwards, as if the hand were pulling the other way. *Stop writing about me.*
G1JournalA.7.short: Then the writing changes, slanting backwards: *Stop writing about me.*

G1JournalA.8.full: A page of accounts, dense with figures. Halfway down, underlined twice: *Lomax, chemist, by the bridge: six phials, paid in cash.* The sum would buy the whole chemist's shop.
G1JournalA.8.easy: It is a page of accounts, full of numbers. Halfway down there is a line underlined twice: *Lomax, chemist, by the bridge: six phials, paid in cash.* With that sum you could buy the whole shop.
G1JournalA.8.short: Accounts. Underlined: *Lomax, chemist: six phials, paid in cash.* A huge sum.

G1JournalA.9.full: Below, in pencil, smaller, as if written in haste: *S. P. knows. S. P. has the key to the cupboard. Tell him nothing, not yet.*
G1JournalA.9.easy: Below, in pencil, smaller, as if written in a hurry: *S. P. knows. S. P. has the key to the cupboard. Tell him nothing, not yet.*
G1JournalA.9.short: In pencil: *S. P. knows. S. P. has the key to the cupboard. Tell him nothing.*

G1JournalA.10.full: A careful drawing of a wooden door with neither handle nor lock, with the measurements of the hinges and an address: the alley behind the estate. Below, a single line: *It opens only from the inside. Remember that, when I am on the other side.*
G1JournalA.10.easy: It is an exact drawing of a wooden door with no handle and no lock, with the measurements of the hinges and an address: the alley behind the estate. Below is a single line: *It opens only from the inside. Remember that, when I am on the other side.*
G1JournalA.10.short: A drawing of a handleless door in the alley behind the estate: *It opens only from the inside. Remember that, when I am on the other side.*

G1JournalA.11.full: On the back, stained with mud, is the print of a shoe: small, too small for a grown man.
G1JournalA.11.easy: On the back, dirty with mud, is the print of a shoe. It is small, too small for a grown man.
G1JournalA.11.short: On the back, the muddy print of a shoe too small for a man.

G1JournalA.12.full: What do you do with the page?

G1JournalA.13.full: You keep it to yourself, among your papers.

G1JournalA.14.full: You read it aloud to everyone, at breakfast.

G1JournalA.15.full: You fold the page in four and slip it among your papers. It is yours, after all: your name is on it, in your father's hand. You will tell the others whatever you like, whenever you like.
G1JournalA.15.easy: You fold the page in four and put it among your papers. After all, it is yours: your name is on it, written by your father. You will tell the others what you want, when you want.
G1JournalA.15.short: You fold it and keep it. It is yours: your name is on it.

G1JournalA.16.full: Gain 1 Chemistry Knowledge. You may tell the others what you read: all of it, some of it or nothing.

G1JournalA.17.full: The next morning, at breakfast, you read the page aloud, word for word, skipping nothing. The others listen in silence, and someone looks at you with gratitude. Someone else, with suspicion: why so generous?
G1JournalA.17.easy: The next morning, at breakfast, you read the page aloud, word for word, skipping nothing. The others listen in silence. Someone looks at you gratefully. Someone else suspiciously: why are you being so generous?
G1JournalA.17.short: At breakfast you read it aloud. One looks grateful. Another, suspicious.

G1JournalA.18.full: Read the text in italics above aloud to the other players. Gain 1VP.

G1JournalFine.2.full: Little is said at breakfast. Those who read their page aloud did so quickly, between the coffee and the bread; the others have folded theirs into a pocket, and watch everyone else's pockets. Pell the notary left at dawn without saying goodbye, and his carriage has left two deep ruts in the mud of the drive.
G1JournalFine.2.easy: Little is said at breakfast. Whoever read their page aloud did it quickly, between the coffee and the bread. The others put theirs in their pockets, and watch everyone else's pockets. Pell the notary left at dawn without saying goodbye, and his carriage left two deep tracks in the mud of the drive.
G1JournalFine.2.short: Little is said at breakfast, and everyone eyes the others' pockets. The notary left at dawn without a word.

G1JournalFine.3.full: From the dining-room windows you can see the village of {0}: half-timbered houses huddled around the square, the market, the bridge over the river. On the hill, where sheep grazed until last year, Lady Carew's workmen have begun to dig the foundations of a great brick building. It will be an asylum, they say, the most modern in the county. Lady Carew has already let it be known that places will be few, and reserved for decent families.
G1JournalFine.3.easy: From the dining-room windows you can see the village of {0}: timber-framed houses crowded round the square, the market, the bridge over the river. On the hill, where there were sheep last year, Lady Carew's workmen have started digging for a big brick building. It will be an asylum, they say, the most modern in the county. Lady Carew has already said there will be few places, and only for respectable families.
G1JournalFine.3.short: From the window you see {0}. On the hill Lady Carew is building a modern asylum, with few places, for respectable families.

G1JournalFine.4.full: It remains to decide what to do with your father's laboratory: a long, low room at the back of the house, with smoke-blackened windows, alembics still dirty and a smell of acid that no draught can carry away.
G1JournalFine.4.easy: You must decide what to do with your father's laboratory. It is a long, low room at the back of the house, with windows black from smoke, alembics still dirty and a smell of acid that no breeze can carry away.
G1JournalFine.4.short: There is still your father's laboratory: blackened windows, dirty alembics, a smell of acid.

G1JournalFine.5.full: What do you do with the laboratory? *(Decide together.)*

G1JournalFine.6.full: You lock it up, just as it is.

G1JournalFine.7.full: You open it again and work there.

G1JournalFine.8.full: You sell the most valuable instruments.

G1JournalFine.9.full: You double-lock the door and hang the key in the kitchen, where everyone can see it. The village finds out, as it finds out everything, and approves: a family that locks up its father's laboratory is a family that wants a quiet life.
G1JournalFine.9.easy: You lock the door twice and hang the key in the kitchen, where everyone can see it. The village finds out, as it always does, and is pleased: a family that locks up its father's laboratory is a family that wants a quiet life.
G1JournalFine.9.short: You lock the laboratory. The village approves.

G1JournalFine.11.full: You throw open the windows, wash the alembics, relight the burners. In the drawers you find reagents of every kind, well kept, carefully labelled. Your father bought in bulk: there is enough for years.
G1JournalFine.11.easy: You open the windows, wash the alembics, light the burners again. In the drawers you find lots of chemicals, well kept and labelled. Your father bought in large amounts: there is enough for years.
G1JournalFine.11.short: You reopen the laboratory. The drawers hold chemicals for years.

G1JournalFine.13.full: A dealer from town comes with a cart and leaves with the brass microscope, the precision scales and two crates of glassware. He pays well, and in cash. The cart crosses the whole village, and everyone sees the old man's instruments jolting under the tarpaulin.
G1JournalFine.13.easy: A dealer comes from town with a cart and takes away the brass microscope, the precision scales and two crates of glassware. He pays well, and in cash. The cart goes right through the village, and everyone sees the old man's instruments bouncing under the cover.
G1JournalFine.13.short: A dealer buys the instruments and pays well. The whole village sees the cart go by.

G1R1.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 4**.

G1R1.4.full: The firm building the asylum has its office at the Builder's Office. The first player to send one of their pieces there,

G1R1.7.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Cemetery,

G1R1.10.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Laborer's Union,

G1R1.13.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Park,

G1R1.16.full: When one of your pieces visits the Fortune Teller, you may pay $1 and have your palm read:

G1R1.19.full: At the market, all the talk is of the funeral, and of the man in the black coat who was laughing at the far end of the cemetery. The baker swears it was the devil; the sexton, that it was a creditor.
G1R1.19.easy: At the market people talk only about the funeral, and about the man in the black coat who was laughing at the back of the cemetery. The baker swears he was the devil. The sexton says he was someone the dead man owed money to.
G1R1.19.short: The market talks of the man in black who laughed at the funeral. The devil, says the baker; a creditor, says the sexton.

G1R1.20.full: Click here at the end of the Round to move on to the next Round...

round.G1R1.end.full: The Early Years of the First Generation have ended.

round.G1R1.then.full: Then perform all Start of Round actions for the Middle Years before continuing.

G1Cantiere.2.full: In the firm's office, among rolls of plans and sample bricks, sits Lady Carew herself: a tall, upright lady dressed in grey, with a leather-bound notebook always open on her knees. She listens to the foreman without looking at him, and takes notes.
G1Cantiere.2.easy: In the firm's office, among rolls of drawings and sample bricks, sits Lady Carew herself. She is a tall, straight-backed lady dressed in grey, with a leather-bound notebook always open on her knees. She listens to the foreman without looking at him, and takes notes.
G1Cantiere.2.short: In the office sits Lady Carew: tall, in grey, a leather notebook on her knees. She listens and takes notes.

G1Cantiere.3.full: When she sees you come in she closes the notebook, smiles and asks whether you are there to see "the future of charity in this county". The asylum will have a hundred beds, she says, and she still does not know how to pay for its roof. Decent families usually contribute. The others usually end up inside.
G1Cantiere.3.easy: When she sees you come in she closes the notebook, smiles and asks if you have come to see "the future of charity in this county". The asylum will have a hundred beds, she says, but she does not yet know how to pay for the roof. Respectable families usually help. The others usually end up inside.
G1Cantiere.3.short: Lady Carew asks for money for the asylum roof. Respectable families help, she says. The others end up inside.

G1Cantiere.5.full: You pay $2 towards the asylum roof.

G1Cantiere.6.full: You ask to see the plans.

G1Cantiere.7.full: You say your family has no need of asylums.

G1Cantiere.8.full: Lady Carew thanks you, writes your name in the notebook in a small, even hand and promises you a brass plaque at the entrance. She sees you to the door with her arm through yours, as one does with relatives, or with patients.
G1Cantiere.8.easy: Lady Carew thanks you, writes your name in the notebook in small, neat writing, and promises you a brass plaque at the entrance. She walks you to the door arm in arm, as one does with relatives. Or with patients.
G1Cantiere.8.short: Lady Carew writes your name down and promises a plaque. She walks you out arm in arm, like a relative. Or a patient.

G1Cantiere.9.full: Pay $2 and gain 2VP. Lady Carew will remember your family.

G1Cantiere.10.full: The foreman unrolls the drawings on the table. A hundred beds, it is true; hot water on every floor. But beneath the gentlemen's ward there is a floor that cannot be seen from the front, with windowless cells and doors that lock only from the outside. Beside it, in Lady Carew's small hand, is written: *interesting cases*.
G1Cantiere.10.easy: The foreman spreads the drawings on the table. A hundred beds, it is true, and hot water on every floor. But under the gentlemen's ward there is a floor you cannot see from outside, with windowless cells and doors that lock only from the outside. Next to it, in Lady Carew's small writing, it says: *interesting cases*.
G1Cantiere.10.short: The plans show a hidden floor with windowless cells. Beside it Lady Carew has written: *interesting cases*.

G1Cantiere.12.full: You say it loudly enough for the foreman to hear, and the errand boy, and the woman scrubbing the stairs. In the village the remark will have made the rounds of the taverns before evening, and many will find it brave. Lady Carew does not. She opens her notebook again and writes something, without ceasing to smile.
G1Cantiere.12.easy: You say it loud enough for the foreman, the errand boy and the woman washing the stairs to hear. By evening the remark will have gone round every tavern in the village, and many will think it brave. Lady Carew does not. She opens her notebook again and writes something, still smiling.
G1Cantiere.12.short: You say it loudly. The village thinks it brave. Lady Carew does not: she smiles, and writes it down.

G1Cantiere.13.full: Gain 1VP. Lady Carew will remember your family.

G1Tomba.2.full: There are fresh flowers on your father's grave. Not the ones from the funeral, long withered: new flowers, every morning, wild violets tied with string. The keeper says he has never seen who brings them. In the soft earth before the headstone are the prints of small, quick shoes, which circle the grave three times and then go away.
G1Tomba.2.easy: There are fresh flowers on your father's grave. Not the ones from the funeral, which are dry now, but new flowers every morning: wild violets tied with string. The keeper says he has never seen who brings them. In the soft earth in front of the headstone are prints of small, quick shoes, which go three times round the grave and then leave.
G1Tomba.2.short: Every morning there are fresh violets on your father's grave. In the earth, small footprints circle the grave three times.

G1Tomba.4.full: You come back at night, and wait.

G1Tomba.5.full: You take the flowers away and throw them in the river.

G1Tomba.6.full: You wait behind a cypress until three, the cold in your bones. Then the gate creaks, and a little man in a black coat comes in whistling, with a posy of violets in his hand. He kneels before the headstone and talks to it, for a long time, in a low voice, the way one talks to a mirror. You cannot make out the words. You make out the laugh, at the end.
G1Tomba.6.easy: You wait behind a cypress until three, cold to the bone. Then the gate creaks, and a little man in a black coat comes in whistling, with a bunch of violets in his hand. He kneels in front of the headstone and talks to it for a long time, quietly, the way you talk to a mirror. You cannot understand the words. At the end you understand the laugh.
G1Tomba.6.short: At three a little man in black comes in with violets. He talks to the headstone for a long time, as to a mirror. Then he laughs.

G1Tomba.7.full: When you come out of your hiding place the cemetery is empty, and the violets are in their place.
G1Tomba.7.easy: When you come out of your hiding place the cemetery is empty, and the violets are where they were.
G1Tomba.7.short: You come out: the cemetery is empty, the violets in place.

G1Tomba.8.full: Gain 1 {icon:Creepy_Icon} and 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}. You have seen Umber up close: you will not forget him.

G1Tomba.9.full: You gather the violets and throw them into the river from the bridge, a handful at a time, as one does with things that bring bad luck. Among the stems is a folded note: *For the old man, who sleeps so soundly.* The handwriting slants backwards.
G1Tomba.9.easy: You take the violets and throw them into the river from the bridge, a handful at a time, as you do with things that bring bad luck. Among the flowers is a folded note: *For the old man, who sleeps so soundly.* The writing slants backwards.
G1Tomba.9.short: You throw the violets in the river. Among them, a backward-slanting note: *For the old man, who sleeps so soundly.*

G1Tomba.10.full: The next morning, on the grave, the flowers are there again.

G1Muratori.2.full: The bricklayers' union meets in a room above the tavern stable, with a stove, a table and thirty men who have not been paid for six weeks. Lady Carew, they say, pays when the work is finished, and the work is never finished, because Lady Carew changes her mind every Monday. Last night someone left an envelope on the table: inside, six weeks' wages for everyone, in cheques. The men do not know whether they can cash them.
G1Muratori.2.easy: The bricklayers' union meets in a room above the tavern stable: a stove, a table and thirty men who have not been paid for six weeks. Lady Carew, they say, pays when the work is finished, but the work never finishes, because she changes her mind every Monday. Last night someone left an envelope on the table with six weeks' pay for everyone, in cheques. The men do not know if they can cash them.
G1Muratori.2.short: The asylum bricklayers have not been paid for six weeks. Last night someone left their wages, in cheques. Can they cash them?

G1Muratori.4.full: You say the cheques are good: cash them.

G1Muratori.5.full: You say they are forged, and pay $2 for bread yourself.

G1Muratori.6.full: You take the envelope to Lady Carew.

G1Muratori.7.full: The cheques are good, of course. The men cash them all on the same day, and the village bank runs out of coin by evening. For a month, at the tavern, they drink to the health of Mr. Umber, the bricklayers' benefactor.
G1Muratori.7.easy: The cheques are good, of course. The men all cash them on the same day, and the village bank has no money left until evening. For a month, in the tavern, they drink to the health of Mr. Umber, the bricklayers' friend.
G1Muratori.7.short: The cheques are good. For a month the tavern drinks to Mr. Umber.

G1Muratori.8.full: Gain 1 {icon:Bodies_Icon}: a grateful bricklayer owes you a favour.

G1Muratori.9.full: The men burn the envelope in the stove, and you pay for bread and soup for a week. Lady Carew, when she hears of it, sends you an icy note: charity, she writes, is done through the proper channels.
G1Muratori.9.easy: The men burn the envelope in the stove, and you pay for bread and soup for a week. When she finds out, Lady Carew sends you an ice-cold note: charity, she writes, must be done properly.
G1Muratori.9.short: They burn the envelope, and you pay for bread. Lady Carew sends you an icy note.

G1Muratori.11.full: Lady Carew opens the envelope in front of you, looks at the cheques one by one and shuts them in her leather-bound notebook, without expression. "Thank you," she says. "You did the right thing. I shall pay the workmen next week." And so she does. With Umber's cheques.
G1Muratori.11.easy: Lady Carew opens the envelope in front of you, looks at the cheques one by one and puts them in her leather notebook, without a flicker on her face. "Thank you," she says. "You did the right thing. I shall pay the workmen next week." And she really does. With Umber's cheques.
G1Muratori.11.short: Lady Carew takes the envelope and thanks you. The next week she pays the workmen. With Umber's cheques.

G1Parco.2.full: In the Park, by the pond, a little boy is playing alone with a paper boat. The boat is a cheque, carefully folded: you can still see the amount, the signature and the handwriting slanting backwards. A tiny gentleman in a black coat gave it to him, he says, "because I was sad".
G1Parco.2.easy: In the Park, by the pond, a little boy is playing alone with a paper boat. The boat is a carefully folded cheque: you can still see the amount, the signature and the writing that slants backwards. A tiny gentleman in a black coat gave it to him, he says, "because I was sad".
G1Parco.2.short: A boy plays with a paper boat made from a cheque. A tiny gentleman in black gave it to him, "because I was sad".

G1Parco.4.full: You buy the boat from him for $1.

G1Parco.5.full: You ask him what the gentleman said.

G1Parco.6.full: You take him back to his mother.

G1Parco.7.full: The boy accepts the coin with the gravity of a banker and hands over the soggy boat. At home you unfold it on the table: the cheque is signed with the name of one of you. You burn it before it dries.
G1Parco.7.easy: The boy takes the coin, as serious as a banker, and gives you the wet boat. At home you open it on the table: the cheque is signed with the name of one of you. You burn it before it dries.
G1Parco.7.short: You buy the boat. The cheque bears one of your names. You burn it.

G1Parco.9.full: The boy thinks for a long time, frowning. "He said he was the grandfather," he answers at last. "Everybody's grandfather. That he had lots of grandchildren, and I wasn't one of them, but he liked me anyway." Then he goes back to his game, and says nothing more.
G1Parco.9.easy: The boy thinks for a long time, frowning. "He said he was the grandfather," he answers at last. "Everybody's grandfather. He had lots of grandchildren, and I wasn't one of them, but he liked me anyway." Then he goes back to his game, and says nothing more.
G1Parco.9.short: "He said he was everybody's grandfather," says the boy. "And that he liked me anyway."

G1Parco.11.full: His mother is a washerwoman, with red hands and a tired voice. When you tell her about the cheque she turns pale, then thanks you, then asks whether your family needs someone for the laundry. It does, you discover: the house is big, and nobody wants to work at the estate.
G1Parco.11.easy: The boy's mother is a washerwoman, with red hands and a tired voice. When you tell her about the cheque she goes pale, then thanks you, then asks whether your family needs someone to do the washing. You do, you find out: the house is big, and nobody wants to work at the estate.
G1Parco.11.short: You take him to his mother, a washerwoman. She thanks you, and offers to do the estate's washing, where nobody will work.

G1Duello.2.full: At dawn, in the Park, by the pond, a young officer on leave is waiting for you, pale with rage, with two seconds and a case of pistols. Last night, at the tavern, a little man in black with his collar turned up spilled wine over him, insulted his sister and handed him a visiting card. On the card was your family's name. The officer demands satisfaction.
G1Duello.2.easy: At dawn, in the Park, by the pond, a young officer on leave is waiting for you. He is pale with anger, with two seconds and a case of pistols. Last night, at the tavern, a little man in black with his collar up spilled wine on him, insulted his sister and gave him a visiting card. On the card was your family's name. The officer wants a duel.
G1Duello.2.short: An officer challenges you to a duel: a little man in black insulted him and left a card bearing your family's name.

G1Duello.5.full: You apologise, and pay $2 for the wine.

G1Duello.6.full: You show him the card: the handwriting is not yours.

G1Duello.7.full: Twenty paces, in the fog. The officer fires first and misses, widely: his hands are shaking. You fire into the air. The seconds shake hands, the officer embraces you and weeps a little, and the village tells the story for a year, better every time.
G1Duello.7.easy: Twenty paces, in the fog. The officer fires first and misses by a long way: his hands are shaking. You fire into the air. The seconds shake hands, and the officer hugs you and cries a little. For a year the village tells the story, and every time it gets better.
G1Duello.7.short: The officer fires and misses. You fire into the air. The village talks of it for a year.

G1Duello.9.full: You apologise for something you did not do, with all the dignity you can find, and pay for the wine. The officer accepts, stiffly. The seconds look disappointed. On the way home you notice that now it is your hands that are shaking.
G1Duello.9.easy: You apologise for something you did not do, with all the dignity you can find, and you pay for the wine. The officer accepts, stiffly. The seconds look disappointed. On the way home you notice that now it is your hands that are shaking.
G1Duello.9.short: You apologise for something you did not do, and pay for the wine. On the way home, your hands shake.

G1Duello.10.full: Pay $2. Move back 1 space on the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track.

G1Duello.11.full: The officer looks at the card, then at your signature, then at the card again. The handwriting on the card slants backwards; yours does not. For a moment he seems disappointed not to be shooting you. Then he offers you his hand, and that same evening takes the card to Inspector Haskett, with your compliments.
G1Duello.11.easy: The officer looks at the card, then at your signature, then at the card again. The writing on the card slants backwards; yours does not. For a moment he seems disappointed he cannot shoot you. Then he shakes your hand, and that same evening takes the card to Inspector Haskett, with your compliments.
G1Duello.11.short: The card's writing slants backwards; yours does not. The officer shakes your hand and takes the card to the Inspector.

G1Duello.12.full: Gain 1VP. Inspector Haskett will remember your family.

G1Parroco.2.full: The parish priest is a fat, kindly man with tobacco-stained fingers and an excellent memory for funerals. He remembers your father's well: the low sky, the thin crowd, the man laughing at the back. Above all he remembers the bearers, who had to stop halfway up the nave to catch their breath. "It weighed like a stone," he says. "I said so to the notary. He told me that grief is heavy."
G1Parroco.2.easy: The parish priest is a fat, kind man with tobacco-stained fingers and a very good memory for funerals. He remembers your father's well: the low sky, the few people, the man laughing at the back. Above all he remembers the bearers, who had to stop halfway up the church to get their breath back. "It was as heavy as a stone," he says. "I told the notary. He said grief is heavy."
G1Parroco.2.short: The priest remembers the funeral: the bearers had to stop. "It weighed like a stone. The notary told me grief is heavy."

G1Parroco.4.full: You offer $2 for a Mass for the dead.

G1Parroco.5.full: You ask him who closed the coffin.

G1Parroco.7.full: The priest accepts, and the following Sunday says a long, well-sung Mass. At the back of the church, during the elevation, someone laughs softly. When you turn round, there is only an old woman asleep.
G1Parroco.7.easy: The priest agrees, and the next Sunday he says a long, well-sung Mass. During the most solemn moment, at the back of the church, someone laughs softly. When you turn round, there is only an old woman asleep.
G1Parroco.7.short: During Mass, someone laughs at the back. You turn: only an old woman asleep.

G1Parroco.9.full: The priest leafs through the register of the dead. "The carpenter nailed it shut the evening before, in the presence of Pell the notary and the village doctor. No one else. The notary insisted that no one should open it again: the wish of the deceased." He closes the register. "At the time it seemed a gesture of affection. Now, I don't know."
G1Parroco.9.easy: The priest leafs through the register of the dead. "The carpenter nailed the coffin shut the evening before, in front of Pell the notary and the village doctor. No one else. The notary wanted no one to open it again: it was the dead man's wish." He closes the register. "At the time it seemed an act of love. Now I don't know."
G1Parroco.9.short: "They closed it the night before, with Pell the notary and the doctor there. The notary wanted no one to reopen it." Now the priest does not know what to think.

G1Parroco.11.full: You thank him and leave. On the church steps you notice the priest watching you from the door, and crossing himself. Perhaps it is for you. Perhaps it is for your father.
G1Parroco.11.easy: You thank him and leave. On the church steps you notice the priest watching you from the door and crossing himself. Perhaps for you. Perhaps for your father.
G1Parroco.11.short: As you leave, you see the priest cross himself. For you, or for your father.

G1Nozze.2.full: The mayor's daughter is getting married in church, and all the village's good society is in the pews, the family from the estate included. Halfway through the ceremony, when the priest asks whether anyone knows any reason why these two should not be wed, someone at the back of the church laughs. Everyone turns. There is no one there, but on the last pew is a wedding present wrapped in black paper, with a card: *From Mr. Umber, with every good wish.*
G1Nozze.2.easy: The mayor's daughter is getting married, and all the important people of the village are in the pews, the family from the estate too. Halfway through, the priest asks if anyone knows a reason why these two should not marry. At the back of the church someone laughs. Everyone turns round. There is no one there, but on the last pew is a wedding present wrapped in black, with a card: *From Mr. Umber, with every good wish.*
G1Nozze.2.short: At the mayor's daughter's wedding someone laughs at the back. On the last pew is a gift wrapped in black: *From Mr. Umber.*

G1Nozze.4.full: You take the package outside before anyone opens it.

G1Nozze.5.full: You let the bride and groom open it.

G1Nozze.6.full: You carry it out under your jacket while the priest resumes the ceremony. In the cemetery, sheltered by a tomb, you open it. Inside is a canteen of silver cutlery, beautiful, engraved with your family's initials. Only the knives are missing.
G1Nozze.6.easy: You take it out under your jacket while the priest carries on with the ceremony. In the cemetery, hidden behind a tomb, you open it. Inside is a set of beautiful silver cutlery, with your family's initials. Only the knives are missing.
G1Nozze.6.short: Outside you open it: silver cutlery with your family's initials. Only the knives are missing.

G1Nozze.7.full: Gain $2: you sell the cutlery in town, no questions asked.

G1Nozze.8.full: The couple open it at the reception, in front of everyone. Inside is a canteen of silver cutlery, beautiful, engraved with your family's initials. The bride thanks the family from the estate for the magnificent gift. The mayor, on the other hand, looks at the initials, and then looks at **{0}**, for a long time.
G1Nozze.8.easy: The couple open it at the party, in front of everyone. Inside is a set of beautiful silver cutlery, with your family's initials. The bride thanks the family from the estate for the wonderful present. But the mayor looks at the initials, and then looks at **{0}**, for a long time.
G1Nozze.8.short: The couple find silver cutlery with your family's initials. The mayor stares at **{0}** for a long time.

G1Nozze.9.full: **{0}** moves up 1 space on the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track. You gain 1VP.

G1Ronda.2.full: The mayor has decided it is time to put an end to the sightings. He wants a night watch: six men with lanterns and cudgels, walking the streets from dusk to dawn. He lacks the men, and he lacks the money. When he sees you come into the town hall he greets you with a broad smile, the way one greets a backer.
G1Ronda.2.easy: The mayor has decided the sightings must stop. He wants a night watch: six men with lanterns and sticks, in the streets from dusk to dawn. But he has no men and no money. When he sees you come into the town hall he greets you with a big smile, the way one greets someone who can pay.
G1Ronda.2.short: The mayor wants a night watch, but lacks men and money. He greets you with a big smile.

G1Ronda.6.full: You say the watch is nonsense.

G1Ronda.7.full: The watch patrols for a whole month, with lanterns and cudgels. It catches no one. But the village sleeps better, and knows who paid for the lanterns.
G1Ronda.7.easy: The watch walks the streets for a whole month, with lanterns and sticks. It catches no one. But the village sleeps better, and knows who paid for the lanterns.
G1Ronda.7.short: The watch catches no one, but the village sleeps better. And knows who paid.

G1Ronda.9.full: You walk the streets with five others, a lantern and a cudgel you do not know how to use. At three o'clock, at the end of the alley behind the estate, you see a small shadow stop, turn and raise its hat to you. The others did not see it. You do not tell them.
G1Ronda.9.easy: You walk the streets with five others, a lantern and a stick you do not know how to use. At three in the morning, at the end of the alley behind the estate, you see a small shadow stop, turn and raise its hat to you. The others did not see it. You do not tell them.
G1Ronda.9.short: At three, in the alley behind the estate, a small shadow raises its hat to you. Only you saw it.

G1Ronda.10.full: Gain 1 {icon:Creepy_Icon} and 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}. Secretly look at one face-down Sighting {icon:S2_HuntTokenFRONT} on the board, without turning it over.

G1Ronda.11.full: The mayor stops smiling. A family that does not want a night watch, he says later at the tavern, is a family that has something to do at night. The tavern agrees.
G1Ronda.11.easy: The mayor stops smiling. Later, at the tavern, he says that a family that does not want a night watch is a family that has something to do at night. Everyone at the tavern agrees.
G1Ronda.11.short: The mayor stops smiling. At the tavern he says whoever refuses a watch has business at night.

G1Ronda.12.full: Gain $1: the money you did not give.

G1Chiromante.3.full: The fortune teller now is the daughter of the one before: the same red headscarf, the same pale eyes, almost white, and a bigger tent, with a cast-iron stove and a portrait of her mother hung on the pole. She takes your left hand, then your right, and smiles. "My mother told me about your family," she says. "She told me to take the money first."
G1Chiromante.3.easy: The fortune teller now is the daughter of the old one: the same red scarf, the same pale, almost white eyes, and a bigger tent, with an iron stove and her mother's portrait hanging on the pole. She takes your left hand, then your right, and smiles. "My mother told me about your family," she says. "She told me to get paid first."
G1Chiromante.3.short: The fortune teller is the old one's daughter. She smiles: "My mother told me to get paid first."

G1Chiromante.4.full: The fortune teller is an old woman with a red scarf on her head and pale eyes, almost white. She takes your left hand, then your right, then your left again, and frowns.
G1Chiromante.4.easy: The fortune teller is an old woman with a red scarf on her head and pale, almost white eyes. She takes your left hand, then your right, then your left again, and frowns.
G1Chiromante.4.short: An old woman with almost white eyes looks at your hands, and frowns.

G1Chiromante.5.full: "Two life lines," she says. "One short and one long. I don't know which one is yours." She closes your fingers over your palm, as if to keep something inside, and will say nothing more.
G1Chiromante.5.easy: "Two life lines," she says. "One short and one long. I don't know which one is yours." She closes your fingers over your palm, as if to keep something inside, and will not say anything else.
G1Chiromante.5.short: "Two life lines. I don't know which is yours." She says no more.

G1Chiromante.6.full: Gain 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon} and one resource of your choice ({icon:Bodies_Icon}, {icon:Chemical_Icon}, {icon:Gears_Icon} or {icon:Animal_Icon}).

G1Chiromante.7.full: "I see money," she says. "A lot of money, and not yours. Signed by someone else." She laughs, with all the teeth she is missing. "Take it while it's there." On the way home you find a wallet in the mud, with no name in it.
G1Chiromante.7.easy: "I see money," she says. "A lot of money, and not yours. Signed by someone else." She laughs, with all the teeth she is missing. "Take it while it's there." On the way home you find a wallet in the mud, with no name in it.
G1Chiromante.7.short: "I see money, signed by someone else." On the way home you find a wallet in the mud.

G1Chiromante.9.full: "I see a door," she says. "You are on this side. Stay on this side." For once it seems excellent advice, and that night you sleep as you have not slept for months.
G1Chiromante.9.easy: "I see a door," she says. "You are on this side. Stay on this side." For once it seems very good advice, and that night you sleep as you have not slept for months.
G1Chiromante.9.short: "I see a door. Stay on this side." That night you sleep well.

G1Chiromante.10.full: Move back 1 space on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track.

G1Chiromante.11.full: The old woman lets go of your hand at once, as if it were burning, and puts the coin back in your pocket. "This hand isn't yours," she says. "You borrowed it. Give it back." Then she closes the tent flap, and does not open it again.
G1Chiromante.11.easy: The old woman drops your hand suddenly, as if it were burning, and puts the coin back in your pocket. "This hand isn't yours," she says. "You borrowed it. Give it back." Then she closes the tent, and does not open it again.
G1Chiromante.11.short: The old woman drops your hand: "This hand isn't yours. Give it back."

G1Sale.3.full: Today, in the laboratory, the floor gave way under my foot: a loose board by the stove that someone had put back with too much care. Under it was a zinc box, and in the box six phials of dark glass, sealed with wax. White salt, fine as sugar, with a yellowish sheen when you hold it to the light. On the label: *Lomax's Pharmacy – first batch*. Tied to the box with string, a note in our father's hand: *A single sip. Then the door.*
G1Sale.3.easy: Today, in the laboratory, the floor moved under my foot: a loose board by the stove, put back with too much care. Under it was a zinc box, and inside six phials of dark glass, sealed with wax. Inside is white salt, as fine as sugar, a little yellow when you hold it up to the light. The label says: *Lomax's Pharmacy – first batch*. Tied to the box with string is a note in our father's writing: *A single sip. Then the door.*
G1Sale.3.short: Under a laboratory floorboard were six phials of white salt: *Lomax's Pharmacy – first batch*. And a note from our father: *A single sip. Then the door.*

G1Sale.4.full: We have not yet decided what to do with them. Meanwhile, in the village, the baker came round to cash a cheque signed by our father, dated last week: more than a year after the funeral. It was given to him by a little man in a black coat too large for him, who bought all the bread in the shop and threw it in the river, one loaf at a time, laughing.
G1Sale.4.easy: We have not yet decided what to do with them. Meanwhile, in the village, the baker came to cash a cheque signed by our father. It is dated last week: more than a year after the funeral. A little man in a black coat too big for him gave it to him, and bought all the bread in the shop and threw it in the river, one loaf at a time, laughing.
G1Sale.4.short: The baker has a cheque signed by our father and dated last week. A little man in black gave it to him and threw all the bread in the river.

G1Sale.5.full: We paid the baker, and had him give us the cheque. The signature is our father's, no doubt about it. But it slants backwards, as if he had written it with the wrong hand.
G1Sale.5.easy: We paid the baker and got the cheque from him. The signature is our father's, there is no doubt. But it slants backwards, as if he had written it with the wrong hand.
G1Sale.5.short: The signature is our father's. But it slants backwards.

G1Sale.6.full: What do you do with the cheque? *({0} decides, after hearing the others.)*

G1Sale.7.full: You burn it, and tell no one.

G1Sale.8.full: You take it to the police.

G1Sale.9.full: The cheque burns quickly, with a greenish flame that no one remarks on. The baker, paid twice, has promised to keep quiet; and keeps his promise for almost a week.
G1Sale.9.easy: The cheque burns quickly, with a greenish flame, and nobody says anything. The baker, paid twice, has promised to keep quiet. And he keeps his promise for almost a week.
G1Sale.9.short: The cheque burns with a green flame. The baker promises silence, for almost a week.

G1Sale.10.full: The village police is one woman alone: Inspector Nell Haskett, tall, thin, with a black notebook and a pencil always sharpened. She holds the cheque up to the light, sniffs it and shuts it in her notebook. "Thank you," she says. "You are the first in this village to bring me something instead of hiding it. I shall remember that." The village, which saw the estate's carriage outside the police station, will remember it too.
G1Sale.10.easy: The village police is just one woman: Inspector Nell Haskett, tall and thin, with a black notebook and a pencil always sharp. She holds the cheque up to the light, sniffs it and puts it in her notebook. "Thank you," she says. "You are the first people in this village to bring me something instead of hiding it. I shall remember that." The village, which saw the estate's carriage at the police station, will remember it too.
G1Sale.10.short: Inspector Nell Haskett takes the cheque: "You are the first to bring me something instead of hiding it. I shall remember."

G1SaleSetup.1.full: From the **Fear of the Unknown** Scenario Box take the **Hunt tokens** {icon:S2_HuntTokenFRONT}: in this scenario they are Mr. Umber's **Sightings**. Keep them next to the board.

G1SaleSetup.2.full: Also take the **Obsession cards** and keep them face down next to the board.

G1SaleSetup.3.full: Take the **Money tokens** {icon:S2_ColoredMoneyToken}: each player takes the one in their colour. They are the **cheques** Umber signs with your name.

G1SaleSetup.4.full: Take the **20 Estate Upgrades** from the box and shuffle them into the Generation I/II Upgrade deck.

G1Cronaca1.3.full: **NEWS FROM THE HILL.** Work continues on Lady Carew's new asylum. The foreman assures us the roof will be finished before winter, and that the cells of the paupers' ward will have, for the first time in the county, a window each. A small one, but a window.
G1Cronaca1.3.easy: **NEWS FROM THE HILL.** Work goes on at Lady Carew's new asylum. The foreman says the roof will be ready before winter. In the paupers' ward, for the first time in the county, each cell will have a window. A small one, but a window.
G1Cronaca1.3.short: **NEWS FROM THE HILL.** The asylum will have its roof before winter, and a small window in every paupers' cell.

G1Cronaca1.4.full: Among the benefactors who contributed to the roof, Lady Carew wished to thank publicly the family from the estate, "who understood sooner than others the value of prevention". The family's name will be engraved on a brass plaque at the entrance.
G1Cronaca1.4.easy: Lady Carew publicly thanked, among those who paid for the roof, the family from the estate, "who understood before others how important it is to treat things early". The family's name will be written on a brass plaque at the entrance.
G1Cronaca1.4.short: Lady Carew publicly thanks the family from the estate. Their name will go on a plaque at the entrance.

G1Cronaca1.5.full: Lady Carew wished to remind the committee, in her address, that "certain families of the county prefer to keep their sick at home, until it is too late". She named no names. At the committee, everyone looked towards the hill where the estate stands.
G1Cronaca1.5.easy: In her speech to the committee Lady Carew said that "certain families of the county prefer to keep their sick at home, until it is too late". She named no names. But everyone turned to look towards the estate on the hill.
G1Cronaca1.5.short: Lady Carew speaks of families who keep their sick at home "until it is too late". Everyone looks towards the estate.

G1Cronaca1.6.full: The cemetery keeper reports that for some time now fresh violets have appeared every morning on the grave of the old man from the estate, and that an heir of the family has been seen wandering among the headstones in the dead of night. This newspaper draws no conclusions.
G1Cronaca1.6.easy: The cemetery keeper says that for some time, every morning, there have been fresh violets on the grave of the old man from the estate. And that an heir of the family has been seen walking among the graves in the middle of the night. This newspaper will say no more.
G1Cronaca1.6.short: Every morning there are fresh violets on the old man's grave. And an heir has been seen at the cemetery at night.

G1Cronaca1.7.full: Meanwhile the dispute of the bricklayers at the building site, left without pay for six weeks, has been settled without incident, in circumstances the union prefers not to discuss.
G1Cronaca1.7.easy: Meanwhile the protest of the building-site bricklayers, who had gone without pay for six weeks, has ended without trouble. How it ended, the union would rather not say.
G1Cronaca1.7.short: The bricklayers' protest is over. The union will not say how.

G1Cronaca1.8.full: A village washerwoman relates that her son was given, in the Park, a cheque folded into a little boat, signed with the name of an heir from the estate. The family, when asked, declined to comment.
G1Cronaca1.8.easy: A village washerwoman says that her son was given, in the Park, a cheque folded like a little boat, signed with the name of an heir from the estate. The family, when we asked, would not answer.
G1Cronaca1.8.short: A child was given a cheque signed by an heir from the estate. The family says nothing.

G1Cronaca1.9.full: At the tavern, of an evening, there is little talk of anything but Mr. Umber and the estate. The priest has urged the faithful from the pulpit not to listen to gossip. Which, naturally, has doubled it.
G1Cronaca1.9.easy: At the tavern, in the evening, people talk about almost nothing but Mr. Umber and the estate. From the pulpit the priest asked people not to listen to gossip. So, of course, the gossip doubled.
G1Cronaca1.9.short: The tavern talks only of Umber. The priest begs people to ignore the gossip, which doubles.

G1Cronaca1.10.full: Otherwise the village is quiet. The harvest was good, the river did not burst its banks, and the man in the black coat has been seen little this year.
G1Cronaca1.10.easy: Otherwise the village is quiet. The harvest was good, the river did not flood, and this year the man in the black coat has not been seen much.
G1Cronaca1.10.short: Otherwise all is quiet. The man in black has been seen little this year.

Assegno.2.full: The shopkeeper takes you into the back room, away from the customers. He has a cheque: the signature is the name of one of your relatives, the handwriting slants backwards, and the bank stamp is genuine. It was brought in last night, in the fog, by a little man in black, who bought every candle in the shop and lit them, one by one, along the pavement.
Assegno.2.easy: The shopkeeper takes you into the back room, away from the customers. He has a cheque: it has the name of one of your relatives, the writing slants backwards, and the bank stamp is real. A little man in black brought it last night, in the fog, and bought every candle in the shop and lit them, one by one, on the pavement.
