Assegno.2.short: The shopkeeper has a cheque with a relative's name, in a backward hand. A little man in black brought it and lit every candle on the pavement.

Assegno.3.full: The shopkeeper is waiting for you at the door, with the air of a man who has prepared his speech. He is holding a cheque: the amount is small, the signature is the name of one of your relatives, and the writing slants backwards. It was cashed last night by a little man in a black coat, who paid for a bottle of wine and smashed it on the pavement to hear the noise.
Assegno.3.easy: The shopkeeper is waiting at the door, like someone who has prepared a speech. He is holding a cheque: the amount is small, it has the name of one of your relatives, and the writing slants backwards. Last night a little man in a black coat cashed it, paid for a bottle of wine and smashed it on the pavement to hear the noise.
Assegno.3.short: The shopkeeper has a cheque with a relative's name, in a backward hand. A little man in black brought it and smashed a bottle to hear it break.

Assegno.4.full: He wants no trouble: he wants his money. Or, if you prefer, he can tell the whole story to the police.
Assegno.4.easy: He does not want trouble: he wants his money. Or, if you prefer, he can tell the police everything.
Assegno.4.short: He wants his money. Or he goes to the police.

Assegno.6.full: You pay $1 to the player who signed the cheque, and keep quiet.

Assegno.7.full: You report it to the police.

Assegno.8.full: Pay $1 to the cheque's owner, who takes it back.

Assegno.9.full: Gain 1VP. The cheque's owner takes it back and moves up 1 on the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track.

Avvistamento.2.full: The footprints in the mud are small and quick, and go in one direction only. You follow them past the market, past the bridge, to the alley behind the estate, where they end in front of a wooden door with neither handle nor lock.
Avvistamento.2.easy: The footprints in the mud are small and quick, and all go the same way. You follow them past the market, past the bridge, to the alley behind the estate. There they stop in front of a wooden door with no handle and no lock.
Avvistamento.2.short: You follow the prints to the alley behind the estate. They stop at a door with no handle.

Avvistamento.3.full: In your pocket is the apprentice's key, the one with the eye-shaped head. There is no keyhole to put it in; but when you bring it close to the wood, something clicks on the other side, and the door opens.
Avvistamento.3.easy: In your pocket is the apprentice's key, the one with the eye-shaped head. There is no keyhole to put it in; but when you hold it near the wood, something on the other side clicks, and the door opens.
Avvistamento.3.short: You hold the apprentice's key to the wood. Something clicks, and the door opens.

Avvistamento.4.full: When you touch it, it opens: someone on the other side forgot to lock it.
Avvistamento.4.easy: You touch it, and it opens: someone on the other side forgot to lock it.
Avvistamento.4.short: The door opens: someone forgot to lock it.

Avvistamento.5.full: Behind it is the study on the alley, the one in the will: a room none of you had ever managed to find, its walls covered in mirrors, with a second door, this one with a handle, that opens onto the estate's corridor. A house with two doors. Through one comes a respectable scientist; through the other goes whoever pleases.
Avvistamento.5.easy: Behind it is the study on the alley, the one in the will: a room none of you had ever managed to find. The walls are covered with mirrors, and there is another door, this one with a handle, that opens into the estate's corridor. It is a house with two doors. Through one comes a respectable scientist; through the other goes whoever likes.
Avvistamento.5.short: It is the study from the will, full of mirrors, with a second door into the estate. A house with two doors.

Avvistamento.6.full: Take the **House on the Hill** from the **Fear of the Unknown** Scenario Box and place it next to your Estate: it is **the house with two doors**. Return the Sighting to the box.

Avvistamento.7.full: The little man in the black coat on the street corner is a boy in his grandfather's coat and a paper hat. He is playing at Umber to frighten his sisters, and doing it very well. When he sees you, he runs off laughing.
Avvistamento.7.easy: The little man in the black coat on the street corner is a boy in his grandfather's coat and a paper hat. He is pretending to be Umber to scare his sisters, and doing it very well. When he sees you, he runs off laughing.
Avvistamento.7.short: It is only a boy in his grandfather's coat, playing at Umber.

Avvistamento.8.full: You find it where they told you: a black coat hung on a fence to dry, collar turned up and a broom handle for shoulders. From a distance, in the fog, it really looked like a man waiting for someone.
Avvistamento.8.easy: You find it where they said: a black coat hung on a fence to dry, with the collar up and a broom handle for shoulders. From far away, in the fog, it really looked like a man waiting for someone.
Avvistamento.8.short: It is only a black coat hung on a fence to dry.

Avvistamento.9.full: It is a drunkard, asleep on a doorstep, wearing a black coat that is not his. When you wake him he swears he got it from a very kind little gentleman, who laughed a great deal, in exchange for a song.
Avvistamento.9.easy: It is a drunk asleep on a doorstep, wearing a black coat that is not his. When you wake him he swears a very kind little gentleman gave it to him, laughing a lot, in exchange for a song.
Avvistamento.9.short: It is a drunk in a black coat, given to him by a little gentleman for a song.

Avvistamento.10.full: There is no one: only a black cat rummaging in the rubbish. On the cobbles, though, lies a wax seal, stamped with a crest you think you have seen before.
Avvistamento.10.easy: There is no one, only a black cat looking for food in the rubbish. But on the ground is a wax seal, with the mark of a crest you think you have seen before.
Avvistamento.10.short: Only a black cat. On the ground, a wax seal you think you know.

Avvistamento.11.full: In the fog, under a street lamp, a little man in a black coat stands waiting, motionless. You approach slowly. It is a tailor's dummy, stolen from a shop window and set there as a joke by some students. Round its neck hangs a sign: *You have wasted your time.*
Avvistamento.11.easy: In the fog, under a street lamp, a little man in a black coat is waiting without moving. You go closer slowly. It is a tailor's dummy, stolen from a shop window and put there as a joke by some students. Round its neck is a sign: *You have wasted your time.*
Avvistamento.11.short: It is a stolen tailor's dummy, with a sign: *You have wasted your time.*

Avvistamento.12.full: It is a short vagrant whom Ada Haskett's constables have already stopped twice. He has taken a liking to it: he walks about at night in a black coat bought for the purpose, and gets himself arrested for a warm bed in a cell.
Avvistamento.12.easy: It is a short tramp whom Ada Haskett's constables have already stopped twice. Now he enjoys it: he walks about at night in a black coat bought specially, and gets arrested to have a warm bed in a cell.
Avvistamento.12.short: It is a tramp who wears a black coat to get arrested and sleep somewhere warm.

Avvistamento.13.full: The shadow you saw slip along the wall belongs to a lamplighter, small and quick, his ladder on his shoulder and his pole in his hand. He greets you politely. He has never seen Umber, he says: and that, it seems, grieves him very much.
Avvistamento.13.easy: The shadow you saw going along the wall is a lamplighter, small and quick, with his ladder on his shoulder and his pole in his hand. He says hello politely. He says he has never seen Umber, and he seems very sorry about it.
Avvistamento.13.short: It is a lamplighter, small and quick. He has never seen Umber, and is sorry.

Avvistamento.14.full: There is no one, but on the wall, at eye level, someone has chalked a little man in a hat. Below it is an arrow pointing to the alley you came from.
Avvistamento.14.easy: There is no one. But on the wall, at eye level, someone has drawn a little man with a hat in chalk. Below it is an arrow pointing to the alley you came from.
Avvistamento.14.short: No one. On the wall, a chalk little man and an arrow towards your alley.

Avvistamento.15.full: It is a false alarm. Gain 1VP. Return the Sighting to the box.

G1R2.2.full: Turn to **page 5** of the Village Chronicle, **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}).

G1R2.4.full: Inspector Haskett receives visitors on the ground floor of the town hall. The first player to send one of their pieces to the Town Hall,

G1R2.7.full: On Thursdays Lomax the chemist keeps a stall at the market. The first player to send one of their pieces to the Farmer's Bazaar,

G1R2.13.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Church,

G1R2.15.full: {icon:Storybook} **The Key Without a Door – Blacksmith's Apprentice**

G1R2.16.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Blacksmith's Apprentice,

G1R2.22.full: Inspector Nell Haskett, the first woman of that rank in the whole county, has opened a file on Umber's cheques. She goes from shop to shop with a black notebook and a pencil always sharpened, and writes everything down: even what you do not tell her.
G1R2.22.easy: Inspector Nell Haskett, the first woman with that rank in the whole county, has opened a file on Umber's cheques. She goes from shop to shop with a black notebook and a pencil that is always sharp, and writes everything down: even what you do not tell her.
G1R2.22.short: Inspector Nell Haskett is investigating Umber's cheques, and writes everything down: even what you do not say.

round.G1R2.end.full: The Middle Years of the First Generation have ended.

round.G1R2.then.full: Then perform all Start of Round actions for the Late Years before continuing.

G1Interrogatorio.2.full: Inspector Haskett's office is a narrow room on the ground floor of the town hall, with a stove that gives no heat and a portrait of the sovereign hanging crooked on the wall. She has you sit down, offers you a tea you do not drink and lays out on the table, side by side, six cheques bearing the names of your family.
G1Interrogatorio.2.easy: Inspector Haskett's office is a narrow room on the ground floor of the town hall, with a stove that does not warm and a portrait of the king hanging crooked. She has you sit down, offers you a tea you do not drink and puts on the table, side by side, six cheques with your family's names on them.
G1Interrogatorio.2.short: The Inspector has you sit, and lays out six cheques bearing your family's names.

G1Interrogatorio.3.full: "I am not accusing you of anything," she says. "I should simply like to know who, in your house, goes out at night."
G1Interrogatorio.3.easy: "I am not accusing you of anything," she says. "I would just like to know who, in your house, goes out at night."
G1Interrogatorio.3.short: "I would just like to know who, in your house, goes out at night."

G1Interrogatorio.5.full: The truth: there is a salt in the family, and someone drinks it.

G1Interrogatorio.6.full: That in your house, at night, people sleep.

G1Interrogatorio.7.full: A name: one of your relatives'.

G1Interrogatorio.8.full: You tell her about the phials, your father's note, the first sip. The Inspector listens without interrupting and without taking notes, and when you have finished she is silent for a long time. Then she closes her notebook. "I cannot arrest a salt," she says. "But from today I know where to look. And I know that one of you, at least, can be trusted."
G1Interrogatorio.8.easy: You tell her about the phials, your father's note, the first sip. The Inspector listens without interrupting and without writing, and when you have finished she is quiet for a long time. Then she closes her notebook. "I cannot arrest a salt," she says. "But from today I know where to look. And I know I can trust at least one of you."
G1Interrogatorio.8.short: You tell her about the salt. "I cannot arrest a salt," she says. "But I know where to look, and whom to trust."

G1Interrogatorio.10.full: You say that at the estate everyone goes to bed early, that the laboratory is locked and that the cheques are surely forgeries. The Inspector nods at every sentence, kindly, and at every sentence writes a word in her notebook. In the end she sees you to the door and wishes you good night, with a certain insistence.
G1Interrogatorio.10.easy: You say that at the estate everyone goes to bed early, that the laboratory is locked and that the cheques must be forged. At every sentence the Inspector nods kindly and writes a word in her notebook. At the end she walks you to the door and wishes you good night, rather pointedly.
G1Interrogatorio.10.short: You say everyone sleeps at the estate. The Inspector nods and writes. Then she wishes you good night, pointedly.

G1Interrogatorio.11.full: Nothing happens. Inspector Haskett, however, will remember your family.

G1Interrogatorio.12.full: You give a name. Not your own. The Inspector writes it in capitals, underlines it twice and thanks you for your cooperation; then she looks at you the way one looks at a dog that has brought a dead rat into the house. On your way back to the estate you pass the relative you named. They greet you. They know nothing yet.
G1Interrogatorio.12.easy: You say a name. Not yours. The Inspector writes it in capitals, underlines it twice and thanks you for your help. Then she looks at you the way you look at a dog that has brought a dead rat into the house. On your way back to the estate you meet the relative you named. They say hello. They know nothing yet.
G1Interrogatorio.12.short: You name a relative. The Inspector writes it down, and looks at you with contempt. In the street the relative greets you. They know nothing.

G1Interrogatorio.13.full: Choose another player: they move up 1 on the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track. You gain 1VP.

G1Lomax.2.full: Lomax the chemist has his stall between the chicken coops and the wheels of cheese: cough syrups, liver pills, salts for every occasion. He is a thin man, still young, with yellow-stained fingers and the air of someone who has been expecting bad news for many years.
G1Lomax.2.easy: Lomax the chemist has his stall between the chicken cages and the wheels of cheese: cough syrups, liver pills, salts for every occasion. He is a thin man, still young, with yellow fingers and the look of someone who has been waiting years for bad news.
G1Lomax.2.short: Lomax the chemist, thin and yellow-fingered, has a market stall. He seems to have been expecting bad news for years.

G1Lomax.3.full: When you ask him about the first batch of salt he sold your father he turns pale and says he does not remember: he has sold a lot of salt, to a lot of people. But he keeps his hand on his ledger, as if it might run away.
G1Lomax.3.easy: When you ask him about the first batch of salt he sold your father he goes pale and says he does not remember: he has sold lots of salt to lots of people. But he keeps his hand on his ledger, as if it might run away.
G1Lomax.3.short: You ask about the first batch of salt. He says he does not remember, but keeps his hand on his ledger.

G1Lomax.5.full: You offer him $3 for a page of the ledger.

G1Lomax.6.full: You grab him by the collar.

G1Lomax.7.full: You buy a phial of his salt.

G1Lomax.8.full: Lomax looks at the money, then at the crowd, then at the money again. He tears a page from the ledger and hands it to you folded in four. *9 November 1859: six phials, white salt, delivered to the gentleman at the estate.* In the column of ingredients, next to the salt, a line has been crossed out so thoroughly that the ink has gone through the paper.
G1Lomax.8.easy: Lomax looks at the money, then at the people, then at the money again. He tears a page from the ledger and gives it to you folded in four. *9 November 1859: six phials, white salt, delivered to the gentleman at the estate.* In the ingredients column, next to the salt, is a line crossed out so hard that the ink has gone through the paper.
G1Lomax.8.short: Lomax sells you the page: *9 November 1859: six phials, white salt.* Beside the salt, a line crossed out so hard it tore the paper.

G1Lomax.9.full: Pay $3. Gain 1 Chemistry Knowledge. The page stays with your family: the Storybook will remember it.

G1Lomax.10.full: You grab him by the collar in front of the whole market. The hens squawk, a wheel of cheese rolls into the mud, and someone runs to fetch the Inspector. Lomax says nothing. He presses a phial of salt into your hand, "the best I have", and begs you to go. That evening, in the glass, the salt turns barely red, and nothing more.
G1Lomax.10.easy: You grab him by the collar in front of the whole market. The hens squawk, a cheese rolls into the mud, and someone runs to get the Inspector. Lomax says nothing. He puts a phial of salt in your hand, "the best I have", and begs you to leave. That evening, in the glass, the salt turns only slightly red, and that is all.
G1Lomax.10.short: You grab him by the collar. Lomax says nothing: he gives you a phial of salt that barely turns red.

G1Lomax.12.full: Lomax wraps it carefully and will not even take your money. "Salt from the second batch," he says. "Perfectly pure. Your father bought pounds of it, afterwards. He never liked it." You try it that very evening, in a glass of water: it turns red and stops there. Nothing happens. This, for some reason, seems to you the worst news of all.
G1Lomax.12.easy: Lomax wraps it carefully and does not even make you pay. "Salt from the second batch," he says. "Very pure. Your father bought kilos of it, later. He never liked it." You try it that evening, in a glass of water: it turns red and stops. Nothing happens. And for some reason, that seems to you the worst news of all.
G1Lomax.12.short: "Salt from the second batch. Very pure." In the glass it turns red and stops. Nothing happens.

G1Apprendista.2.full: The blacksmith's apprentice is a boy black to the elbows and with a loose tongue. While he works he tells you that last month a little gentleman in a black coat ordered a strange key from him: no teeth, with an eye-shaped head, "for a door that opens only from the inside". He paid for it with a cheque. The boy kept the mould, just in case.
G1Apprendista.2.easy: The blacksmith's apprentice is a boy with arms black up to the elbows who loves to talk. While he works he tells you that last month a little gentleman in a black coat ordered a strange key: no teeth, with an eye-shaped head, "for a door that opens only from the inside". He paid with a cheque. The boy kept the mould, just in case.
G1Apprendista.2.short: The apprentice made a toothless key for a little gentleman in black, "for a door that opens only from the inside". He kept the mould.

G1Apprendista.4.full: You pay $2 for a copy of the key.

G1Apprendista.5.full: You report him to Inspector Haskett.

G1Apprendista.7.full: It takes the boy all afternoon. The key he hands you is still warm, heavy, useless: there is no lock in the world it could fit. And yet, when you grip it, it seems to pull gently towards the alley behind the estate, like a compass needle.
G1Apprendista.7.easy: It takes the boy all afternoon. The key he gives you is still warm, heavy, and useless: there is no lock in the world it would fit. And yet, when you hold it tight, it seems to pull gently towards the alley behind the estate, like a compass needle.
G1Apprendista.7.short: The key fits no lock. But it pulls gently towards the alley behind the estate, like a compass.

G1Apprendista.8.full: Pay $2. You have the apprentice's key: the next time you turn over a Sighting, it may come in useful.

G1Apprendista.9.full: The Inspector confiscates the mould and thanks you. The boy spends a night in a cell and comes out with a black eye and a very low opinion of your family. The mould disappears from the police store three days later.
G1Apprendista.9.easy: The Inspector takes the mould and thanks you. The boy spends a night in a cell and comes out with a black eye and a very bad opinion of your family. Three days later the mould disappears from the police store.
G1Apprendista.9.short: The Inspector seizes the mould. Three days later, it vanishes.

G1Apprendista.11.full: You leave the boy to his chatter and his anvil. On the way home you pass through the alley behind the estate without meaning to, and without meaning to you look for a door with no handle. You do not see one. Which does not mean it is not there.
G1Apprendista.11.easy: You leave the boy to his chatter and his anvil. On the way home you go through the alley behind the estate without meaning to, and without meaning to you look for a door with no handle. You do not see it. But that does not mean it is not there.
G1Apprendista.11.short: On your way back you pass the alley and look for a handleless door. You do not see it. That does not mean it is not there.

G1Manicomio.3.full: **THE NEW ASYLUM OPENS ITS DOORS.** Yesterday morning, in the presence of the bishop and the finest families of the county, Lady Carew opened the asylum on the hill: a hundred beds, hot water on every floor, gardens for walking and a ward for gentlefolk, separated from the paupers' ward by a wall four metres high.
G1Manicomio.3.easy: **THE NEW ASYLUM OPENS ITS DOORS.** Yesterday morning, with the bishop and the most important families of the county, Lady Carew opened the asylum on the hill. There are a hundred beds, hot water on every floor, gardens for walking and a ward for gentlefolk, kept apart from the paupers' ward by a wall four metres high.
G1Manicomio.3.short: **THE NEW ASYLUM OPENS ITS DOORS.** A hundred beds, hot water, gardens and a ward for gentlefolk, walled off from the poor.

G1Manicomio.4.full: In her speech Lady Carew urged decent families not to be ashamed: madness, she said, is not a fault but an illness, and is best treated when caught early. Anyone with a relative at home who sleeps too little, goes out at night or sees things others do not see has a duty to report it.
G1Manicomio.4.easy: In her speech Lady Carew told respectable families not to be ashamed. Madness, she said, is not a fault but an illness, and it is easier to cure if you catch it early. Anyone with a relative at home who sleeps little, goes out at night or sees things others do not see must report it.
G1Manicomio.4.short: Lady Carew asks families to report anyone who sleeps little, goes out at night or sees strange things.

G1Manicomio.5.full: This newspaper has learned that the first report has already arrived, anonymously, and concerns one of the heirs of the estate. The letter is written in a small hand that slants backwards.
G1Manicomio.5.easy: This newspaper knows that the first report has already arrived, unsigned, and is about one of the heirs of the estate. The letter is written in small handwriting that slants backwards.
G1Manicomio.5.short: The first report, unsigned, names an heir of the estate. The handwriting slants backwards.

G1Manicomio.6.full: Lady Carew, whose plaque at the entrance bears the family's name, wished to make clear that anyone reported will receive the very best care, in the gentlefolk's ward.
G1Manicomio.6.easy: Lady Carew, who has the family's name on a plaque at the entrance, said that anyone who is reported will get the best care, in the gentlefolk's ward.
G1Manicomio.6.short: Lady Carew promises the best care, in the gentlefolk's ward, to anyone reported.

G1Manicomio.7.full: Lady Carew added that certain families "with no need of asylums" would do well to remember that the asylum, on the other hand, has need of them.
G1Manicomio.7.easy: Lady Carew also said that certain families "with no need of asylums" should remember that the asylum, however, needs them.
G1Manicomio.7.short: Lady Carew notes that the asylum needs certain families, even if they do not need it.

G1ManicomioVoto.2.full: Each player takes a Voting token and chooses in secret. When everyone has chosen, reveal your votes together.

G1ManicomioVoto.3.full: YAY: the heir who has drunk the most times is committed *(only those who drank know: they may lie)*.

G1ManicomioEsito.5.full: The asylum carriage arrives early in the morning, with two attendants in white aprons and a form already filled in. The family signs without meeting one another's eyes. Lady Carew, who wished to escort her first patient of quality in person, thanks everyone for their public spirit; and the village, for a few months, stops talking about the estate.
G1ManicomioEsito.5.easy: The asylum carriage arrives early in the morning, with two attendants in white aprons and a form ready to sign. The family signs without looking at each other. Lady Carew, who wanted to escort her first important patient herself, thanks everyone for doing their duty. And for a few months the village stops talking about the estate.
G1ManicomioEsito.5.short: The family signs, and the asylum carriage takes an heir away. For a few months the village is silent.

G1ManicomioEsito.6.full: The player who has drunk the most times *(their choice; if no one admits it, the Start Player)* places their Self on the Lost for the whole of the next Round, and gains 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}: the gentlefolk's ward is comfortable.

G1ManicomioEsito.7.full: The player who has drunk the most times *(their choice; if no one admits it, the Start Player)* places their Self on the Lost for the whole of the next Round, and gains 2 {icon:Insanity_Icon}.

G1ManicomioEsito.8.full: The family shuts the gate and does not answer letters. Lady Carew drives past the estate twice without stopping; the third time she stops, looks for a long while at the laboratory windows and writes something in her leather-bound notebook. In the village they say the gentlefolk at the estate have something to hide. In the village, for once, they are right.
G1ManicomioEsito.8.easy: The family shuts the gate and does not answer letters. Lady Carew drives past the estate twice without stopping. The third time she stops, looks for a long time at the laboratory windows and writes something in her leather notebook. In the village they say the people at the estate have something to hide. And for once they are right.
G1ManicomioEsito.8.short: The family shuts the gate. Lady Carew drives by, studies the laboratory and writes in her notebook. The village says you have something to hide. It is right.

G1Cronaca2.2.full: **Letter from Inspector Nell Haskett to her sister – *1874.***

G1Cronaca2.3.full: Dear Margaret, I write to you from my office, with the stove out because the council will not pay for wood. The Umber case keeps me awake. For thirteen years I have been collecting cheques in the same handwriting, and for thirteen years that family has smiled at me on its doorstep.
G1Cronaca2.3.easy: Dear Margaret, I am writing from my office, with the stove out because the council will not pay for wood. The Umber case keeps me awake. For thirteen years I have been collecting cheques in the same handwriting, and for thirteen years that family has smiled at me on its doorstep.
G1Cronaca2.3.short: Dear Margaret, the Umber case keeps me awake. For thirteen years I have collected cheques in the same hand, and that family smiles at me.

G1Cronaca2.4.full: I must say that not all of them lie to me. Someone up at the estate has told me the truth more than once, even when it cost them. I do not know whether it is courage or weariness. Either way, I remember it.
G1Cronaca2.4.easy: I must say not all of them lie to me. Someone up at the estate has told me the truth more than once, even when it cost them. I do not know if it is courage or tiredness. Either way, I remember it.
G1Cronaca2.4.short: Someone at the estate has told me the truth, even when it cost them. I remember it.

G1Cronaca2.5.full: They all lie to me, up there, with a courtesy that makes me want to arrest them on principle. I have learned to recognise their lies by the way they straighten their cuffs.
G1Cronaca2.5.easy: Up there they all lie to me, so politely that I want to arrest them on principle. I have learned to tell when they are lying by the way they straighten their cuffs.
G1Cronaca2.5.short: They all lie to me, politely. I can tell by how they straighten their cuffs.

G1Cronaca2.6.full: I hear that one of them bought a page of Lomax the chemist's ledger, at the market, in front of half the village. I do not know what was written on it. Since then Lomax has closed his shop at six.
G1Cronaca2.6.easy: I heard that one of them bought a page of Lomax the chemist's ledger, at the market, in front of half the village. I do not know what was on it. Since then Lomax has closed his shop at six.
G1Cronaca2.6.short: One of them bought a page of Lomax's ledger. Since then Lomax closes at six.

G1Cronaca2.7.full: One of them grabbed Lomax the chemist by the collar in the middle of the market. Lomax would not press charges. A man who will not press charges, Margaret, is a man afraid of something worse than the police.
G1Cronaca2.7.easy: One of them grabbed Lomax the chemist by the collar in the middle of the market. Lomax would not report it. A man who will not report it, Margaret, is afraid of something worse than the police.
G1Cronaca2.7.short: One of them attacked Lomax at the market. Lomax will not report it: he fears something worse than the police.

G1Cronaca2.8.full: The blacksmith's apprentice told me, after two beers, about a toothless key made for a little gentleman, and a copy made for the estate. I have looked for the door it opens. I have not found it. I believe it is the door that must find me.
G1Cronaca2.8.easy: The blacksmith's apprentice, after two beers, told me about a toothless key made for a little gentleman, and a copy made for the estate. I looked for the door it opens. I did not find it. I think the door has to find me.
G1Cronaca2.8.short: The apprentice made a toothless key, and a copy for the estate. I cannot find the door it opens.

G1Cronaca2.9.full: Last month an officer on leave challenged an heir of the estate to a duel, over an insult received at the tavern from a little man in a black coat. It ended without injury. I leave the rest to your imagination: the village talked of nothing else for weeks.
G1Cronaca2.9.easy: Last month an officer challenged an heir of the estate to a duel, because of an insult from a little man in a black coat at the tavern. It ended with no one hurt. You can imagine the rest: the village talked of nothing else for weeks.
G1Cronaca2.9.short: An officer challenged an heir to a duel over the man in black's insult. No one was hurt, but the village talks of nothing else.

G1Cronaca2.10.full: One of the heirs has been committed to Lady Carew's asylum, in the gentlefolk's ward. The family signed without argument. The cheques, since then, have not grown fewer.
G1Cronaca2.10.easy: One of the heirs has been shut away in Lady Carew's asylum, in the gentlefolk's ward. The family signed without arguing. But the cheques have not become fewer.
G1Cronaca2.10.short: An heir has been committed. The cheques have not grown fewer.

G1Cronaca2.11.full: Tomorrow I write to the capital to ask for a handwriting expert. If they send me the one I hope for, in a few years we shall at least know who writes those cheques. I am afraid I know already. Give my love to the children. Yours, Nell.
G1Cronaca2.11.easy: Tomorrow I am writing to the capital to ask for a handwriting expert. If they send the one I hope for, in a few years we shall at least know who writes those cheques. I am afraid I know already. Give my love to the children. Yours, Nell.
G1Cronaca2.11.short: I shall ask for a handwriting expert. I fear I already know who writes the cheques. Yours, Nell.

G1R3.2.full: Turn to **page 6** of the Village Chronicle, **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}).

G1R3.3.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **A Time of War** section ({icon:S3_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 21**.

G1R3.5.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Asylum Program, to visit the committed relative,

G1R3.11.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Blacksmith,

G1R3.14.full: The fortune teller has left with the caravan, but comes back to town with it. When one of your pieces visits the Traveling Caravan, you may pay $1 and have your palm read:

G1R3.20.full: The mayor is looking for volunteers and money for a night watch. The first player to send one of their pieces to the Town Hall,

G1R3.26.full: Inspector Haskett has sent to the capital for a handwriting expert, a little man with thick spectacles and a case full of lenses. He has asked the family for a letter from each of them, and to see the father's Journal, at the estate, in front of the notary.
G1R3.26.easy: Inspector Haskett has brought a handwriting expert from the capital, a little man with thick glasses and a case full of lenses. He has asked the family for a letter from each of them, and to see the father's Journal, at the estate, in front of the notary.
G1R3.26.short: The handwriting expert has arrived. He wants a letter from each of you and the father's Journal.

G1R3.27.full: Click here at the End of the Generation to continue...

round.G1R3.end.full: The Late Years of the First Generation have ended.

round.G1R3.then.full: Perform the End of Round actions, then continue with the Storybook before the End of the Generation.

G1Fucina.3.full: The forge is closed, but there is a light inside. The blacksmith is asleep on his bench, his head in his arms. By the fire, sitting on an anvil as if on a throne, is a little man in a black coat too large for him. He is warming his hands, and smiles at you as if he had been expecting you for years.
G1Fucina.3.easy: The forge is closed, but there is a light inside. The blacksmith is asleep on his bench, his head in his arms. By the fire, sitting on an anvil like a throne, is a little man in a black coat that is too big for him. He is warming his hands, and he smiles at you as if he had been waiting for you for years.
G1Fucina.3.short: In the forge, sitting on an anvil, is a little man in black. He smiles, as if he had been waiting for you.

G1Fucina.4.full: "Family at last," he says. He has a young voice and an old laugh. From his pocket he takes a page torn from the Journal, dense with formulas. "This is yours. You can have it in exchange for a signature: a blank cheque, with your name. It won't cost you anything. Not right away."
G1Fucina.4.easy: "Someone from the family at last," he says. He has a young voice and an old laugh. From his pocket he takes a page torn from the Journal, full of formulas. "This is yours. You can have it if you sign a blank cheque, with your name. It won't cost you anything. Not right away."
G1Fucina.4.short: "Family at last." He offers you a page of the Journal in exchange for a blank cheque with your signature.

G1Fucina.8.full: You run to fetch the constables.

G1Fucina.9.full: You sign, with a trembling hand. Umber blows on the ink, folds the cheque and tucks it into his breast pocket, over his heart. The page he gives you is written in your father's hand, the upright one, the respectable one, and it is the most beautiful thing you have ever read. When you look up, the anvil is empty.
G1Fucina.9.easy: You sign, with a shaking hand. Umber blows on the ink, folds the cheque and puts it in his breast pocket, near his heart. The page he gives you is in your father's handwriting, the upright, respectable one, and it is the most beautiful thing you have ever read. When you look up, there is no one on the anvil.
G1Fucina.9.short: You sign. The page is in your father's hand, and beautiful. When you look up, Umber is gone.

G1Fucina.10.full: Gain 1 Chemistry Knowledge and 2 {icon:Chemical_Icon}. The player on your left places your Money token on a Location of their choice: it is the cheque you signed.

G1Fucina.11.full: You lunge at him. He is as light as a child and as quick as a cat: he slips out of your arms, leaves you holding his empty coat and runs off into the alley, laughing. There is nothing in the coat's pockets. There is only a smell, and you recognise it: sweet tobacco and laboratory acid. The smell of your father.
G1Fucina.11.easy: You jump at him. He is as light as a child and as quick as a cat: he slips out of your arms, leaves you holding his empty coat and runs off into the alley laughing. The pockets are empty. There is only a smell, and you know it: sweet tobacco and laboratory acid. The smell of your father.
G1Fucina.11.short: He slips away and leaves you his coat. It smells of your father.

G1Fucina.13.full: When you come back with the constables, lanterns and cudgels, the forge is dark, the blacksmith is snoring on his bench and on the anvil there is only a cheque for a penny, made out to you, "for your trouble". The constables laugh all the way back. Inspector Haskett does not: she asks for the cheque and shuts it in her notebook.
G1Fucina.13.easy: When you come back with the constables, their lanterns and sticks, the forge is dark and the blacksmith is snoring on his bench. On the anvil there is only a cheque for a penny, made out to you, "for your trouble". The constables laugh all the way back. Inspector Haskett does not: she takes the cheque and puts it in her notebook.
G1Fucina.13.short: The constables find only a penny cheque for you. They laugh. Inspector Haskett does not.

G1Fucina.14.full: Gain 1 {icon:Creepy_Icon}. Inspector Haskett will remember your family.

G1Asilo.2.full: The gentlefolk's ward has carpets, velvet curtains and bars painted white so they look like picture frames. Your committed relative sits by the window in a dressing gown, writing letters to no one. They greet you kindly, as one greets a stranger. They are writing with their left hand.
G1Asilo.2.easy: The gentlefolk's ward has carpets, velvet curtains and bars painted white so they look like picture frames. Your relative sits by the window in a dressing gown, writing letters they never send. They greet you kindly, the way one greets a stranger. They are writing with their left hand.
G1Asilo.2.short: Your committed relative greets you like a stranger. They write letters with their left hand.

G1Asilo.3.full: Lady Carew shows you round in person. When she is called away into the corridor she leaves her leather-bound notebook on the desk, open.
G1Asilo.3.easy: Lady Carew shows you round herself. When someone calls her into the corridor, she leaves her leather notebook on the desk, open.
G1Asilo.3.short: Lady Carew steps out and leaves her notebook open on the desk.

G1Asilo.6.full: You pay the attendant $2 to let your relative out early.

G1Asilo.7.full: You leave $1 in the asylum's offering box.

G1Asilo.8.full: It is pages of names, and beside each name a diagnosis and a sum. Your relative's name is there, underlined: *interesting case*. At the back, on a separate page, the accounts of the gentlefolk's ward. The asylum is not paid for by decent families. For seven years it has been paid for by a monthly cheque, always for the same amount, always with the same signature: *Umber*.
G1Asilo.8.easy: There are pages of names, and next to each name an illness and an amount. Your relative's name is there too, underlined: *interesting case*. At the back, on a separate page, are the accounts of the gentlefolk's ward. Respectable families do not pay for the asylum. For seven years it has been paid by a cheque every month, always the same amount, always with the same signature: *Umber*.
G1Asilo.8.short: Your relative is marked *interesting case*. And for seven years the gentlefolk's ward has been paid for by Umber.

G1Asilo.9.full: When Lady Carew comes back, the notebook is closed, exactly where she left it. She smiles at you. You smile at her. Neither of you believes it.
G1Asilo.9.easy: When Lady Carew comes back, the notebook is closed, exactly where she left it. She smiles at you. You smile at her. Neither of you believes it.
G1Asilo.9.short: Lady Carew returns and smiles. You smile. Neither of you believes it.

G1Asilo.11.full: The attendant counts the coins without shame. That evening your relative comes home to the estate in a hired carriage, dressing gown under their coat, and asks straight away about the laboratory. At dinner they use their fork in the right hand, as always. Almost always.
G1Asilo.11.easy: The attendant counts the coins without shame. That evening your relative comes back to the estate in a hired carriage, dressing gown under their coat, and asks straight away about the laboratory. At dinner they hold their fork in their right hand, as always. Almost always.
G1Asilo.11.short: You pay the attendant, and your relative comes home. At dinner they hold the fork in their right hand. Almost always.

G1Asilo.12.full: Pay $2. The committed player takes their Self back from the Lost straight away.

G1Asilo.13.full: Lady Carew sees the coin drop into the box and thanks you with a nod, as one thanks someone who has understood the rules. Before you leave she promises that your relative will be treated with every consideration. She says it looking at her notebook.
G1Asilo.13.easy: Lady Carew sees the coin fall into the box and thanks you with a nod, the way you thank someone who has understood the rules. Before saying goodbye she promises your relative will be treated very well. She says it looking at her notebook.
G1Asilo.13.short: Lady Carew thanks you, and promises your relative will be well treated. She says it looking at her notebook.

G1Asilo.14.full: Pay $1 and gain 1VP. Lady Carew will remember your family.

G1Silas.2.full: It is night, and there is a lantern on your father's grave. Silas Pell the notary is standing before the headstone, alone, hat in hand. He has aged a great deal in these years. You see him take a paper twist from his waistcoat and sprinkle a pinch of grey powder on the grave, carefully, the way one salts soup.
G1Silas.2.easy: It is night, and there is a lantern on your father's grave. Silas Pell the notary is standing in front of the headstone, alone, holding his hat. He has grown much older in these years. You see him take a small paper packet from his waistcoat and sprinkle a pinch of grey powder on the grave, carefully, the way you salt soup.
G1Silas.2.short: At night, on your father's grave, Silas Pell the notary sprinkles a pinch of grey powder.

G1Silas.3.full: "We both fell for it, old friend," he says to the headstone. "You over there. Me over here."
G1Silas.3.easy: "We both fell for it, old friend," he says to the headstone. "You over there. Me over here."
G1Silas.3.short: "We both fell for it, old friend. You over there. Me over here."

G1Silas.5.full: You ask him what "S. P. knows" means.

G1Silas.6.full: You wait for him to leave, and gather the powder.

G1Silas.8.full: The notary starts, and the lantern shakes in his hand. For a moment he seems about to tell you everything. Then he puts his hat back on. "Your father wrote many things," he says. "Not all of them true, and none of them for you. My cupboard is locked, and I keep the key. See that it stays that way." He leaves without wishing you good night.
G1Silas.8.easy: The notary jumps, and the lantern shakes in his hand. For a moment he seems about to tell you everything. Then he puts his hat back on. "Your father wrote many things," he says. "Not all of them true, and none of them for you. My cupboard is locked, and I have the key. Make sure it stays that way." He leaves without saying good night.
G1Silas.8.short: The notary almost tells you everything, then thinks better of it: "My cupboard is locked, and I have the key. Keep it that way."

G1Silas.9.full: Gain 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon} and $2: the next day the notary sends you an envelope "for your trouble". Silas Pell will remember your family.

G1Silas.10.full: You wait for the lantern to disappear beyond the gate, then gather the grey powder from the headstone with a handkerchief. It tastes of nothing. In the laboratory you dissolve a pinch of it in a glass with salt from Lomax's second batch: the colour turns red, then violet, and stops there, as if something were still missing. Or as if there were too little of it.
G1Silas.10.easy: You wait for the lantern to disappear past the gate, then gather the grey powder from the headstone with a handkerchief. It tastes of nothing. In the laboratory you dissolve a pinch in a glass with salt from Lomax's second batch: the colour turns red, then violet, and stops there, as if something were still missing. Or as if there were too little of it.
G1Silas.10.short: You gather the grey powder. With Lomax's salt the colour reaches violet, and stops. Something is still missing.

G1Silas.12.full: You go back slowly, among the headstones, without a sound. Behind you the notary goes on talking to the grave in a low voice, for a long time. Once only, it seems to you, the grave answers. But it may have been the wind, or an owl, or your imagination.
G1Silas.12.easy: You go back quietly, among the graves, without a sound. Behind you the notary goes on talking softly to the grave, for a long time. Just once, it seems to you, the grave answers him. But perhaps it is the wind, or an owl, or your imagination.
G1Silas.12.short: You slip away. Once, it seems, the grave answers the notary.

G1Perizia.2.full: **Report of the handwriting expert to Inspector Haskett – *1877.***

G1Perizia.3.full: As requested, the undersigned has examined the twenty-three cheques collected from the shops of the village over the last sixteen years, signed with various names, and has compared them with the letters of the heirs of the estate and with the Journal of their late father.
G1Perizia.3.easy: As you asked, I have examined the twenty-three cheques collected from the village shops over the last sixteen years, signed with different names. I have compared them with the letters of the heirs of the estate and with the Journal of their dead father.
G1Perizia.3.short: I compared twenty-three cheques from sixteen years with the heirs' letters and their father's Journal.

G1Perizia.4.full: The conclusions are as follows. First: the cheques were all written by the same hand. Second: that hand belongs to none of the heirs, whose handwriting is, for the purposes of this report, surprisingly innocent. Third: that hand is the same as the Journal's.
G1Perizia.4.easy: Here are the conclusions. First: all the cheques were written by the same hand. Second: that hand does not belong to any of the heirs, whose writing is, for this report, surprisingly innocent. Third: that hand is the same as the Journal's.
G1Perizia.4.short: All the cheques are in one hand. Not the heirs'. It is the Journal's.

G1Perizia.5.full: The pressure of the pen, the *g* closed like a knot, the signature rising to the right: everything matches, except the slant. In the Journal the writing leans forward, like that of any respectable person; in the cheques it leans backwards. The undersigned has seen something similar only once, in a man who had learned to write with his left hand after losing his right.
G1Perizia.5.easy: The pressure of the pen, the *g* closed like a knot, the signature going up to the right: everything is the same, except the slant. In the Journal the writing leans forward, like any respectable person's; in the cheques it leans backwards. I have seen something like it only once, in a man who learned to write with his left hand after losing his right.
G1Perizia.5.short: Everything matches but the slant: in the Journal the writing leans forward, in the cheques backwards.

G1Perizia.6.full: The undersigned notes one exception. Among the most recent cheques is one filled in by the usual hand, but genuinely signed by an heir, in their own handwriting and with their own slant. Someone in the family has signed for him.
G1Perizia.6.easy: I report one exception. Among the newest cheques is one filled in by the usual hand, but really signed by an heir, in their own writing and with their own slant. Someone in the family has signed for him.
G1Perizia.6.short: One recent cheque is truly signed by an heir. Someone in the family signed for him.

G1Perizia.7.full: The undersigned adds, unasked, that one of the cheques is dated last week.
G1Perizia.7.easy: I add, though nobody asked me, that one of the cheques is dated last week.
G1Perizia.7.short: One of the cheques is from last week.

G1Bara.3.full: At two in the morning, with the magistrate's authorisation and in the presence of the heirs and of Silas Pell the notary, we had the grave of the deceased opened. The notary objected to the very last; then he signed, and looked elsewhere.
G1Bara.3.easy: At two in the morning, with the judge's permission and in front of the heirs and Silas Pell the notary, we had the dead man's grave opened. The notary was against it to the end; then he signed, and looked the other way.
G1Bara.3.short: At two in the morning we opened the grave. Pell the notary refused; then he signed, looking away.

G1Bara.4.full: The coffin was intact, closed with the carpenter's nails. Inside, wrapped in a sheet bearing the family's initials, were river stones, weighing some seventy kilograms. On top of the stones, folded in four, lay a bearer cheque signed *Umber*, with a note in the same slanting hand: *The notary was right: the circumstances were not doubtful. They were false.*
G1Bara.4.easy: The coffin was whole, closed with the carpenter's nails. Inside, wrapped in a sheet with the family's initials, were river stones: about seventy kilograms. On top of the stones was a cheque folded in four, signed *Umber*, with a note in the same slanting writing: *The notary was right: the circumstances were not doubtful. They were false.*
G1Bara.4.short: The coffin held only river stones. And a note from Umber: *The circumstances were not doubtful. They were false.*

G1Bara.5.full: The priest, present at the opening, crossed himself and said only: "It weighed like a stone. I told him so."
G1Bara.5.easy: The priest, who was there, crossed himself and said only: "It weighed like a stone. I told him so."
G1Bara.5.short: The priest crossed himself: "It weighed like a stone. I told him so."

G1Bara.6.full: One of the heirs, who years ago spent a night in this cemetery, recognised in the mud around the grave the same prints as back then: small, quick, fresh.
G1Bara.6.easy: One of the heirs, who spent a night in this cemetery years ago, recognised in the mud around the grave the same footprints as back then: small, quick, fresh.
G1Bara.6.short: An heir recognised the footprints from years ago in the mud: small, and fresh.

G1Bara.7.full: The village doctor, questioned at dawn, admitted to having signed the death certificate without seeing the body. He had been paid with a cheque.
G1Bara.7.easy: The village doctor, questioned at dawn, admitted he signed the death certificate without seeing the body. He was paid with a cheque.
G1Bara.7.short: The doctor signed the death certificate without seeing the body. He was paid with a cheque.

G1Bara.8.full: **The father is not dead. The father is Mr. Umber.**

G1PadreVoto.2.full: Inspector Haskett gives you one night to decide, and two constables at the gate. She remembers every lie you have told her. Without the Journal she has nothing that would stand up in court: a handwriting, a coffin full of stones, a doctor who has changed his story. With the Journal, she will have a warrant for the arrest of a dead man.
G1PadreVoto.2.easy: Inspector Haskett gives you one night to decide, and puts two constables at the gate. She remembers every lie you have told her. Without the Journal she has no proof that will stand up in court: a handwriting, a coffin of stones, a doctor who changed his story. With the Journal, she can have a dead man arrested.
G1PadreVoto.2.short: The Inspector gives you a night, with two constables at the gate. Without the Journal she has no proof. With it, she can arrest a dead man.

G1PadreVoto.3.full: Inspector Haskett gives you one night to decide. Without the Journal she has nothing that would stand up in court: a handwriting, a coffin full of stones, a doctor who has changed his story. With the Journal, she will have a warrant for the arrest of a dead man.
G1PadreVoto.3.easy: Inspector Haskett gives you one night to decide. Without the Journal she has no proof that will stand up in court: a handwriting, a coffin of stones, a doctor who changed his story. With the Journal, she can have a dead man arrested.
G1PadreVoto.3.short: The Inspector gives you a night. Without the Journal she has no proof. With it, she can arrest a dead man.

G1PadreVoto.4.full: Before leaving she shakes your hands, one by one. "I asked you for the truth, and you gave it to me," she says. "Whatever you decide, I shall not forget it."
G1PadreVoto.4.easy: Before she leaves she shakes your hands, one by one. "I asked you for the truth, and you told me," she says. "Whatever you decide, I shall not forget it."
G1PadreVoto.4.short: She shakes your hands: "You told me the truth. I shall not forget it."

G1PadreVoto.6.full: YAY: you hand the father's Journal over to the Inspector.

G1PadreVoto.7.full: NAY: you burn it, and the father stays dead for everyone.

G1PadreVoto.8.full: Tally the votes *(in case of a tie, the Start Player decides)*.

G1Lapide.2.full: The river stones go back to the river. The empty coffin stays in the open grave for three days, in the rain, until the cemetery keeper asks the family what to do with it. The headstone, with the father's name and the two dates, is still in its place. One of the two dates, now, is a lie.
G1Lapide.2.easy: The river stones go back to the river. The empty coffin stays in the open grave for three days, in the rain, until the cemetery keeper asks the family what to do with it. The headstone, with the father's name and the two dates, is still there. But now one of the two dates is a lie.
G1Lapide.2.short: The empty coffin lies in the open grave. On the headstone, one of the two dates is now a lie.

G1Lapide.3.full: What do you do with the grave? *(Decide together.)*

G1Lapide.4.full: You close it again as it is, with the name and the dates.

G1Lapide.5.full: You have the name removed from the headstone.

G1Lapide.6.full: You have engraved beneath the name: *Come back soon.*

G1Lapide.7.full: The keeper fills in the grave and sets the headstone back in place. For the village the father is dead, and stays dead. The violets, the next morning, are there again.
G1Lapide.7.easy: The keeper fills in the grave and puts the headstone back. For the village the father is dead, and stays dead. The next morning the violets are there again.
G1Lapide.7.short: The keeper closes the grave. The next day the violets are back.

G1Lapide.9.full: The stonemason hammers the name away, letter by letter. What remains is a smooth stone with two dates and a cross. The village approves: a man who is not dead has no right to a grave. The violets, the next morning, are gone.
G1Lapide.9.easy: The stonemason hammers the name away, one letter at a time. What is left is a smooth stone with two dates and a cross. The village approves: a man who is not dead has no right to a grave. The next morning the violets are gone.
G1Lapide.9.short: The name is chiselled away. The next day the violets are gone.

G1Lapide.11.full: The stonemason carves the three words beneath the name, in letters smaller than the rest, and asks twice whether he has understood correctly. The village finds it in the worst possible taste. The next morning, on the grave, beside the violets, there is a note: *You can count on it.*
G1Lapide.11.easy: The stonemason carves the three words under the name, in smaller letters, and asks twice if he has understood correctly. The village thinks it is in very bad taste. The next morning, on the grave, next to the violets, there is a note: *You can count on it.*
G1Lapide.11.short: You have *Come back soon* carved under the name. The next day, among the violets, a note: *You can count on it.*

G1Chiusura.2.full: Inspector Haskett hunts a dead man for two years. She has his portrait printed on posters all over the county, with the word WANTED and a reward; but the portrait is of a tall, distinguished man, and no one has ever seen Umber like that. The posters end up wrapping fish.
G1Chiusura.2.easy: Inspector Haskett hunts a dead man for two years. She has his portrait printed on posters all over the county, with WANTED and a reward. But the portrait shows a tall, elegant man, and nobody has ever seen Umber like that. The posters end up wrapping fish.
G1Chiusura.2.short: The Inspector hunts the father for two years. But the posters show a tall, elegant man, and Umber is not like that.

G1Chiusura.3.full: In the winter of 1879, on the bridge, they find a black coat too large for its owner, carefully folded, its pockets full of labels from Lomax's pharmacy. Of the father, nothing else.
G1Chiusura.3.easy: In the winter of 1879, on the bridge, they find a black coat that is too big, carefully folded, with its pockets full of labels from Lomax's pharmacy. They find nothing else of the father.
G1Chiusura.3.short: In 1879 a folded black coat is found on the bridge. Of the father, nothing.

G1Chiusura.4.full: The Journal burns in the library fireplace, one page at a time, while the Inspector waits in her carriage outside the gate. When the family tells her the notebook was lost years ago, she writes something in her notebook and does not insist.
G1Chiusura.4.easy: The Journal burns in the library fireplace, one page at a time, while the Inspector waits in her carriage outside the gate. When the family tells her the notebook was lost years ago, she writes something in her notebook and does not insist.
G1Chiusura.4.short: You burn the Journal and tell the Inspector it was lost years ago. She writes something, and lets it go.

G1Chiusura.5.full: The last page, lifted by the heat, flies up the chimney before anyone can catch it. The next morning the baker finds it in the gutter and brings it back to the estate. It is blank. On the back, in the backward-slanting hand, there is a single word: *thank you*.
G1Chiusura.5.easy: The last page, lifted by the heat, flies up the chimney before anyone can catch it. The next morning the baker finds it in the gutter and brings it back to the estate. It is blank. But on the back, in the backward-slanting writing, there is a single word: *thank you*.
G1Chiusura.5.short: The last page flies away. The next day it is back: blank, with one word on the back, slanting backwards: *thank you*.

G1Chiusura.7.full: The heirs of the first generation died in the years that followed, all of natural causes, all in their beds; and this time my father checked every coffin in person before it was closed. The sightings, on the other hand, went on.
G1Chiusura.7.easy: The heirs of the first generation died in the years after, all of natural causes, all in their beds. This time my father checked every coffin himself before it was closed. The sightings, however, went on.
G1Chiusura.7.short: The heirs died in their beds, and my father checked every coffin. The sightings went on.

G1Chiusura.8.full: My father closed the file in 1880, with a note in the margin: *Case closed*. Many years later, beneath it, I added: *Not yet.*
G1Chiusura.8.easy: My father closed the file in 1880, with a note in the margin: *Case closed*. Many years later, underneath, I added: *Not yet.*
G1Chiusura.8.short: My father wrote: *Case closed*. Years later, I added: *Not yet.*

G1Chiusura.9.full: Remove all pieces from the board and perform the End of the Generation. Return unused {icon:StorybookToken} tokens to the supply. The Sightings {icon:S2_HuntTokenFRONT} on the board go back next to the board; the Money tokens go back to the players.

SaleG2Intro.2.full: **Note by Ezra Pell, notary, for the file – *1886.***

SaleG2Intro.3.full: My father died two years ago, pen in hand, halfway through a deed of sale. He left me his practice, his clients, a locked cupboard whose key I have never found, and this file, which I should never have reopened.
SaleG2Intro.3.easy: My father died two years ago, pen in hand, while writing a contract. He left me his practice, his clients, a locked cupboard whose key I have never found, and this file, which I should never have opened again.
SaleG2Intro.3.short: My father died two years ago. He left me his practice, a locked cupboard with no key and this file.

SaleG2Intro.4.full: In his last years my father no longer slept in his bed. Ever since one of the heirs of the estate had gone looking for him in the cemetery, at night, to ask him questions, he slept in his office, in an armchair, in front of the cupboard.
SaleG2Intro.4.easy: In his last years my father stopped sleeping in his bed. Ever since one of the heirs of the estate went looking for him in the cemetery, at night, to ask him questions, he slept in his office, in an armchair, in front of the cupboard.
SaleG2Intro.4.short: After an heir sought him out at the cemetery, my father slept in an armchair, in front of the cupboard.

SaleG2Intro.5.full: In twenty-five years the village has become a town. The half-timbered houses have fallen one after another, and in their place have grown houses of grey stone, all alike, with gas lamps outside the door. The railway has come, and with the railway the soot. Of the old man nothing more has been heard: in law he died in 1861, and no one has any wish to reopen the matter.
SaleG2Intro.5.easy: In twenty-five years the village has become a town. The wooden houses have fallen one after another, and in their place are houses of grey stone, all the same, with gas lamps outside the door. The train has come, and with the train the soot. Nothing more has been heard of the old man: by law he died in 1861, and no one wants to talk about it again.
SaleG2Intro.5.short: The village has become a town of stone, with trains and soot. Nothing more is known of the old man.

SaleG2Intro.6.full: The sightings of Mr. Umber, on the other hand, have never stopped. A little man in a black coat, not a day older, who pays with cheques signed by respectable people and laughs at the end of the street. Today the heirs of the estate are the old man's grandchildren. None of them has ever seen the phials of salt, and all of them know where they are.
SaleG2Intro.6.easy: But the sightings of Mr. Umber have never stopped. A little man in a black coat, not one day older, pays with cheques signed by respectable people and laughs at the end of the street. Today the heirs of the estate are the old man's grandchildren. None of them has ever seen the phials of salt, but they all know where they are.
SaleG2Intro.6.short: But Umber is still seen: not a day older. The heirs are the old man's grandchildren, and know where the phials are.

SaleG2Intro.7.full: They grew up on the stories, the way one grows up on bread: the grandfather who was not dead, the coffin full of stones, the door with no handle. At school their classmates dared each other to touch the estate's gate. Now the classmates are lawyers, doctors, town councillors, and cross to the other side of the street.
SaleG2Intro.7.easy: They grew up with these stories, the way you grow up with bread: the grandfather who was not dead, the coffin full of stones, the door with no handle. At school their friends dared each other to touch the estate's gate. Now those friends are lawyers, doctors, councillors, and they cross the street when they see them.
SaleG2Intro.7.short: They grew up on stories of their grandfather. Their schoolfriends now cross the street.

SaleG2Intro.9.full: Take the **Vanity Estate Upgrades** from the **Fear of the Unknown** Scenario Box and add them to those available.

G2SognoA.3.full: You wake before dawn on top of the covers, still dressed. Your shoes are caked with river mud. In your pocket is a cheque signed with your name, in your own hand: but the writing slants backwards. You have never touched the salt. You did not need to: whoever came before you drank it for you. You are Umber. You always have been.
G2SognoA.3.easy: You wake before dawn on top of the covers, fully dressed. Your shoes are dirty with river mud. In your pocket is a cheque signed with your name, in your hand: but the writing slants backwards. You have never touched the salt. You did not need to: whoever came before you drank it for you. You are Umber. You always were.
G2SognoA.3.short: You wake with muddy shoes and a cheque signed by you, slanting backwards. You never drank the salt. You are Umber.

G2SognoA.4.full: **You are the Heir in the Shadow.** Tell no one. Gain 1VP for each of your cheques that is still on a Location at the end of a Round. At the End of the Generation the family will accuse someone.

G2SognoA.5.full: What do you do with the cheque?

G2SognoA.8.full: You dream of the alley behind the estate, the door with no handle, a laugh coming from behind you that you have always known. You wake with a start, your heart in your mouth. The bed is neat, your shoes are clean by the door, your pockets empty. And yet, for a moment, you would have sworn your hands were muddy.
G2SognoA.8.easy: You dream of the alley behind the estate, the door with no handle, and a laugh behind you that you have always known. You wake suddenly, your heart racing. The bed is tidy, your shoes are clean by the door, your pockets empty. And yet, for a moment, you would have sworn your hands were muddy.
G2SognoA.8.short: You dream of the alley and a laugh. You wake: all is in order. But for a moment your hands seem muddy.

G2SognoA.9.full: You are not the Heir in the Shadow. One of you may be, or perhaps no one: watch who places cheques, and when.

G2SognoA.11.full: You search the coat hanging in the hall.

G2SognoA.13.full: At the bank the cashier looks at the signature, looks at you, and counts out the money without a word.
G2SognoA.13.easy: At the bank the cashier looks at the signature, then at you, and counts out the money without saying anything.
G2SognoA.13.short: The cashier looks at the signature, and pays.

G2SognoA.14.full: In the coat pocket there is money you do not remember putting there.
G2SognoA.14.easy: In the coat pocket there is some money you do not remember putting there.
G2SognoA.14.short: In the pocket, money you do not remember.

G2SognoA.16.full: The paper burns quickly, with a greenish flame. You feel better, almost.
G2SognoA.16.easy: The paper burns quickly, with a slightly green flame. You feel better, almost.
G2SognoA.16.short: It burns with a green flame. You feel better, almost.

G2SognoA.17.full: Sleep comes at once, deep and dreamless. You feel better, almost.
G2SognoA.17.easy: You fall asleep at once, deeply, without dreams. You feel better, almost.
G2SognoA.17.short: You sleep without dreams. You feel better, almost.

G2SognoFine.2.full: Where the village market used to be there now stands the Jail: a red-brick building with barred windows that people call "the new hotel". Half the river has been covered over, and carriages run on top of it.
G2SognoFine.2.easy: Where the village market used to be there is now the Jail: a red-brick building with barred windows that people call "the new hotel". Half the river has been covered, and carriages drive over it.
G2SognoFine.2.short: Where the market stood is now the Jail, "the new hotel". Half the river is covered.

G2SognoFine.3.full: Inspector Nell Haskett has retired. She lives in a little house near the station, with a cat and her old black notebook, and still receives visits from her successor: her niece, Inspector Ada Haskett, who has the same eyes and a sharper pencil. The first file Ada opened, on the day of her appointment, was Mr. Umber's.
G2SognoFine.3.easy: Inspector Nell Haskett has retired. She lives in a little house near the station, with a cat and her old black notebook. She still gets visits from the person who took her place: her niece, Inspector Ada Haskett, who has the same eyes and an even sharper pencil. The first file Ada opened, on her first day, was Mr. Umber's.
G2SognoFine.3.short: Nell Haskett has retired. Her niece, Inspector Ada Haskett, has taken her place. Her first file: Mr. Umber.

G2SognoFine.4.full: Meanwhile a gentleman from the railway company arrives at the estate, with a waxed moustache and a leather portfolio. The new line must run along the edge of the estate, right behind the alley. The company offers a good price for the strip of land, and an even better one if the family signs quickly.
G2SognoFine.4.easy: Meanwhile a gentleman from the railway company comes to the estate, with a shiny moustache and a leather case. The new railway line must run along the edge of the estate, right behind the alley. The company offers a good price for that strip of land, and an even better one if the family signs quickly.
G2SognoFine.4.short: The railway wants to buy the land along the alley, and pays well if you sign quickly.

G2SognoFine.6.full: You sell the land along the alley.

G2SognoFine.8.full: You sign quickly, and the company pays quickly. A month later the workmen pull down the boundary wall and lay the rails ten metres from the alley. Now goods trains pass at night, and no one hears anything any more: neither footsteps nor laughter.
G2SognoFine.8.easy: You sign quickly, and the company pays quickly. A month later the workmen knock down the wall and lay the rails ten metres from the alley. Now goods trains go by at night, and nobody hears anything any more: no footsteps, no laughter.
G2SognoFine.8.short: You sell. Now trains pass at night, and no one hears footsteps or laughter any more.

G2SognoFine.10.full: You refuse. The gentleman with the waxed moustache leaves shaking his head, and the line makes a wide curve around the estate, which on the company's maps is shaded grey, like the marshes. In town they say the family has something to hide behind that wall. They are not entirely wrong.
G2SognoFine.10.easy: You refuse. The gentleman with the shiny moustache leaves shaking his head. The railway makes a wide curve round the estate, and on the company's maps the estate is marked in grey, like the marshes. In town they say the family is hiding something behind that wall. They are not entirely wrong.
G2SognoFine.10.short: You refuse. The railway curves round the estate, and the town says you are hiding something. It is not wrong.

G2R1.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 8**.

G2R1.4.full: Inspector Ada Haskett has her office in the new Jail. The first player to send one of their pieces there,

G2R1.7.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Bank,

G2R1.10.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Town Hall,

G2R1.16.full: The railway workers are on strike. The first player to send one of their pieces to the Laborer's Union,

G2R1.19.full: The old fortune teller still reads palms, or perhaps it is her daughter. When one of your pieces visits the Fortune Teller, you may pay $1:

G2R1.22.full: Umber's cheques turn up in the shops again, signed with your names. No one in the family admits to having drunk the salt.
G2R1.22.easy: Umber's cheques turn up in the shops again, signed with your names. No one in the family says they drank the salt.
G2R1.22.short: Umber's cheques return with your names. No one admits to drinking the salt.

round.G2R1.end.full: The Early Years of the Second Generation have ended.

G2Ada.2.full: The new Jail has steam heating, numbered cells and an office on the first floor with a window onto the yard. Inspector Ada Haskett is young, younger than you expected, with her aunt's eyes and an even sharper pencil. On her desk is a single file, as thick as a missal. On the cover is written *Umber*.
G2Ada.2.easy: The new Jail has steam heating, numbered cells and an office on the first floor with a window onto the yard. Inspector Ada Haskett is young, younger than you expected. She has her aunt's eyes and an even sharper pencil. On the desk there is a single file, as thick as a prayer book. On the cover it says *Umber*.
G2Ada.2.short: Inspector Ada Haskett is young, with her aunt's eyes. On her desk is a single file: *Umber*.

G2Ada.3.full: "My aunt told me about your family," she says, before you have even opened your mouth. "She says one can talk to you. I hope she's right. She usually is."
G2Ada.3.easy: "My aunt told me about your family," she says, before you can speak. "She says you are people one can talk to. I hope she is right. She usually is."
G2Ada.3.short: "My aunt says you are people one can talk to. She is usually right."

G2Ada.4.full: "My aunt told me about your family," she says, before you have even opened your mouth. "She told me not to believe a word you say. She's usually right."
G2Ada.4.easy: "My aunt told me about your family," she says, before you can speak. "She told me not to believe anything you tell me. She is usually right."
G2Ada.4.short: "My aunt says not to believe a word you tell me. She is usually right."

G2Ada.5.full: "My aunt told me about your family," she says. "She didn't tell me whether to trust you. I think she wanted to leave me the pleasure of finding out."
G2Ada.5.easy: "My aunt told me about your family," she says. "She did not tell me whether to trust you. I think she wanted to leave me the pleasure of finding out myself."
G2Ada.5.short: "My aunt did not say whether to trust you. I shall find out myself."

G2Ada.7.full: You offer her your help against Umber.

G2Ada.8.full: You ask her to leave your family in peace.

G2Ada.9.full: You pay $2 to learn where Umber was last seen.

G2Ada.10.full: Ada looks at you for a long time, as if searching for the point where you are lying. Then she opens a drawer and gives you a brass whistle, the kind constables carry. "If you see him, blow it," she says. "And if one day you have to tell me something you'd rather not, come to me before I come to you."
G2Ada.10.easy: Ada looks at you for a long time, as if she were looking for the lie. Then she opens a drawer and gives you a brass whistle, like the constables' ones. "If you see him, blow it," she says. "And if one day you have to tell me something you don't like, come to me before I come to you."
G2Ada.10.short: Ada gives you a whistle: "If you see him, blow it. And come to me before I come to you."

G2Ada.11.full: Gain 1VP. Inspector Ada Haskett will remember your family.

G2Ada.12.full: Ada smiles. "Gladly," she says. "The day Umber leaves the town in peace, I'll leave you in peace." She writes a line in the file, closes it and wishes you a good day. It is the first time a good day has ever sounded to you like a threat.
G2Ada.12.easy: Ada smiles. "Gladly," she says. "When Umber leaves the town in peace, I shall leave you in peace." She writes a line in the file, closes it and wishes you a good day. It is the first time "good day" has sounded like a threat.
G2Ada.12.short: "When Umber leaves the town alone, I shall leave you alone." Her good day sounds like a threat.

G2Ada.14.full: Ada counts the coins in front of you, one by one, and locks them in the drawer labelled *Evidence*. Then she tells you where Umber was last seen, and thanks you: "I'll add this to the file."
G2Ada.14.easy: Ada counts the coins in front of you, one at a time, and locks them in the drawer labelled *Evidence*. Then she tells you where Umber was last seen, and thanks you: "That goes in the file."
G2Ada.14.short: Ada locks the coins in the *Evidence* drawer, tells you where Umber was last seen and thanks you.

G2Ada.15.full: Pay $2. Secretly look at one face-down Sighting {icon:S2_HuntTokenFRONT} on the board, without turning it over. Inspector Ada Haskett will remember your family.

G2Elezioni.2.full: The town council election is under way, and at the town hall the candidates' posters cover the walls up to the ceiling. One has neither picture nor programme: only a name, *U. Mber*, and the promise of "street lamps lit all night, so that everyone may see who walks beside them". The town clerk swears the candidacy is in order: the deposit was paid with a cheque.
G2Elezioni.2.easy: There is an election for the town council, and at the town hall the candidates' posters cover the walls up to the ceiling. One poster has no picture and no programme. There is only a name, *U. Mber*, and a promise: "lamps lit all night, so that everyone can see who walks beside them". The town clerk swears the candidacy is in order: the deposit was paid with a cheque.
G2Elezioni.2.short: At the election there is a candidate with no picture: *U. Mber*. He promises lamps lit all night. He paid the deposit with a cheque.

G2Elezioni.6.full: You vote for him, to see what happens.

G2Elezioni.7.full: You tear them all down, one by one, in front of the town hall, in broad daylight. A constable watches you without stepping in, then writes something in his notebook. At dawn the posters are back in their place, bigger.
G2Elezioni.7.easy: You tear down every poster, one at a time, in front of the town hall, in broad daylight. A constable watches you and does nothing, then writes something in his notebook. At dawn the posters are back, bigger.
G2Elezioni.7.short: You tear down the posters. At dawn they are back, bigger.

G2Elezioni.9.full: You have posters printed, shake hands at the market, promise new sewers and less fog. You lose, naturally, but with honour. *U. Mber* gets a single vote, and no one knows whose: the returning officer swears he counted three times. And yet on the evening of the count, in the town hall, someone laughs for an hour.
G2Elezioni.9.easy: You have posters printed, shake hands at the market, promise new drains and less fog. Of course you lose, but with honour. *U. Mber* gets just one vote, and no one knows who cast it: the teller swears he counted three times. And yet on the evening of the count, at the town hall, someone laughs for a whole hour.
G2Elezioni.9.short: You stand and lose with honour. *U. Mber* gets one vote. That evening, at the town hall, someone laughs for an hour.

G2Elezioni.11.full: In the polling booth you write his name with your pencil, in your own handwriting, and halfway through you notice the letters are slanting backwards. As you leave, the returning officer wishes you good night by your Christian name, although you have never met.
G2Elezioni.11.easy: In the booth you write his name with your pencil, in your handwriting. Halfway through you notice the letters are slanting backwards. When you come out, the teller wishes you good night by your first name, though you have never met.
G2Elezioni.11.short: You vote for him, and your letters slant backwards. The teller, a stranger, calls you by name.

G2Elezioni.12.full: Gain 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon} and $1: someone has slipped a coin into your coat pocket.

G2Lapide.2.full: On your grandfather's grave, beneath the name, the words your parents had engraved can still be read: *Come back soon*. Someone has recut them with a chisel recently: the grooves are white and clean. Before the headstone, the usual violets.
G2Lapide.2.easy: On your grandfather's grave, under the name, you can still read the words your parents had carved: *Come back soon*. Someone has gone over them with a chisel recently: the grooves are white and clean. In front of the headstone are the usual violets.
G2Lapide.2.short: Under your grandfather's name, *Come back soon* has been recut. And the usual violets are there.
