G2Lapide.3.full: Your grandfather's nameless headstone is covered in moss, except in one place: where the name used to be, someone has scraped the moss away with a fingernail, letter by letter, and the name can be read again, green on grey. Before the headstone, after so many years, the violets have come back.
G2Lapide.3.easy: Your grandfather's nameless headstone is covered in moss, except in one place. Where the name used to be, someone has scraped off the moss with a fingernail, one letter at a time, and the name can be read again, green on grey. In front of the headstone, after so many years, the violets have come back.
G2Lapide.3.short: Someone has scraped your grandfather's name back into the moss. And the violets have come back.

G2Lapide.4.full: Your grandfather's grave is as your parents left it: the name, the two dates, a cross. The earth in front is disturbed every so often, as if someone slept on it. Before the headstone, the usual violets.
G2Lapide.4.easy: Your grandfather's grave is as your parents left it: the name, the two dates, a cross. Every now and then the earth in front is disturbed, as if someone slept on it. In front of the headstone are the usual violets.
G2Lapide.4.short: The earth before your grandfather's grave is sometimes disturbed. And the usual violets are there.

G2Lapide.6.full: You have the grave watched, at night, for a week.

G2Lapide.7.full: You leave a note under the violets.

G2Lapide.8.full: The keeper keeps watch for six nights and sees nothing. On the seventh he falls asleep. In the morning the violets are fresh, and on his hat, propped against the headstone, there is a cheque: his week's wages, "for the courtesy".
G2Lapide.8.easy: The keeper keeps watch for six nights and sees nothing. On the seventh he falls asleep. In the morning the violets are fresh, and on his hat, leaning against the headstone, there is a cheque: a week's wages, "for your kindness".
G2Lapide.8.short: The keeper watches six nights. On the seventh he dozes, and finds a cheque on his hat, "for your kindness".

G2Lapide.10.full: You write a few lines: *Who are you? What do you want?* The next day the note is gone. In its place is another, in the backward-slanting hand: *I am family. I want what you want.*
G2Lapide.10.easy: You write a few lines: *Who are you? What do you want?* The next day the note is gone. In its place there is another, in the backward-slanting hand: *I am family. I want what you want.*
G2Lapide.10.short: *Who are you? What do you want?* The answer: *I am family. I want what you want.*

G2Chiave.2.full: The toothless key, the one with the eye-shaped head, has lain for twenty years at the bottom of a drawer. When you take it in your hand it is warm, and it pulls: gently, patiently, towards the back of the house, towards the alley, like a compass needle. At night, in the silence, you can even hear a faint hum.
G2Chiave.2.easy: The toothless key, the one with the eye-shaped head, has lain for twenty years at the bottom of a drawer. When you pick it up it is warm, and it pulls: gently, patiently, towards the back of the house and the alley, like a compass needle. At night, in the silence, you can even hear a faint hum.
G2Chiave.2.short: The toothless key is warm, and pulls towards the alley like a compass. At night it hums.

G2Chiave.5.full: You throw it in the river.

G2Chiave.6.full: The key leads you along the corridor, down the servants' stairs, to a wall where there is no door. You put it against the wall, and the wall opens: it is the study of mirrors. At the desk, with their back to you, someone is writing, the pen scratching the paper. They are wearing a black coat. They do not turn round. You do not stay to see who it is.
G2Chiave.6.easy: The key leads you down the corridor and the service stairs, to a wall with no door. You hold it against the wall, and the wall opens: it is the study of mirrors. At the desk, back turned, someone is writing, the pen scratching the paper. They wear a black coat. They do not turn round. You do not stay to see who it is.
G2Chiave.6.short: The key opens a wall: the study of mirrors. At the desk, back turned, someone in a black coat writes. You leave.

G2Chiave.8.full: You throw it from the bridge, by day, in front of everyone. It sinks at once, without a sound. That night you sleep as you have not slept for years. The next morning, on your bedside table, there is a puddle of river water, small, in the shape of a key.
G2Chiave.8.easy: You throw it off the bridge, in daylight, in front of everyone. It sinks at once, without a sound. That night you sleep as you have not slept for years. The next morning, on your bedside table, there is a small puddle of river water in the shape of a key.
G2Chiave.8.short: You throw it in the river. Next morning, on your bedside table, there is a puddle shaped like a key.

G2Sindacato.2.full: The railway workers have been on strike for three weeks. The union meets in a smoky room above a tavern, with odd chairs and the portrait of an old bearded union man hanging crooked. The strike should have ended long ago, because the workers have not a penny left. And yet they hold out. Someone pays them their week's wages every Friday, with a cheque.
G2Sindacato.2.easy: The railway workers have been on strike for three weeks. The union meets in a smoky room above a tavern, with odd chairs and the crooked portrait of an old bearded union man. The strike should have ended long ago, because the workers have no money left. And yet they hold out. Every Friday someone pays their week's wages, with a cheque.
G2Sindacato.2.short: The railway strike has lasted three weeks. The workers hold out because every Friday someone pays them by cheque.

G2Sindacato.4.full: You give $2 to the strike fund.

G2Sindacato.5.full: You ask to see one of the cheques.

G2Sindacato.7.full: The workers applaud you, the union secretary shakes your hand with his coal-black hands. For a week, in town, the family from the estate is "the one that stands with the workers". The gentlemen at the club will never forgive you; the workers will never forget it.
G2Sindacato.7.easy: The workers clap, and the union secretary shakes your hand with his coal-black hands. For a week, in town, the family at the estate is "the one that stands with the workers". The gentlemen at the club will not forgive you. The workers will not forget it.
G2Sindacato.7.short: The workers cheer. The club will not forgive you; the workers will not forget.

G2Sindacato.9.full: The secretary hesitates, then shows you last Friday's cheque. It is made out to the union and signed with the name of one of you, in the backward-slanting hand. On the back, in pencil, someone has written: *Hold out. It's good for your health.*
G2Sindacato.9.easy: The secretary hesitates, then shows you last Friday's cheque. It is made out to the union and signed with the name of one of you, in the backward-slanting hand. On the back, in pencil, someone has written: *Hold out. It's good for your health.*
G2Sindacato.9.short: The cheque bears one of your names, slanting backwards. On the back: *Hold out. It's good for your health.*

G2Sindacato.11.full: The company thanks you and has the cheques stopped at the bank. The strike ends within a week, from hunger. That very night, on the estate wall, someone writes in charcoal: *UMBER'S SPY*.
G2Sindacato.11.easy: The company thanks you and has the cheques stopped at the bank. The strike ends in a week, because the workers are hungry. That same night, on the estate wall, someone writes in charcoal: *UMBER'S SPY*.
G2Sindacato.11.short: The cheques are stopped and the strike ends in hunger. On your wall someone writes: *UMBER'S SPY*.

G2Banca.2.full: The manager of the Bank is a pink, round man who speaks softly, as if in church. He explains, with great embarrassment, that your grandfather's account has never been closed. The will leaves it to Mr. Umber, and the notary has never given permission to close it. So the account lives on: every week someone draws on it with a cheque, and every month someone pays in, in cash, always the same amount.
G2Banca.2.easy: The manager of the Bank is a pink, round man who speaks softly, as if in church. He explains, very embarrassed, that your grandfather's account has never been closed. The will leaves it to Mr. Umber, and the notary has never given permission to close it. So the account is still alive: every week someone draws money with a cheque, and every month someone pays in cash, always the same amount.
G2Banca.2.short: Your grandfather's account is still open, in Mr. Umber's name. Every week someone draws, every month someone pays in.

G2Banca.3.full: Among last month's cheques there is one the manager shows you separately, holding it between two fingers: the signature is one of your parents', and it is genuine. It is dated 1877. It was filled in last week.
G2Banca.3.easy: Among last month's cheques the manager shows you one separately, holding it with two fingers. The signature is one of your parents', and it is genuine. It is dated 1877. But it was written last week.
G2Banca.3.short: One cheque bears a parent's genuine signature, dated 1877. It was written last week.

G2Banca.5.full: You pay the manager $2 to learn who makes the deposits.

G2Banca.6.full: You ask for the account to be closed.

G2Banca.7.full: The manager leafs through the ledger, licks his finger, leafs again. The deposits are brought by a young clerk in sleeve protectors, always the same one, who leaves no name and asks for no receipt. The manager knows him by sight: he is the clerk of **Pell's notary practice**. The deposits began before old Silas died. And they have continued since.
G2Banca.7.easy: The manager leafs through the ledger, licks his finger, leafs again. The deposits are brought by a young clerk with oversleeves, always the same one. He leaves no name and asks for no receipt. The manager knows him by sight: he is the clerk from the **Pell, Notary**. The deposits began before old Silas died. And they went on afterwards.
G2Banca.7.short: The deposits are brought by the clerk from the **Pell, Notary**. They began before Silas died, and go on.

G2Banca.9.full: The manager spreads his hands. Without the notary's permission he cannot, and Ezra Pell the notary, when asked, has already said no: "The account will remain open until Mr. Umber comes to close it in person." In town, meanwhile, word spreads that the family from the estate wants Umber's money.
G2Banca.9.easy: The manager spreads his hands. Without the notary's permission he can do nothing, and Ezra Pell the notary has already said no: "The account will stay open until Mr. Umber comes to close it himself." Meanwhile the rumour goes round town that the family at the estate wants Umber's money.
G2Banca.9.short: Ezra Pell the notary refuses: the account stays open until Umber closes it himself. And the town says you want his money.

G2Banca.10.full: Gain $2: the manager, by way of apology, refunds you the costs of an old mistake.

G2BigliettoA.3.full: A note folded in four, slipped under your bedroom door. You recognise the paper: it is from your own writing desk. You recognise the handwriting: it is yours. *Tonight, at the market. You know already.*
G2BigliettoA.3.easy: There is a note folded in four, pushed under your bedroom door. You know the paper: it is from your writing desk. You know the handwriting: it is yours. *Tonight, at the market. You already know.*
G2BigliettoA.3.short: A note under your door, on your paper, in your hand: *Tonight, at the market. You already know.*

G2BigliettoA.4.full: This Round, place your Money token on the Farmer's Market, even if you did not drink.

G2BigliettoA.5.full: A note folded in four, slipped under your bedroom door. The paper is the estate's. The handwriting is small, quick, slanting backwards. *Watch who goes to the market.*
G2BigliettoA.5.easy: There is a note folded in four, pushed under your bedroom door. The paper is the estate's. The handwriting is small, quick, and slants backwards. *See who goes to the market.*
G2BigliettoA.5.short: A note under your door, slanting backwards: *See who goes to the market.*

G2BigliettoA.6.full: You need do nothing. But remember who places a cheque on the Farmer's Market.

G2BigliettoA.7.full: What do you do with the note?

G2BigliettoA.8.full: You burn it in the candle.

G2BigliettoA.9.full: You keep it in your Journal.

G2BigliettoA.10.full: The paper curls and turns to ash in an instant. The smell remains, and the sentence, which you keep repeating to yourself until dawn.
G2BigliettoA.10.easy: The paper curls up and turns to ash in a moment. What is left is the smell, and the sentence, which you keep repeating to yourself until dawn.
G2BigliettoA.10.short: It turns to ash. The words stay in your head until dawn.

G2BigliettoA.12.full: You slip it between the pages of your Journal, where no one will look for it. Now and then, at night, you read it again. Each time the handwriting seems a little more familiar.
G2BigliettoA.12.easy: You put it between the pages of the Journal, where no one will look for it. Every so often, at night, you read it again. Each time the handwriting looks a little more familiar.
G2BigliettoA.12.short: You hide it in the Journal. Each time you reread it, the handwriting looks more familiar.

G2BigliettoFine.2.full: That autumn a yellow fog comes down from the hill and settles on the town like a lid. It smells of sulphur and river. The street lamps are lit at noon and are not enough to see the other side of the street; carriages go at a walking pace, with a boy in front waving a lantern.
G2BigliettoFine.2.easy: That autumn a yellow fog comes down from the hill and settles on the town like a lid. It smells of sulphur and river. The lamps are lit at noon, but it is not enough to see across the street. Carriages go at walking pace, with a boy in front waving a lantern.
G2BigliettoFine.2.short: That autumn a yellow fog covers the town. The lamps are lit at noon, and it is not enough.

G2BigliettoFine.3.full: In the fog, they say, Umber walks more easily. Ada Haskett's constables have orders to stop every short man in a black coat. In one week they stop forty, and let them all go.
G2BigliettoFine.3.easy: They say Umber walks more easily in the fog. Ada Haskett's constables have orders to stop every short man in a black coat. In a week they stop forty, and let them all go.
G2BigliettoFine.3.short: Ada's constables stop every short man in a black coat: forty in a week, all released.

G2BigliettoFine.4.full: The forty-first person stopped is **{0}**: at two in the morning, on the bridge, hatless, shoes wet and without an explanation that satisfies the constables. They spend the night in a cell at the Jail. At dawn the family can pay bail, or let them answer Ada Haskett's questions until she is satisfied.

G2Cronaca2.3.short: Three months and no proof: a stick, a maid, an impatient town. My aunt says there is usually more than one to blame.

G2Cronaca2.4.full: Half the hall, on the night of the party, saw Lady Carew talking in a low voice with someone from the estate. She had promised to give them a name the next day. She died first. I do not know whether the person she spoke to is a witness or an accomplice. I know they are afraid.
G2Cronaca2.4.easy: On the night of the party half the room saw Lady Carew talking quietly with someone from the estate. She had promised to give them a name, the next day. She died first. I do not know if that person is a witness or an accomplice. I know they are afraid.
G2Cronaca2.4.short: Lady Carew was to give someone from the estate a name. I do not know if they are a witness or an accomplice. I know they are afraid.

G2Cronaca2.5.full: Lady Carew's leather-bound notebook, the one she never let out of her sight, was found neither on the body nor in her house. Someone took it. I have half an idea who.
G2Cronaca2.5.easy: Lady Carew's leather notebook, the one she always carried, was not on the body and not in her house. Someone took it. I have an idea who.
G2Cronaca2.5.short: Lady Carew's notebook is gone. I have an idea who took it.

G2Cronaca2.6.full: The town still talks about *The Doctor and His Double*, the caravan's play, and there are those who go looking for Lady Carew's murderer among the actors, as one goes to the circus. I asked the manager who played the double. He does not know. He never knew.
G2Cronaca2.6.easy: The town still talks about *The Doctor and His Double*, the travelling players' show, and some people go looking for Lady Carew's murderer among the actors, as if going to the circus. I asked the manager who played the double. He does not know. He never knew.
G2Cronaca2.6.short: I asked the manager who played the double. He never knew.

G2Cronaca2.7.full: One of the heirs borrowed the old man's book from the library, the one reserved every month by Pell's practice. The next day the notary's clerk came to ask for it back, with an insistence that struck me as odd. I took note.
G2Cronaca2.7.easy: One of the heirs borrowed the old man's book from the library, the one the Pell office reserves every month. The next day the notary's clerk came to ask for it back, so insistently that it struck me as odd. I made a note.
G2Cronaca2.7.short: An heir borrowed the old man's book, and Pell's clerk demanded it back. I made a note.

G2Cronaca2.8.full: The gravedigger at the new cemetery says that months ago he received an order for a grave in the name of a living man, paid with a cheque from Umber, undated. I asked him not to fill it in. He laughed.
G2Cronaca2.8.easy: The gravedigger at the new cemetery says that months ago he got an order for a grave for someone still alive, paid with a cheque from Umber, with no date. I asked him not to fill it in. He laughed.
G2Cronaca2.8.short: Umber paid for a grave for someone living, undated. I asked the gravedigger not to fill it in. He laughed.

G2Cronaca2.9.full: Tomorrow I start again from the beginning, at the estate. My aunt says that is where one always ends up.
G2Cronaca2.9.easy: Tomorrow I start again from the beginning, at the estate. My aunt says that is always where it ends.
G2Cronaca2.9.short: Tomorrow I start again at the estate. My aunt says it always ends there.

G2R3.2.full: Turn to **page 19** of the Village Chronicle, **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}): the town is watched, but not locked down.

G2R3.3.full: Turn to **page 21** of the Village Chronicle, **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}): the curfew.

G2R3.8.full: Lomax has closed his pharmacy, but still sells his salts at a counter in the General Store. The first player to send one of their pieces there,

G2R3.14.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Foundry,

G2R3.17.full: During the curfew the church stays open all night. The first player to send one of their pieces there,

G2R3.20.full: Christmas is long past, and there is no culprit. Ada Haskett has stopped searching the streets: now she searches the estate.
G2R3.20.easy: Christmas is long past, and there is no one to blame. Ada Haskett has stopped searching the streets: now she is searching the estate.
G2R3.20.short: Christmas has passed, and Ada Haskett now looks for the culprit at the estate.

round.G2R3.end.full: The Late Years of the Second Generation have ended.

G2Ricatto.2.full: A letter is waiting for you at the Bank, left at the counter by a boy who ran off at once. Inside, letters of every size, cut from newspapers, make up a single sentence: *I KNOW WHICH OF YOU GOES OUT AT NIGHT. LEAVE THE MONEY IN SAFE DEPOSIT BOX 14, OR THE INSPECTOR WILL KNOW TOO.* Box 14, says the cashier, is in the name of Pell's notary practice, which has not used it for years.
G2Ricatto.2.easy: At the Bank there is a letter for you, left at the counter by a boy who ran straight off. Inside, letters of every size cut from newspapers make up a single sentence: *I KNOW WHICH OF YOU GOES OUT AT NIGHT. LEAVE THE MONEY IN SAFE DEPOSIT BOX 14, OR THE INSPECTOR WILL KNOW TOO.* The cashier says box 14 belongs to the Pell's notary practice, but the office has not used it for years.
G2Ricatto.2.short: An anonymous letter: *I KNOW WHICH OF YOU GOES OUT AT NIGHT. LEAVE THE MONEY IN SAFE DEPOSIT BOX 14, OR THE INSPECTOR WILL KNOW TOO.* The box is the Pell office's.

G2Ricatto.4.full: You pay, and tell no one.

G2Ricatto.5.full: You take the letter to Ada Haskett.

G2Ricatto.7.full: You leave the money in box 14, in an envelope with no name. A week later you go back to check: the envelope is gone, and in its place is a handwritten note, in the backward-slanting hand: *Thank you. I shall bear it in mind.*
G2Ricatto.7.easy: You leave the money in box 14, in an unmarked envelope. A week later you go back to check. The envelope is gone, and in its place is a handwritten note, in the backward-slanting hand: *Thank you. I shall bear it in mind.*
G2Ricatto.7.short: You pay. A week later, in the box, a note slanting backwards: *Thank you. I shall bear it in mind.*

G2Ricatto.9.full: Ada reads the letter, turns it over, sniffs it and seals it in a police envelope. She has box 14 opened with a warrant: inside there is only dust, and an old empty pen case. "Someone knew you would come to me," she says. "Or hoped you wouldn't."
G2Ricatto.9.easy: Ada reads the letter, turns it over, sniffs it and seals it in a police envelope. She has box 14 opened with a warrant. Inside there is only dust, and an old empty pen case. "Someone knew you would come to me," she says. "Or hoped you wouldn't."
G2Ricatto.9.short: Ada has the box opened: just dust and an empty pen case. "Someone knew you would come to me. Or hoped not."

G2Ricatto.11.full: You tear it into eight pieces and drop it in the bank's wastepaper basket. Two days later, in the Gazette's gossip column, a riddle in verse appears about a family "that goes out by night and tears up its post by day". The town laughs for a week.
G2Ricatto.11.easy: You tear it into eight pieces and drop it in the bank's wastepaper basket. Two days later, in the Gazette's gossip column, there is a rhyming riddle about a family "that goes out by night and tears up its post by day". The town laughs for a week.
G2Ricatto.11.short: You tear it up. Two days later the Gazette prints a riddle about a family "that goes out by night and tears up its post by day".

G2Bastone.2.full: The foreman of the foundry is a huge man with burn-scarred arms and an archivist's memory. When you describe to him the silver handle of the stick found beside Lady Carew, he nods at once. "We cast it," he says. "Forty years ago, for the old man at the estate. One of a kind. That stick, the old man always carried it."
G2Bastone.2.easy: The foundry foreman is a huge man with burn-scarred arms and a memory like an archive. When you describe the silver handle of the stick found near Lady Carew, he nods at once. "We cast it," he says. "Forty years ago, for the old man at the estate. One of a kind. The old man always carried that stick."
G2Bastone.2.short: The foreman knows the stick's handle: "We cast it, for the old man at the estate. He always carried it."

G2Bastone.4.full: You ask him to testify that the stick has not been yours for thirty years.

G2Bastone.5.full: You ask him whether he ever cast a copy.

G2Bastone.6.full: The foreman thinks it over for a long time. Then he agrees, for a small fee and for the love of truth, in that order. Before Inspector Haskett he will swear that the stick belonged to the old man, vanished nearly thirty years ago, and that no one in the family has seen it since.
G2Bastone.6.easy: The foreman thinks for a long time. Then he agrees, for a small fee and for the love of truth, in that order. Before Inspector Haskett he will swear that the stick belonged to the old man, gone for nearly thirty years, and that no one in the family has seen it since.
G2Bastone.6.short: For a small fee he will swear to the Inspector that the stick was the old man's, and none of you has seen it since.

G2Bastone.7.full: Pay $2. The foreman will testify for the family.

G2Bastone.8.full: "A copy, no," says the foreman. "But three years ago a gentleman came to have the handle polished. With the whole stick. A short gentleman, in a black coat too large for him. He paid with a cheque." He laughs. "The cheque was good."
G2Bastone.8.easy: "No copy," says the foreman. "But three years ago a gentleman came to have the handle polished. With the whole stick. A small gentleman, in a black coat too big for him. He paid with a cheque." He laughs. "And the cheque was good."
G2Bastone.8.short: "Three years ago a small gentleman in a black coat had it polished. He paid by cheque. And it was good."

G2Ezra.2.full: On Silas Pell's grave there is a new headstone, of white marble, too big for a man who never liked to be noticed. Before it stands his son, Ezra Pell the notary: thin, dressed in black, with the eyes of a man who sleeps little. He greets you with a bow, as one greets a client. He is your family's notary now, and he has read the whole file.
G2Ezra.2.easy: On Silas Pell's grave there is a new headstone of white marble, too big for a man who did not like to be noticed. In front of it stands his son, Ezra Pell the notary: thin, dressed in black, with the eyes of someone who sleeps little. He greets you with a bow, the way one greets a client. He is your family's notary now, and he has read the whole file.
G2Ezra.2.short: At Silas's grave stands his son, Ezra Pell, thin and tired. He is your notary now, and has read the file.

G2Ezra.3.full: "My father was fond of you," he says. "In his way."

G2Ezra.4.full: Then, after a moment: "In his last years, though, he was afraid of you. Of one of you, at least. He never told me why."
G2Ezra.4.easy: Then, after a moment: "In his last years, though, he was afraid of you. Of one of you, at least. He never told me why."
G2Ezra.4.short: "In his last years he was afraid of one of you. He never told me why."

G2Ezra.6.full: You tell him about the salt and the cheques.

G2Ezra.7.full: You ask him about his father's cupboard.

G2Ezra.8.full: You leave a flower on Silas's grave, and go.

G2Ezra.9.full: Ezra listens without interrupting, with a strange, almost hungry attention: he asks you the colour of the salt in the glass, how many sips, how many hours it lasts. At the end he thanks you, shakes your hand and offers to keep the family's papers in his office, "safe, under lock and key". His fingers are cold.
G2Ezra.9.easy: Ezra listens without interrupting, with a strange, almost hungry attention. He asks you the colour of the salt in the glass, how many sips, how many hours it lasts. In the end he thanks you, shakes your hand and offers to keep the family's papers in his office, "safe, under lock and key". His fingers are cold.
G2Ezra.9.short: Ezra listens hungrily: colour, sips, hours. Then he offers to keep your papers "under lock and key". His fingers are cold.

G2Ezra.10.full: Gain 1VP. Ezra Pell the notary will remember your family.

G2Ezra.11.full: Ezra laughs, a short, nervous laugh. "The cupboard! I've never found the key. I had two locksmiths in, and neither of them could open it. My father kept his powders there, when he was young and wanted to be an apothecary." He strokes his waistcoat, where his father once kept the paper twist. "If I open it, you'll be the first to know."
G2Ezra.11.easy: Ezra laughs, a short, nervous laugh. "The cupboard! I have never found the key. I called in two locksmiths, and neither could open it. My father kept his powders there, when he was young and wanted to be an apothecary." He touches his waistcoat, where his father kept the little packet. "If I open it, you will be the first to know."
G2Ezra.11.short: "The cupboard? I never found the key. My father kept his powders there." He touches his waistcoat. "If I open it, you will be the first to know."

G2Ezra.13.full: You leave a posy of violets on the headstone. Ezra looks at it and turns pale. "Violets," he says. "Someone used to bring them to your grandfather too, every morning. My father told me about it." Then he collects himself, thanks you and walks you to the gate.
G2Ezra.13.easy: You leave a little bunch of violets on the headstone. Ezra looks at it and turns pale. "Violets," he says. "Someone used to bring them to your grandfather too, every morning. My father told me." Then he recovers, thanks you and walks you to the gate.
G2Ezra.13.short: You leave violets. Ezra turns pale: "Someone used to bring them to your grandfather every morning."

G2Ezra.14.full: Move back 1 space on the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track. Ezra Pell the notary will remember your family.

G2Lomax.2.full: Lomax has grown old now. He has closed his pharmacy and sells his salts at a counter at the back of the General Store, between the brooms and the paraffin lamps. His fingers are still stained yellow, and he has the same air of a man expecting bad news: the difference is that now he seems to know which.
G2Lomax.2.easy: Lomax is old now. He has closed his pharmacy and sells his salts from a counter at the back of the General Store, among the brooms and oil lamps. His fingers are still stained yellow, and he still looks like a man waiting for bad news. The difference is that now he seems to know which.
G2Lomax.2.short: Old Lomax sells his salts at the back of the General Store. He seems to await bad news, and to know which.

G2Lomax.3.full: He recognises you at once: you are from the family that grabbed him by the collar at the market, years ago. He does not say a word to you.
G2Lomax.3.easy: He recognises you at once: you are from the family that grabbed him by the collar at the market, years ago. He will not speak to you.
G2Lomax.3.short: He knows you: the family from the market. He will not speak to you.

G2Lomax.4.full: He recognises you at once. "Do you still have my page?" he asks quietly. "Keep it safe. One day you'll need it."
G2Lomax.4.easy: He recognises you at once. "Do you still have my page?" he asks quietly. "Keep it safe. One day you will need it."
G2Lomax.4.short: "Do you still have my page? Keep it safe. One day you will need it."

G2Lomax.7.full: You ask him what was in the first batch.

G2Lomax.8.full: Lomax wraps it with trembling hands. "It's the best," he says. "It's pure. That's the trouble." That evening, in the glass, the colour stops at the first red, as always.
G2Lomax.8.easy: Lomax wraps it for you with shaking hands. "It's the best," he says. "It's pure. And that's the trouble." That evening, in the glass, the colour stops at the first red, as always.
G2Lomax.8.short: "It's the best. It's pure. And that's the trouble." In the glass it stops at red, as always.

G2Lomax.10.full: Lomax calls the shopkeeper in a faint voice. The shopkeeper shows you to the door, politely, in front of all the customers. On the pavement, a lady recognises you and crosses herself.
G2Lomax.10.easy: Lomax calls the shopkeeper in a faint voice. The shopkeeper shows you to the door, politely, in front of all the customers. On the pavement a lady recognises you and crosses herself.
G2Lomax.10.short: Lomax calls the shopkeeper, who shows you out. Outside, a lady crosses herself.

G2Lomax.12.full: Lomax looks around, then leans towards you. His breath smells of mint and fear. "Grey," he whispers. "It was grey, the powder. A teaspoon for each phial. Don't ask me whose it was." Then he goes back to counting his boxes, and says nothing more.
G2Lomax.12.easy: Lomax looks around, then leans towards you. His breath smells of mint and fear. "Grey," he whispers. "The powder was grey. A teaspoon per phial. Don't ask me whose it was." Then he goes back to counting his boxes, and says nothing more.
G2Lomax.12.short: "Grey," Lomax whispers. "The powder was grey. A teaspoon per phial. Don't ask me whose it was."

G2Chiesa.3.full: The church is full of people who do not want to sleep at home: whole families in the pews, with blankets and lanterns, praying under their breath. The confessional is at the back, in the dark. You kneel. Behind the grille a tired voice says: "Go on."
G2Chiesa.3.easy: The church is full of people who do not want to sleep at home: whole families on the pews, with blankets and lanterns, praying softly. The confessional is at the back, in the dark. You kneel. Behind the grille a tired voice says: "Go on."
G2Chiesa.3.short: The church is full of people afraid to sleep at home. In the confessional, a tired voice: "Go on."

G2Chiesa.5.full: You confess to having drunk the salt.

G2Chiesa.6.full: You confess to something you did not do.

G2Chiesa.8.full: You tell everything, even what you do not remember. The priest is silent for a long time. Then, very quietly: "The other one came here too, last night. He confessed the same things, in the same order. In your voice." When you come out of the confessional, the other side of the grille is empty.
G2Chiesa.8.easy: You tell everything, even what you do not remember. The priest is silent for a long time. Then, very quietly: "The other one came here too, last night. He confessed the same things, in the same order. With your voice." When you leave the confessional, the other side of the grille is empty.
G2Chiesa.8.short: You tell everything. The priest whispers: "The other one came last night. He confessed the same things. With your voice."

G2Chiesa.9.full: Move back 2 spaces on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track and gain 1 {icon:Creepy_Icon}.

G2Chiesa.10.full: You confess an invented sin, small and plausible, to see what happens. "Liar," says the voice behind the grille, and laughs. It is not the priest's voice. When you draw back the curtain, the priest is only now arriving from the sacristy, stole in hand, to apologise for being late.
G2Chiesa.10.easy: You confess an invented sin, small and believable, to see what happens. "Liar," says the voice behind the grille, and laughs. It is not the priest's voice. When you open the curtain, the priest is only now coming from the sacristy, stole in hand, apologising for being late.
G2Chiesa.10.short: You confess a made-up sin. "Liar," the voice laughs. But the priest is only now arriving from the sacristy.

G2Chiesa.12.full: You say nothing. On the other side of the grille someone breathes softly, for a long time, then gets up and leaves. On the step of the confessional you find a cheque folded in four, payable to bearer, in the backward-slanting hand. It is alms. For you.
G2Chiesa.12.easy: You say nothing. On the other side of the grille someone breathes slowly, for a long time, then gets up and leaves. On the confessional step you find a cheque folded in four, payable to bearer, in the backward-slanting hand. It is alms. For you.
G2Chiesa.12.short: You stay silent. Someone breathes behind the grille, then leaves. On the step, a backward-slanting cheque: alms for you.

G2Accusa.2.full: Inspector Ada Haskett comes to the estate one winter evening, alone, with the broken stick wrapped in a handkerchief. She sits down in the library without taking off her coat and lays it on the table, between you.
G2Accusa.2.easy: One winter evening Inspector Ada Haskett comes to the estate, alone, with the broken stick wrapped in a handkerchief. She sits down in the library without taking off her coat and lays it on the table, between you.
G2Accusa.2.short: One evening Ada Haskett comes alone and lays the broken stick on the table between you.

G2Accusa.3.full: "I don't believe in ghosts," she says, "nor in men who never grow old. I believe in initials on handles and in muddy shoes. Umber is in this room. Either you tell me, or I choose."
G2Accusa.3.easy: "I don't believe in ghosts," she says, "nor in men who don't grow old. I believe in initials on handles and in muddy shoes. Umber is in this room. Either you tell me, or I choose."
G2Accusa.3.short: "I don't believe in ghosts. I believe in initials and mud. Umber is in this room. You tell me, or I choose."

G2Accusa.4.full: On the table, beside the stick, there is also the statement of the foundry foreman: the stick was the old man's, and no one in the family had seen it for nearly thirty years. Ada touches it with one finger, as if to see whether it is hot.
G2Accusa.4.easy: On the table, beside the stick, is the foundry foreman's statement too: the stick was the old man's, and no one in the family had seen it for nearly thirty years. Ada touches it with one finger, as if to see whether it is hot.
G2Accusa.4.short: Beside it lies the foreman's statement: the stick was the old man's. Ada touches it as if it burned.

G2Accusa.5.full: Then she adds, more quietly: "You helped me, and I don't forget it. If you're wrong, I won't be the one to make you pay."
G2Accusa.5.easy: Then she adds, more quietly: "You helped me, and I don't forget it. If you get it wrong, I won't be the one who makes you pay."
G2Accusa.5.short: "You helped me. If you get it wrong, I won't make you pay."

G2Accusa.6.full: Then she opens the file and lays on the table, in plain sight, the coins you gave her. "These," she says, "are already on record."
G2Accusa.6.easy: Then she opens the file and puts on the table, in plain view, the coins you gave her. "These," she says, "are already on record."
G2Accusa.6.short: Then she lays your coins on the table. "These are already on record."

G2Accusa.7.full: Each player secretly takes in hand as much money as they wish to offer the Inspector *to close the investigation without a name*, even nothing. When everyone is ready, reveal your offers together.

G2Accusa.9.full: Each player secretly points at another player (a finger on the table, on the count of three). Whoever gets the most fingers is accused *(in case of a tie, the Start Player decides)*.

G2Accusa.10.full: Click when you have chosen the accused...

G2Offerta.2.full: Is the total offer at least ${0}?

G2Offerta.3.full: Yes: the Inspector closes the investigation.

G2Offerta.4.full: No: the Inspector chooses for herself.

G2Verdetto.2.full: Ada Haskett counts the money twice, slips it into an envelope and writes on the envelope: *for police widows*. Then she closes the file, gets up and leaves without saying goodbye. The next day the Gazette writes that Lady Carew's murderer was a vagrant, drowned in the river.
G2Verdetto.2.easy: Ada Haskett counts the money twice, puts it in an envelope and writes on it: *for police widows*. Then she closes the file, stands and leaves without saying goodbye. The next day the Gazette reports that Lady Carew's murderer was a tramp, drowned in the river.
G2Verdetto.2.short: Ada puts the money in an envelope *for police widows* and leaves. The Gazette says the murderer was a drowned tramp.

G2Verdetto.3.full: No one in town believes it. They say the family from the estate bought the silence of the police; and people, when they cannot have a culprit, gladly make do with a suspicion.
G2Verdetto.3.easy: No one in town believes it. They say the family at the estate bought the police's silence. And people, when they cannot have someone to blame, are happy to settle for a suspicion.
G2Verdetto.3.short: No one believes it. They say you bought the police, and a suspicion is enough.

G2Verdetto.4.full: The offers go to the supply. The {icon:AngryMob_Icon} marker moves up 1 space.

G2Verdetto.5.full: The constables search the accused's room. In the wardrobe they find shoes caked with river mud; in the pocket of a black coat too tight for its owner, a bundle of signed cheques; under the mattress, the other half of the stick. The handwriting on the cheques slants backwards.
G2Verdetto.5.easy: The constables search the accused's room. In the wardrobe they find shoes caked with river mud. In the pocket of a black coat that is too tight they find a bundle of signed cheques. Under the mattress is the other half of the stick. The handwriting on the cheques slants backwards.
G2Verdetto.5.short: In the accused's room they find muddy shoes, backward-slanting cheques and the other half of the stick.

G2Verdetto.6.full: At the trial the accused swears to remember nothing, and everyone in court laughs. Everyone except Ada Haskett, who looks at them for a long time, the way one looks at someone telling the truth. That night, for the first time in thirty years, no one sees Umber in town.
G2Verdetto.6.easy: At the trial the accused swears they remember nothing, and everyone in court laughs. Everyone except Ada Haskett, who looks at them for a long time, the way one looks at someone telling the truth. That night, for the first time in thirty years, no one sees Umber in town.
G2Verdetto.6.short: At the trial the accused remembers nothing. All laugh but Ada. That night, for the first time in thirty years, no one sees Umber.

G2Verdetto.7.full: **The accused was the Heir in the Shadow.** They lose 5VP and take the **Loose Lips** Maladjustment that was set aside. The other players gain 2VP.

G2Verdetto.8.full: The constables search the accused's room and find nothing: no muddy shoes, no cheques, no other half of the stick. Ada Haskett takes them away all the same, because the town wants it; but the next morning she releases them for lack of evidence, and tells the Gazette that the investigation continues.
G2Verdetto.8.easy: The constables search the accused's room and find nothing: no muddy shoes, no cheques, no half of the stick. Ada Haskett takes them away anyway, because the town wants it. But the next morning she lets them go for lack of evidence, and tells the Gazette the investigation continues.
G2Verdetto.8.short: The accused's room holds nothing. Ada takes them in, but frees them next morning: the investigation goes on.

G2Verdetto.9.full: That night, while the family celebrates the return of the accused, someone at the end of the alley laughs.
G2Verdetto.9.easy: That night, while the family celebrates the homecoming, someone laughs at the end of the alley.
G2Verdetto.9.short: That night you celebrate. At the end of the alley, someone laughs.

G2Verdetto.10.full: **The accused was innocent.** They gain 3VP for the wrong they suffered.

G2Verdetto.11.full: The constables search the accused's room and find nothing: no muddy shoes, no cheques, no other half of the stick. They take them away all the same, because the town wants a culprit and Christmas is long past. The Jail has a free cell, with a window onto the alley.
G2Verdetto.11.easy: The constables search the accused's room and find nothing: no muddy shoes, no cheques, no half of the stick. They take them away anyway, because the town wants someone to blame and Christmas is long past. The Jail has a free cell, with a window onto the alley.
G2Verdetto.11.short: The accused's room holds nothing, but they take them anyway. Their cell looks onto the alley.

G2Verdetto.12.full: That night, while the accused looks at the stars between the bars, someone at the end of the alley laughs.
G2Verdetto.12.easy: That night, while the prisoner watches the stars between the bars, someone laughs at the end of the alley.
G2Verdetto.12.short: That night, at the end of the alley, someone laughs.

G2Boccette.2.full: The old man's six phials are empty: someone in the family has drunk or thrown away the last grain, and no one admits to it. They are still in the zinc box, under the loose board by the stove, with their broken seals and faded labels: *Lomax's Pharmacy – first batch*. At the bottom of the glass there remains a greyish film that will not come off even with boiling water.
G2Boccette.2.easy: The old man's six phials are empty: someone in the family drank or threw away the last grain, and no one admits it. They are still in the zinc box, under the loose board by the stove, with broken sealing wax and faded labels: *Lomax's Pharmacy – first batch*. On the glass at the bottom there is a greyish film that will not come off, even with boiling water.
G2Boccette.2.short: The six phials are empty, and no one admits emptying them. A grey film clings to the bottom.

G2Boccette.3.full: What do you do with the phials? *(Decide together.)*

G2Boccette.4.full: You keep them in the laboratory.

G2Boccette.5.full: You entrust them to Ezra Pell the notary.

G2Boccette.6.full: You throw them in the river.

G2Boccette.7.full: You put them back in the zinc box, and the box under the board. No one knows what use empty phials could be. No one has the heart to throw them away.
G2Boccette.7.easy: You put them back in the zinc box, and the box back under the board. No one knows what empty phials could be good for. But no one has the heart to throw them away.
G2Boccette.7.short: You put them back. They are useless, but no one can throw them away.

G2Boccette.9.full: Ezra Pell receives them in his office, examines them one by one against the light from the window and locks them in a glass-fronted cabinet, with a care that moves you. "They'll be safe," he says. "Safer than with you."
G2Boccette.9.easy: Ezra Pell receives them in his office, studies them one by one against the light of the window and locks them in a glass cabinet, with a care that moves you. "They will be safe," he says. "Safer than with you."
G2Boccette.9.short: You give them to Ezra Pell, who locks them away with great care. "Safer than with you."

G2Boccette.11.full: You throw them from the bridge, one at a time, on a moonless night. The river swallows them without a sound. A week later a fisherman fishes one out and sells it to the junk dealer as a keepsake of the old man from the estate.
G2Boccette.11.easy: You throw them off the bridge, one at a time, on a moonless night. The river swallows them without a sound. A week later a fisherman pulls one out and sells it to the junk dealer as a souvenir of the old man at the estate.
G2Boccette.11.short: You throw them in the river. A fisherman fishes one out and sells it to the junk dealer.

G2Chiusura.2.full: Lomax the chemist, now an old man, still sells the salt: white, fine, with the new label and the old price. But in the glass the colour no longer changes as it used to. It turns red and stops there. When people ask him why, old Lomax looks at the ground and says that today's salt is too pure.
G2Chiusura.2.easy: Lomax the chemist, now old, still sells the salt: white, fine, with a new label and the old price. But in the glass the colour no longer changes as it used to. It turns red and stops there. When people ask him why, old Lomax looks at the floor and says today's salt is too pure.
G2Chiusura.2.short: Lomax still sells the salt. But in the glass it stops at red: "Today's salt is too pure."

G2Chiusura.4.full: In the winter of 1895 an old man with no papers died in a rented room by the river: small, thin, in a black coat too large for him. They buried him in a pauper's grave. I was the only one at the funeral: I had read the file, and I knew who he was.
G2Chiusura.4.easy: In the winter of 1895, in a rented room near the river, an old man with no papers died: small, thin, in a black coat too big for him. They buried him in the common grave. I was the only one at the funeral. I had read the file, and I knew who he was.
G2Chiusura.4.short: In the winter of 1895 a nameless old man died by the river, small, in a black coat. I alone was at the funeral. I knew who he was.

G2Chiusura.5.full: That same winter, going through my father's papers, I finally found the key to the cupboard: it was sewn into the lining of his coat. I will not write here what I found inside. I will write only that since then I have slept little, and that the cupboard, now, is empty.
G2Chiusura.5.easy: That same winter, going through my father's papers, I finally found the key to the cupboard: it was sewn into the lining of his coat. I shall not write here what I found inside. I write only that since then I sleep little, and that the cupboard is now empty.
G2Chiusura.5.short: That winter I found the cupboard key, sewn into my father's coat. I shall not write what was inside. The cupboard is empty now.

G2Chiusura.6.full: I did not tell the family from the estate, although I had promised they would be the first to know. They had trusted me. It was the worst mistake of their lives, and the most useful of mine.
G2Chiusura.6.easy: I did not tell the family at the estate, though I had promised they would be the first to know. They had trusted me. It was the worst mistake of their lives, and the most useful of mine.
G2Chiusura.6.short: I did not tell the family, who trusted me. It was their worst mistake, and my most useful.

SaleG3Intro.2.full: **Note by Ezra Pell, notary, for the file – *1911.***

SaleG3Intro.3.full: The town has electric light, a tramway and two newspapers that hate each other: a liberal one, which blames everything on the rich, and a conservative one, which blames everything on the poor. On one thing they agree: Mr. Umber sells copies. On the hill, beside the asylum, an Institute of science has risen, all glass and brass, and its professors write to the papers that the estate's salt is a country superstition.
SaleG3Intro.3.easy: The town has electric light, trams and two newspapers that hate each other. One is liberal and blames everything on the rich. The other is conservative and blames everything on the poor. On one thing they agree: Mr. Umber sells copies. On the hill, near the asylum, a new Institute of Science has gone up, all glass and brass. Its professors write to the papers that the estate's salt is a country superstition.
SaleG3Intro.3.short: The town has electric light and two papers that hate each other, but Umber sells copies of both. The new Institute's professors call the salt a superstition.

SaleG3Intro.4.full: They are wrong, but not entirely. In recent years some young people of the town bought the new salt from Lomax, for a bet or out of despair, and drank it. The new salt works: the other one goes out, as always. But in the morning it does not come back. Two of them are in the asylum, laughing day and night; the third has not been seen since. I knew him. He was my neighbour's son, and always raised his hat to me.
SaleG3Intro.4.easy: They are wrong, but not entirely. In recent years some young people in town bought the new salt from Lomax, for a bet or out of despair, and drank it. The new salt works: the other one comes out, as always. But in the morning it does not go back. Two of them are in the asylum, laughing day and night. No one has seen the third again. I knew him. He was my neighbour's son, and he always raised his hat to me.
SaleG3Intro.4.short: They are wrong. Three young people drank the new salt: the other came out, but never went back. Two laugh in the asylum, the third has vanished.

SaleG3Intro.5.full: As for me, I am fifty-six, with a cough the doctors cannot cure. I sleep little, I write badly, I wear gloves even in summer because of an eczema on my hands. The practice runs on by force of habit, with the old clerk treating me like a sick son. I have decided to keep this file in order to the end. Whoever reads it after me will judge whether it was worth it.
SaleG3Intro.5.easy: As for me, I am fifty-six, with a cough the doctors cannot cure. I sleep little, write badly and wear gloves even in summer, because of eczema on my hands. The practice runs by itself, with the old clerk treating me like a sick son. I have decided to keep this file in order to the end. Whoever reads it after me will judge whether it was worth it.
SaleG3Intro.5.short: I am fifty-six, with a cough no one can cure. I sleep little, write badly, wear gloves even in summer for eczema. I shall keep this file in order to the end.

G3LetteraA.3.full: An envelope from Pell's practice, with your name written by hand, in writing so shaky that the postman had to ask twice for the address. Inside, a few lines. The notary begs you, "for the good of the family and in the name of the friendship that has always bound our families", to bring him something from the estate in secret, without telling anyone.
G3LetteraA.3.easy: An envelope has come from the Pell's notary practice, with your name handwritten so shakily that the postman had to ask the address twice. Inside are a few lines. The notary begs you, "for the good of the family and in the name of the friendship that has always bound our families", to bring him something from the estate in secret, without telling anyone.
G3LetteraA.3.short: A letter from Pell the notary, in a shaky hand. He asks you to bring him something from the estate in secret.

G3LetteraA.4.full: *A page of the old man's Journal, any page, as long as it is written in his night-time hand.*
G3LetteraA.4.easy: *A page of the old man's Journal, any page, as long as it is in his night-time hand.*
G3LetteraA.4.short: *A page of the Journal, in the night-time hand.*

G3LetteraA.5.full: *A pinch of the new salt you use in the laboratory, in a well-sealed paper.*
G3LetteraA.5.easy: *A pinch of the new salt you use in the laboratory, well wrapped in paper.*
G3LetteraA.5.short: *A pinch of the new salt, well wrapped.*

G3LetteraA.6.full: *A copy of the key to your gate, which I shall return to you within the week.*
G3LetteraA.6.easy: *A copy of the key to your gate, which I shall return within the week.*
G3LetteraA.6.short: *A copy of the gate key, for a week.*

G3LetteraA.7.full: *A hair of the old man's, from the silver brush that should still be on his dresser.*
G3LetteraA.7.easy: *A hair of the old man's, from the silver brush that should still be on his chest of drawers.*
G3LetteraA.7.short: *A hair of the old man's, from his silver brush.*

G3LetteraA.9.full: You bring the notary what he asks for.

G3LetteraA.11.full: You show the letter to the others.

G3LetteraA.12.full: You take it to his office the next day, in an unmarked envelope. The clerk takes it without looking you in the face. Two days later a note of thanks arrives, and some money, "for your trouble".
G3LetteraA.12.easy: The next day you take it to the office, in an unmarked envelope. The clerk takes it without looking you in the face. Two days later a thank-you note arrives, with some money, "for your trouble".
G3LetteraA.12.short: You take it to the office. Two days later come thanks and money, "for your trouble".

G3LetteraA.13.full: Gain $3. Do not tell the others what you did.

G3LetteraA.14.full: You put the letter in a drawer and do not answer. The notary does not insist. But the shaky handwriting, for some reason, comes back to you every time you open the drawer.
G3LetteraA.14.easy: You put the letter in a drawer and do not reply. The notary does not insist. But that shaky handwriting, who knows why, comes back to you every time you open the drawer.
G3LetteraA.14.short: You do not reply. But that shaky hand comes back to you every time you open the drawer.

G3LetteraA.16.full: You show the letter to the others at dinner, and read it aloud. Someone laughs: the old notary is losing his mind. Someone else does not laugh at all, and wants to know whether the others have received one too.
G3LetteraA.16.easy: At dinner you show the letter to the others and read it aloud. Someone laughs: the old notary is losing his mind. Someone else does not laugh at all, and wants to know whether the others have received one too.
G3LetteraA.16.short: You read it at dinner. Someone laughs. Someone else does not, and asks if the others got one too.

G3LetteraA.17.full: Read the letter aloud to the other players. Gain 1VP.

G3LetteraFine.2.full: At breakfast no one speaks of letters. The tram passes the gate at eight o'clock sharp, as every morning, and the liberal paper's reporter is already posted across the street, notebook in hand.
G3LetteraFine.2.easy: At breakfast no one mentions letters. The tram passes the gate at eight o'clock sharp, as it does every morning. The reporter from the liberal paper is already waiting across the street, notebook in hand.
G3LetteraFine.2.short: At breakfast no one mentions letters. Outside, the reporter waits with his notebook.

G3Rivelazione.2.full: Inspector Ada Haskett, before retiring, had the handwriting examination redone on every cheque of the last twenty years. The result lies on the library table, in a police envelope: not one was written by a member of the family. None of you was Umber, nor ever has been.
G3Rivelazione.2.easy: Before retiring, Inspector Ada Haskett had all the cheques of the last twenty years examined again. The result is on the library table, in a police envelope: none of them was written by anyone in the family. None of you was Umber, and none of you ever has been.
G3Rivelazione.2.short: Ada Haskett's new report says none of the cheques was written by you. None of you has ever been Umber.

G3Rivelazione.3.full: And yet the cheques keep coming, with your names. The slanting hand is always the same, the old man's: only wearier, slower, like the hand of a man growing old. Who signs them, then?
G3Rivelazione.3.easy: And yet the cheques keep coming, with your names. The slanting hand is always the same, the old man's. Only it is more tired and slower, like the hand of a man growing old. So who is signing them?
G3Rivelazione.3.short: Yet the cheques still come, in the old man's hand, only wearier. Who signs them?

G3Rivelazione.5.full: The Heir in the Shadow died in prison many years ago, remembering nothing, and the town celebrated. But blood cannot be arrested. No one in the family says it aloud, yet everyone has noticed: when the youngest write in a hurry, their hand begins to slant backwards.
G3Rivelazione.5.easy: The Heir in the Shadow died in prison many years ago, remembering nothing, and the town celebrated. But blood does not stop. No one in the family says it aloud, but everyone has noticed: when the youngest write in a hurry, their hand begins to slant backwards.
G3Rivelazione.5.short: The Heir in the Shadow died in prison. But when the youngest write fast, their hand slants backwards.

G3Rivelazione.7.full: One evening at dinner, the one who carries the blood of the Heir in the Shadow puts down their knife and fork and tells everything: the nights, the muddy shoes, the cheques, the stick broken in the alley. No one interrupts. At the end someone pours a drink for everyone, and dinner goes on. There is nothing left to hide: Umber runs in the family, like the silver and the debts.
G3Rivelazione.7.easy: One evening at dinner, whoever carries the blood of the Heir in the Shadow puts down their knife and fork and tells everything: the nights, the muddy shoes, the cheques, the broken stick in the alley. No one interrupts. At the end someone pours everyone a drink, and dinner goes on. There is nothing left to hide: Umber is family, like the silver and the debts.
G3Rivelazione.7.short: At dinner the one with the Heir in the Shadow's blood tells all. No one interrupts. Umber is family, like the silver and the debts.

G3Rivelazione.8.full: **{0}** was the Heir in the Shadow: they gain 3VP. In the final vote, their vote counts double.

G3Rivelazione.13.full: From the **Fear of the Unknown** Scenario Box take the **3 Collaborative Experiments** and the **Collaboration tokens** {icon:S2_CollaborativeToken}: they are **the antidote**. Place the Experiments face up next to the board, available to everyone.

G3Rivelazione.14.full: The family still has the page of Lomax's ledger bought at the market so many years ago: it is a step forward. Return one of the Collaborative Experiments to the box, your choice: two are enough for the antidote.

G3Cappotto.2.full: In the attic, in a trunk tied with string, there is a black coat. It is too large for a small man and too short for a tall one; its pockets are worn, a horn button has been replaced with a bone one and, in the lining, there is a dark stain nobody wants to smell. No one knows who put it there. Everyone knows whose it is.
G3Cappotto.2.easy: In the attic, in a trunk tied with string, there is a black coat. It is too wide for a small man and too short for a tall one. The pockets are worn, a horn button has been replaced with a bone one and, in the lining, there is a dark stain no one wants to sniff. No one knows who put it there. Everyone knows whose it is.
G3Cappotto.2.short: In the attic is a black coat with a dark stain in the lining. No one knows who put it there. Everyone knows whose it is.

G3Cappotto.3.full: What do you do with the coat? *(Decide together.)*

G3Cappotto.4.full: You burn it in the garden.

G3Cappotto.5.full: You hang it in the hall, where it can be seen.

G3Cappotto.6.full: You give it to the theatre company.

G3Cappotto.7.full: The coat burns badly, with a thick, greasy black smoke that smells of tobacco and acid. The neighbours, from their windows, see the bonfire and talk of it for days: the family from the estate is burning the evidence.
G3Cappotto.7.easy: The coat burns badly, with thick black smoke that smells of tobacco and acid. From their windows the neighbours see the fire and talk about it for days: the family at the estate is burning the evidence.
G3Cappotto.7.short: You burn it. The neighbours say you are burning the evidence.

G3Cappotto.9.full: You hang it on the hall coat stand, beside your own. Visitors notice it at once, and no one dares ask. Some mornings it seems to have moved one hook along. Some mornings its sleeves are wet.
G3Cappotto.9.easy: You hang it on the hall coat stand, next to your own. Visitors notice it at once, and no one dares ask. Some mornings it seems to have moved one hook along. Some mornings its sleeves are wet.
G3Cappotto.9.short: You hang it in the hall. Some mornings it has moved a hook, or its sleeves are wet.

G3Cappotto.11.full: The company that plays *The Doctor and His Double* accepts it with delight: it is the perfect costume. From that evening the actor who plays Umber wears it on stage, and swears he feels good in it. Too good.
G3Cappotto.11.easy: The company performing *The Doctor and His Double* takes it gladly: it is the perfect costume. From that evening the actor who plays Umber wears it on stage, and swears he feels good in it. Too good.
G3Cappotto.11.short: You give it to the players. The actor who plays Umber feels good in it. Too good.

G3R1.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **A Time of War** section ({icon:S3_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 19**.

G3R1.10.full: Your great-grandfather's six empty phials are still in the laboratory. When your Self takes an action at the Estate,

G3R1.15.full: {icon:Storybook} **Two Newspapers – The Morning Liberal, Conservative Report**

G3R1.16.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to The Morning Liberal or the Conservative Report,

G3R1.19.full: When one of your pieces visits the Farmer's Market, you may pay $1 and look at yourself in a mirror:

G3R1.22.full: The town's two newspapers are fighting over Umber. For the liberal one he is a rich man amusing himself at the expense of the poor; for the conservative one, a poor man dressed up as a rich one. Both send a reporter to the estate, every morning.
G3R1.22.easy: The town's two papers fight over Umber. For the liberal paper he is a rich man amusing himself at the expense of the poor. For the conservative one he is a poor man dressed up as a rich one. Both send a reporter to the estate, every morning.
G3R1.22.short: One paper says Umber is rich, the other poor. Both send a reporter to the estate.

round.G3R1.end.full: The Early Years of the Third Generation have ended.

VociG3.2.full: When your Self takes an action at the Estate, you may drink the chemist's new salt:

VociG3.5.full: When the players complete one of the Collaborative Experiments,

G3Antidoto.2.full: The third experiment succeeds at dawn, after a whole night of broken glass and matches. In the glass, at last, the colour changes as it used to: red, then deep violet, then the green of a pond. Then, slowly, it turns as clear as water. It is not the old man's salt: it is its opposite. Whoever drinks it comes back as one, for ever.
G3Antidoto.2.easy: The third experiment succeeds at dawn, after a whole night of broken glass and matches. In the glass, at last, the colour changes as it used to: red, then dark violet, then pond green. Then, slowly, it turns clear as water. It is not the old man's salt: it is its opposite. Whoever drinks it becomes one person again, for ever.
G3Antidoto.2.short: At dawn it works: red, violet, green, then clear. It is the salt's opposite. Whoever drinks it is one person again, for ever.

G3Antidoto.3.full: It remains to be seen whether it really works. Someone has to taste it first.

G3Antidoto.5.full: You taste it yourself, since you completed the experiment.

G3Antidoto.6.full: You try it on a laboratory rat.

G3Antidoto.7.full: You take it to the son of the woman in black.

G3Antidoto.8.full: A step forward. In the glass the colour reaches violet and stops there, stubbornly, as if waiting for something. One ingredient is still missing, and none of your books can say which: the impurity that was in the first batch, and that no one ever wrote down.
G3Antidoto.8.easy: A step forward. In the glass the colour reaches violet and stops there, stubbornly, as if waiting for something. One ingredient is still missing, and none of your books says which: the impurity that was in the first batch, which no one ever wrote down.
G3Antidoto.8.short: It reaches violet, and stops. The first batch's impurity is missing, and no one ever wrote it down.

G3Antidoto.9.full: Someone in the family remembers old Lomax's words at the General Store: *grey, it was grey*. The problem is not knowing what colour it was. It is knowing where to find it.
G3Antidoto.9.easy: Someone in the family remembers old Lomax's words at the General Store: *grey, it was grey*. The problem is not knowing its colour. It is knowing where to find it.
G3Antidoto.9.short: *Grey, it was grey*, said Lomax. But where to find it?

G3Antidoto.11.full: You drink it in one gulp. It tastes of nothing, like water. For an hour nothing happens; then you sit down, grow sleepy, and wake the next morning with a strange silence in your head, like when the rain stops. You look in the mirror. There is only one face.
G3Antidoto.11.easy: You drink it in one gulp. It tastes of nothing, like water. For an hour nothing happens. Then you sit down, grow sleepy, and wake the next morning with a strange silence in your head, like when the rain stops. You look in the mirror. There is only one face.
G3Antidoto.11.short: You drink it. You fall asleep, and wake with silence in your head. In the mirror there is one face.

G3Antidoto.12.full: Move back 2 spaces on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track and gain 1VP.

G3Antidoto.13.full: The rat drinks, washes its whiskers and falls asleep. The next morning it is alive, alert and perfectly normal. It is also, for the first time since it was caged, entirely uninterested in escaping. You do not know whether that is good news.
G3Antidoto.13.easy: The mouse drinks, washes its whiskers and falls asleep. The next morning it is alive, awake and perfectly normal. It is also, for the first time since it was caged, not interested in escaping at all. You are not sure that is good news.
G3Antidoto.13.short: The mouse drinks and sleeps. Next morning it is normal, and no longer wants to escape. Good news?

G3Antidoto.15.full: At the asylum, the son of the woman in black drinks the glass without asking questions, laughing. He stops laughing halfway through the afternoon. In the evening he asks for his mother, in his own voice, and she comes running, in her dressing gown, through the rain.
G3Antidoto.15.easy: At the asylum, the son of the woman in black drinks the glass without asking anything, laughing. By mid-afternoon he stops laughing. In the evening he asks for his mother, in his own voice, and she comes running, in her dressing gown, through the rain.
G3Antidoto.15.short: The son of the woman in black drinks, and stops laughing. That evening he asks for his mother, in his own voice.

G3Madre.2.full: In the new church, all stucco and gold, a woman in black lights one candle after another before the altar, until the sexton tells her that is enough. Her son is one of the boys of the new salt: two years ago he drank it for a bet, and since then he has lived in the gentlefolk's ward, laughing.
G3Madre.2.easy: In the new church, all stucco and gold, a woman in black lights one candle after another before the altar, until the sexton tells her that is enough. Her son is one of the new-salt boys. Two years ago he drank it for a bet, and since then he has lived in the gentlefolk's ward, laughing.
G3Madre.2.short: In church a woman in black lights candles. Her son drank the new salt for a bet, and has laughed in the asylum ever since.

G3Madre.3.full: She recognises you: the whole town knows the family from the estate. She does not accuse you. She only asks, in the voice of someone who has already asked everyone, whether there is a way to bring him back.
G3Madre.3.easy: She recognises you: the whole town knows the family at the estate. She does not accuse you. She only asks, in the voice of someone who has already asked everyone, whether there is a way to bring him back.
G3Madre.3.short: She knows you, but does not accuse you. She only asks if there is a way to bring him back.

G3Madre.5.full: You promise her you will find an antidote.

G3Madre.6.full: You give her $2 for her son's care.

G3Madre.7.full: You tell her the truth: there is no way.

G3Madre.8.full: The woman takes your hand in both of hers and squeezes it hard, without a word. She leaves the church standing straighter than when she came in. You stay there, before the candles, wondering how many promises this family has made in fifty years, and how many it has kept.
G3Madre.8.easy: The woman takes your hand in hers and squeezes it hard, without a word. She leaves the church standing straighter than when she came in. You stay there, before the candles, wondering how many promises this family has made in fifty years, and how many it has kept.
G3Madre.8.short: She squeezes your hand and leaves standing straighter. You wonder how many promises your family has kept.

G3Madre.9.full: Gain 1VP. If the antidote is ever ready, she will remember.

G3Madre.10.full: The woman takes the money and thanks you, loudly, so that everyone can hear. Soon the town is saying that the family from the estate pays for the care of the salt boys. Some see it as an admission of guilt. Most, for once, as a kindness.
G3Madre.10.easy: The woman takes the money and thanks you loudly, so that everyone hears. Soon the town is saying the family at the estate pays for the new-salt boys' care. Some see it as an admission of guilt. Most, for once, see a kindness.
G3Madre.10.short: She takes the money and thanks you aloud. The town says you pay for the salt boys' care: guilt to some, kindness to most.

G3Madre.12.full: You tell her gently, in the simplest words you can find. She nods, as if she knew already. Then she tells you about her son: that he does not sleep, does not eat, writes letters with his left hand and signs them with a name that is not his. She tells you everything, for a whole hour, and you listen.
G3Madre.12.easy: You tell her gently, in the simplest words you can find. She nods, as if she already knew. Then she tells you about her son: he does not sleep, does not eat, writes letters with his left hand and signs them with a name that is not his. She tells you everything, for a whole hour, and you listen.
G3Madre.12.short: You tell her the truth. She already knew. Then she talks of her son for an hour, and you listen.

G3Giornali.2.full: The offices of the two newspapers face each other across the same square, and their editors have not spoken in twenty years. Both of them, hearing you are in the square, send a boy out to you with a visiting card. Both offer you the same thing: the front page, an exclusive interview about the family and about Umber, and whichever version of events you prefer.
G3Giornali.2.easy: The two papers' offices face each other across the same square, and their editors have not spoken in twenty years. As soon as they hear you are in the square, both send a boy to you with a visiting card. And both offer you the same thing: the front page, an exclusive interview about the family and Umber, and the facts told the way you prefer.
G3Giornali.2.short: Both papers offer you the front page: an interview about Umber, told the way you like.

G3Giornali.4.full: You speak to the liberal paper.

G3Giornali.5.full: You speak to the conservative paper.

G3Giornali.6.full: You sell the true story to both.

G3Giornali.7.full: The liberal paper writes that Umber is a bored rich man, perhaps a professor at the Institute, who enjoys frightening the poor. The conservative paper replies that the liberal paper is in the pay of the estate. For a week the town argues about the newspapers, and no one looks your way.
G3Giornali.7.easy: The liberal paper writes that Umber is a bored rich man, perhaps a professor at the Institute, who enjoys frightening the poor. The conservative paper replies that the liberal paper is paid by the estate. For a week the town argues over the papers, and no one looks your way.
G3Giornali.7.short: The liberal paper calls Umber a bored rich man. The other says it is paid by you. For a week no one looks your way.

G3Giornali.9.full: The conservative paper writes that Umber is a poor man dressed up as a gentleman, one of the many who sleep in the lodging houses by the station. The next night the police raid the lodging houses. None of those they arrest is Umber. The estate, for a while, has peace.
G3Giornali.9.easy: The conservative paper writes that Umber is a poor man dressed as a gentleman, one of the many who sleep in the lodging houses by the station. The next night the police raid the lodging houses. None of those arrested is Umber. For a while the estate has peace.
G3Giornali.9.short: The conservative paper says Umber is poor. The police raid the lodging houses. For a while you have peace.

G3Giornali.10.full: Gain 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}: it is not a pleasant peace.

G3Giornali.11.full: You tell the true story twice, to two different reporters, and get paid twice. The next day both papers come out with the same headline, for the first time in their history: *THE SALT OF THE ESTATE*. The town talks of nothing else. On the estate's door, in the morning, someone has chalked a little man in a black coat.

In the morning, on the estate door, someone has drawn in chalk a little man in a black coat.

G3Specchi.3.full: At the market there is a new stall, covered in mirrors of every size: pocket mirrors, dressing-table mirrors, wall mirrors, with gilt frames and frames of rough wood. The seller has a white beard and a glass eye. "True mirrors," he says. "They show what's there." You pick one at random and look into it.

The seller has a white beard and a glass eye. "True mirrors," he says. "They show what is there." You pick one at random and look into it.
G3Specchi.3.short: At the market a man with a glass eye sells "true mirrors, that show what is there". You look into one.

G3Specchi.4.full: You see yourself old, much older than now, with the eyes of the portrait in the estate library. The seller nods, satisfied. "You look like someone," he says. "Everyone looks like someone."
G3Specchi.4.easy: You see yourself old, much older than now, with the eyes of the portrait in the estate library. The seller nods, pleased. "You look like someone," he says. "Everyone looks like someone."
G3Specchi.4.short: You see yourself old, with the eyes of the library portrait. "Everyone looks like someone," says the seller.

G3Specchi.6.full: There is nothing in the mirror: the market behind you, the people, the stall, but not you. The seller gives you back your coin without a word, and turns his back on you.
G3Specchi.6.easy: There is nothing in the mirror: the market behind you, the people, the stall, but not you. The seller gives you back your coin without a word and turns his back on you.
G3Specchi.6.short: The mirror shows everything but you. The seller returns your coin and turns away.

G3Specchi.8.full: Behind you, in the mirror, there is a little man in a black coat, waving at you. You turn round: no one. When you look back into the mirror, the man is further away, and waves again, the way one waves to someone leaving.
G3Specchi.8.easy: Behind you, in the mirror, is a little man in a black coat, waving at you. You turn round: no one. When you look in the mirror again, the man is farther away, and waves again, the way you wave to someone leaving.
G3Specchi.8.short: In the mirror, behind you, a little man in black waves. You turn: no one. He is farther now, and waves again.

G3Specchi.10.full: Behind you, in the mirror, stands Ezra Pell the notary, hat in hand, smiling. You turn to greet him: no one. The seller looks at the mirror, then at you, then at the mirror again, and covers the stall with a cloth. "That's enough for today," he says.
G3Specchi.10.easy: Behind you, in the mirror, stands Ezra Pell the notary, hat in hand, smiling. You turn to greet him: no one. The seller looks at the mirror, then at you, then at the mirror again, and covers the stall with a cloth. "That's enough for today," he says.

G3Archivio.2.full: Ezra Pell the notary has donated his father's archive to the Library: forty years of deeds, wills and correspondence, in a hundred cardboard boxes, carefully catalogued. The librarian is immensely proud of it. Only one box is missing, number 61, the one for the year 1861. The notary, she says, kept it for himself, "for family reasons".
G3Archivio.2.easy: Ezra Pell the notary has given the Library his father's archive: forty years of deeds, wills and letters, in a hundred cardboard boxes, carefully catalogued. The librarian is very proud of it. Only one box is missing, number 61, for the year 1861. The notary, she says, kept it, "for family reasons".
G3Archivio.2.short: Ezra Pell gave the Library his father's archive. Only box 61, for 1861, is missing: he kept it.

G3Archivio.4.full: You read Silas Pell's correspondence with the old man.

G3Archivio.5.full: You ask the librarian to write to the notary about box 61.

G3Archivio.6.full: The old man's letters to Silas are short, affectionate, full of formulas and jokes. The last ones, from 1860, are different: shorter, more nervous, in a hand that is beginning to slant. The very last says only: *Forgive me for the cupboard. I could not ask you: you would have said no.* Silas never replied. Or the reply is in box 61.
G3Archivio.6.easy: The old man's letters to Silas are short, fond, full of formulas and jokes. The last ones, from 1860, are different: shorter, more nervous, in handwriting that is starting to slant. The very last says only: *Forgive me for the cupboard. I could not ask you: you would have said no.* Silas never replied. Or the reply is in box 61.
G3Archivio.6.short: The old man's last letter to Silas, from 1860, says: *Forgive me for the cupboard. I could not ask you: you would have said no.* The reply, if any, is in box 61.

G3Archivio.8.full: The librarian writes. The notary replies by return of post, in handwriting so shaky that the librarian has to read it with a magnifying glass: box 61 was destroyed in a small fire in his office, many years ago. The librarian says she is sorry. You wonder why a fire should choose a single box.
