G3Archivio.8.short: The notary replies, in a shaking hand, that box 61 burned years ago. Just one box?

G3Boccette.2.full: Your great-grandfather's six phials are still in the zinc box, under the loose board by the stove: broken seals, faded labels, *Lomax's Pharmacy – first batch*. At the bottom of the glass remains the same greyish film as ever. No one in the family has ever had the courage to scrape it off.
G3Boccette.2.easy: Your great-grandfather's six phials are still in the zinc box, under the loose board by the stove: broken sealing wax, faded labels, *Lomax's Pharmacy – first batch*. On the glass at the bottom is the same greyish film as ever. No one in the family has ever had the courage to scrape it off.
G3Boccette.2.short: Your great-grandfather's six phials are still under the board. The grey film still clings to the bottom.

G3Boccette.4.full: You scrape the film from the bottom of the phials.

G3Boccette.5.full: You sell them to the Institute, for $3.

G3Boccette.6.full: With a needle and a great deal of patience you gather, from all six, a pinch of grey powder, so little it fits on the tip of a knife. In the glass, with the new salt, the colour reaches violet, hesitates, and for an instant turns green.
G3Boccette.6.easy: With a needle and great patience you gather from all six a pinch of grey powder, so little it fits on the tip of a knife. In the glass, with the new salt, the colour reaches violet, hesitates, and for an instant turns green.
G3Boccette.6.short: You scrape out a pinch of grey powder. With the new salt the colour reaches violet, and for a moment turns green.

G3Boccette.7.full: The antidote takes a step forward: return one of the Collaborative Experiments not yet completed to the box.

G3Boccette.9.full: The rector of the Institute buys them without haggling, and displays them in a case in the main corridor, with a handwritten card: *The original phials.* The students pass them every day. Someone, at night, leaves a violet there.
G3Boccette.9.easy: The Institute's rector buys them without haggling, and puts them in a display case in the main corridor, with a handwritten card: *The original phials.* The students walk past them every day. At night, someone leaves a violet there.
G3Boccette.9.short: You sell them to the Institute, which displays them. At night someone leaves a violet there.

G3Patto.2.full: At the land registry, in the town hall, the clerk shows you with some embarrassment a deed of purchase just filed. Someone has bought the strip of land along the alley behind the estate, paying with a cheque. The cheque is genuine: it is signed by one of your grandparents, in 1877, in their upright hand. The amount and the payee's name, however, were written last week, in the backward-slanting hand.
G3Patto.2.easy: At the land registry, in the town hall, the clerk shows you with embarrassment a deed of purchase just filed. Someone has bought the strip of land along the alley behind the estate, and paid with a cheque. The cheque is genuine: it is signed by one of your grandparents, in 1877, in their upright hand. But the amount and the payee's name were written last week, in the backward-slanting hand.
G3Patto.2.short: Someone bought the alley with a cheque one of your grandparents signed in 1877. The amount and name, though, are from last week, slanting backwards.

G3Patto.4.full: You honour the cheque: the signature is family.

G3Patto.5.full: You report it as a forgery.

G3Patto.6.full: You pay, and the alley, from today, is the property of one Mr. Umber, by due notarial deed. It was drawn up, you notice, by Pell's practice. The notary charged no fee.
G3Patto.6.easy: You pay, and from today the alley belongs to a certain Mr. Umber, with a proper notarial deed. It was drawn up, you notice, by the Pell office. And the notary charged no fee.
G3Patto.6.short: You pay. The alley now belongs to Mr. Umber, by a deed from the Pell office. Free of charge.

G3Patto.8.full: The judge finds in your favour, after a month of hearings. The signature is genuine, but the cheque is not valid: the signatory has been dead for thirty years. The town, however, has followed the whole case, and now knows that an heir of the estate, in 1877, signed a blank cheque to Mr. Umber.
G3Patto.8.easy: After a month of hearings the judge finds in your favour. The signature is genuine, but the cheque is void: the signer has been dead for thirty years. But the town followed the whole trial, and now it knows that in 1877 an heir of the estate signed a blank cheque to Mr. Umber.
G3Patto.8.short: You win the case. But now the whole town knows that in 1877 one of your grandparents signed Umber a blank cheque.

G3Fabbro.2.full: The blacksmith is an old man whose arms are still strong and whose tongue is still loose: forty years ago he was the apprentice, the one with the toothless key. He remembers the little gentleman in the black coat very well. "Paid with cheques," he says. "Always good ones."
G3Fabbro.2.easy: The blacksmith is an old man with arms still strong and a tongue still loose: forty years ago he was the apprentice, the one with the toothless key. He remembers the little gentleman in the black coat perfectly. "He paid with cheques," he says. "Always good."
G3Fabbro.2.short: The blacksmith was the apprentice of the toothless key. He remembers the little gentleman in black: "Paid by cheque. Always good."

G3Fabbro.3.full: Then he takes a closer look at you. "You're from the estate. I made a copy of that key for your family, years ago. And another one, last year."
G3Fabbro.3.easy: Then he looks at you more closely. "You're from the estate. I made a copy of that key for your family, years ago. And another one last year."
G3Fabbro.3.short: "You're from the estate. I made you a copy years ago. And another last year."

G3Fabbro.4.full: Then he lowers his voice. "I kept the mould, you know. And last year it came in handy."
G3Fabbro.4.easy: Then he lowers his voice. "I kept the mould, you know. And last year it came in handy."
G3Fabbro.4.short: "I kept the mould. And last year it came in handy."

G3Fabbro.6.full: You pay $2 for him to tell you who the last key was for.

G3Fabbro.7.full: You buy the mould from him, for $3.

G3Fabbro.8.full: The blacksmith pockets the coins and scratches his beard. "An elderly gentleman, distinguished, wearing gloves," he says. "Never took his gloves off. Paid in cash, this time, and wanted a receipt. The receipt had the stamp of a practice on it."
G3Fabbro.8.easy: The blacksmith pockets the coins and scratches his beard. "An elderly gentleman, distinguished, with gloves," he says. "Never took his gloves off. This time he paid cash, and wanted a receipt. The receipt had an office stamp on it."
G3Fabbro.8.short: "An elderly gentleman in gloves he never took off. Paid cash. The receipt had an office stamp."

G3Fabbro.10.full: The blacksmith sells it to you with some regret, wrapped in a greasy cloth. It is a small block of plaster bearing the imprint of a toothless key with an eye-shaped head. At home you put it on the mantelpiece. The next morning it is cracked, as if someone had squeezed it too hard.
G3Fabbro.10.easy: The blacksmith sells it to you somewhat reluctantly, wrapped in an oily cloth. It is a block of plaster with the print of a toothless key with an eye-shaped head. At home you put it on the mantelpiece. The next morning it is cracked, as if someone had squeezed it too hard.
G3Fabbro.10.short: You buy the key's mould. The next morning it is cracked, as if someone had squeezed it too hard.

G3Statua.2.full: For the fiftieth anniversary of the laying of the asylum's foundation stone, the town council has decided to honour "the benefactors of the town's science", and in the Foundry a bronze statue of the old man from the estate is being cast: tall, distinguished, the Journal under his arm, as in the portrait. The foreman shows you the mould with pride. The committee, he says, paid with a very generous anonymous donation.
G3Statua.2.easy: For the asylum's fiftieth anniversary, the town council has decided to honour "the benefactors of the town's science". At the Foundry a bronze statue of the old man of the estate is being cast: tall, distinguished, with the Journal under his arm, as in the portrait. The foreman proudly shows you the mould. He says the committee paid with a very generous anonymous donation.
G3Statua.2.short: The Foundry is casting a statue of the old man, tall and distinguished as in the portrait. An anonymous donor paid for it.

G3Statua.5.full: You ask them to change the statue's face.

G3Statua.6.full: You sabotage the mould, at night.

G3Statua.7.full: The family's name is engraved on the pedestal, beneath the old man's, in smaller letters. At the unveiling the mayor gives a speech on progress, and the band plays. The statue gazes sternly over the square. At night, someone puts a black hat on its head.
G3Statua.7.easy: The family's name is carved on the pedestal, under the old man's, in smaller letters. At the unveiling the mayor makes a speech about progress, and the band plays. The statue looks sternly over the square. At night someone puts a black hat on its head.
G3Statua.7.short: Your name goes on the pedestal. The band plays at the unveiling. At night someone puts a black hat on the statue.

G3Statua.9.full: The foreman looks at you as if you were mad, but for a tip he remakes the head. The new face is that of an ordinary man, ageless, expressionless. The committee does not notice. Nor does the town. Only Pell the notary, at the unveiling, stops before the statue and says quietly: "That's a better likeness."
G3Statua.9.easy: The foreman looks at you as if you were mad, but for a tip he redoes the head. The new face is that of an ordinary man, ageless and expressionless. The committee does not notice, nor does the town. Only Pell the notary, at the unveiling, stops before the statue and says quietly: "That's a better likeness."
G3Statua.9.short: The statue now has an ordinary face. No one notices but Pell the notary: "That's a better likeness."

G3Statua.11.full: At night you get into the foundry and pour a bucket of water into the still-hot mould. The bronze cracks with the sound of a broken bell. At dawn the statue has a split running across its face, from forehead to chin, and the town talks of nothing else. The police open a file.
G3Statua.11.easy: At night you get into the foundry and pour a bucket of water into the still-hot mould. The bronze cracks with the sound of a broken bell. At dawn the statue has a crack across its face, from forehead to chin, and the town talks of nothing else. The police open a file.
G3Statua.11.short: At night you pour water into the hot mould. The statue's face cracks. The police open a file.

G3FuneraleLomax.2.full: Lomax's funeral is poor and brief: the priest, two bored nephews, an old woman who sold soap beside his counter, and not a single customer. Ezra Pell the notary is in the front row, in black gloves. During the blessing he pulls off a glove and lays a posy of violets on the coffin.
G3FuneraleLomax.2.easy: Lomax's funeral is poor and short: the priest, two bored great-nephews, an old woman who sold soap beside his counter, and no customers. Ezra Pell the notary is in the front row, in black gloves. During the blessing he takes off one glove and lays a little bunch of violets on the coffin.
G3FuneraleLomax.2.short: At Lomax's poor funeral, Ezra Pell wears black gloves. He removes one and lays violets on the coffin.

G3FuneraleLomax.4.full: You pay $2 for a proper headstone.

G3FuneraleLomax.5.full: You go up to the notary.

G3FuneraleLomax.6.full: You stay at the back, watching.

G3FuneraleLomax.7.full: The stonemason carves Lomax's name, the dates and a line you choose: *He sold salt. It was pure.* The nephews find the phrase incomprehensible. The notary, when he reads it, takes off his hat.
G3FuneraleLomax.7.easy: The stonemason carves Lomax's name, the dates and a line of your choosing: *He sold salt. It was pure.* The great-nephews cannot make sense of it. The notary, when he reads it, takes off his hat.
G3FuneraleLomax.7.short: You have carved: *He sold salt. It was pure.* The notary takes off his hat.

G3FuneraleLomax.9.full: Ezra greets you with a nod and keeps you beside him for the whole service, as one keeps a relative close. At the end he squeezes your arm. "He was a good man," he says. "He carried a secret for more than fifty years. I know how heavy that is."
G3FuneraleLomax.9.easy: Ezra greets you with a nod and keeps you beside him for the whole service, the way one keeps a relative close. At the end he squeezes your arm. "He was a good man," he says. "He carried a secret for more than fifty years. I know how heavy it is."
G3FuneraleLomax.9.short: Ezra keeps you close like a relative. "He carried a secret for fifty years. I know how heavy it is."

G3FuneraleLomax.11.full: You stay at the back, by the door. From there you see what cannot be seen from the front row: when the notary pulls off his glove, the fingers of his right hand are stained violet, and shaking. When he puts it back on, they stop shaking.
G3FuneraleLomax.11.easy: You stay at the back, by the door. From there you see what cannot be seen from the front row: when the notary takes off his glove, his right hand has violet-stained fingers, and it trembles. When he puts the glove back on, it stops trembling.
G3FuneraleLomax.11.short: From the back you see the notary's ungloved hand: violet-stained fingers, trembling.

G3Recita.2.full: The company that has been playing *The Doctor and His Double* for more than twenty years gives its last performance, then disbands: the manager is old, the actors are tired, and the town has the cinematograph. The tent is full. In the front row sit the mayor, the rector of the Institute and Ezra Pell the notary, in his gloves.

The tent is full. In the front row are the mayor, the Institute's rector and Ezra Pell the notary, in his gloves.
G3Recita.2.short: Last show of *The Doctor and His Double*. In the front row, among others, Ezra Pell, in gloves.

G3Recita.3.full: The actor who plays Umber is wearing the black coat you gave him. Tonight, they say, he is better than ever.
G3Recita.3.easy: The actor playing Umber wears the black coat you gave him. They say tonight he is better than ever.
G3Recita.3.short: The actor playing Umber wears your coat. Tonight he is superb.

G3Recita.6.full: You go backstage, during the second act.

G3Recita.7.full: In the third act the doctor chases the double across the rooftops, catches him and snatches off his hat. Tonight, under the hat, there is not his son's face: there is an old, thin, tired face. The actor has never been made up like that, the manager swears afterwards. Pell the notary, in the front row, leaves before the applause.
G3Recita.7.easy: In the third act the doctor chases the double across the rooftops, catches him and pulls off his hat. Tonight, under the hat, is not his son's face: it is an old, thin, tired face. The manager swears afterwards that the actor was never made up like that. Pell the notary, in the front row, leaves before the applause.
G3Recita.7.short: Tonight, under the double's hat, is an old, tired face no one made up. Pell the notary leaves before the applause.

G3Recita.9.full: Backstage, among the hanging costumes, you find the actor who plays Umber sitting on a trunk, his head in his hands. "I don't know when I stop acting any more," he tells you. "Twenty years inside this part. Some nights I walk out of the tent and go about the town, and people run, and I like it." He asks you for money for the train. He wants to leave tonight.
G3Recita.9.easy: Backstage, among the hanging costumes, you find the actor who plays Umber sitting on a trunk, head in his hands. "I don't know any more when I stop acting," he tells you. "Twenty years inside this character. Some nights I leave the tent and walk about, and people run, and I like it." He asks you for money for the train. He wants to leave tonight.
G3Recita.9.short: The actor who plays Umber is in despair: "I don't know when I stop acting. People run, and I like it." He wants money to leave tonight.

G3Tomba.2.full: The old man's nameless headstone, the one the family had scraped clean so many years ago, has been cleaned. Someone has carved the name again, in small, careful letters, and beneath it, smaller still: *Not yet.*
G3Tomba.2.easy: The old man's nameless headstone, the one the family had scraped clean years ago, has been cleaned. Someone has carved the name again, in small, careful letters, and underneath, even smaller: *Not yet.*
G3Tomba.2.short: Someone has recarved the old man's name on the headstone. And beneath it: *Not yet.*

G3Tomba.3.full: Beneath the old man's name and the words *Come back soon*, which the family had engraved so many years ago, someone has added with a nail, in a hand that slants backwards: *Nearly.*
G3Tomba.3.easy: Under the old man's name and the words *Come back soon*, which the family had carved years ago, someone has added with a nail, in a backward-slanting hand: *Almost.*
G3Tomba.3.short: Under *Come back soon*, someone has scratched with a nail, slanting backwards: *Almost.*

G3Tomba.4.full: On the old man's grave the headstone is in its place, with the name and the two dates. The earth in front, though, has been freshly turned, as if someone had dug and filled it in again, at night, with care.
G3Tomba.4.easy: On the old man's grave the headstone is in place, with the name and the two dates. But the earth in front has been freshly turned, as if someone had dug and filled it in again at night, carefully.
G3Tomba.4.short: The old man's headstone is in place. But the earth is freshly turned, as if dug at night.

G3Tomba.5.full: On the stone lies a posy of fresh violets, tied with string.
G3Tomba.5.easy: On the stone is a little bunch of fresh violets, tied with string.

G3Tomba.7.full: You have the grave opened again.

G3Tomba.9.full: The keeper grumbles, but for an hour's work and a few coins he opens it. The coffin is still there, empty. At the bottom, though, there is something that was not there fifty years ago: a notary's leather document case, empty too, its initials scraped off.
G3Tomba.9.easy: The keeper grumbles, but for an hour's work and a few coins he opens it again. The coffin is still there, empty. But at the bottom there is something that was not there fifty years ago: a notary's leather case, empty too, with the initials scraped off.
G3Tomba.9.short: You have the grave opened. In the empty coffin now lies a notary's case, its initials scraped off.

G3Tomba.11.full: You take them away, and the next day they are back. The keeper, questioned, swears he has never seen who brings them. Then, after a tip, he admits he has sometimes seen, at dawn, an elderly gentleman wearing gloves. "A respectable sort," he says. "Nothing to worry about."
G3Tomba.11.easy: You take them away, and the next day they are back. The keeper swears he has never seen who brings them. Then, after a tip, he admits he has sometimes seen, at dawn, an elderly gentleman with gloves. "A respectable sort," he says. "Don't you worry."
G3Tomba.11.short: You remove them, and they return. For a tip the keeper admits: at dawn an elderly gentleman in gloves comes.

G3Istituto.2.full: The Memorial Institute is all glass and brass, with corridors smelling of carbolic acid and professors in white coats walking quickly, as if someone were chasing them. The rector receives you in a study full of microscopes. In front of him lies a newspaper cutting about the estate's salt, underlined in red.
G3Istituto.2.easy: The Memorial Institute is all glass and brass. The corridors smell of carbolic acid, and the professors in white coats walk fast, as if someone were chasing them. The rector receives you in an office full of microscopes. In front of him is a newspaper cutting about the estate's salt, underlined in red.
G3Istituto.2.short: The Memorial Institute's rector receives you among microscopes, with an article on the salt underlined in red.

G3Istituto.3.full: He wants the formula. He wants the family's notes, the Journal, everything. In exchange he offers a sum that makes your head spin, and a chair named after the old man.
G3Istituto.3.easy: He wants the formula. He wants the family's notes, the Journal, everything. In return he offers a sum that makes your head spin, and a chair named after the old man.
G3Istituto.3.short: He wants the formula and the Journal. He offers a fortune and a chair in the old man's name.

G3Istituto.6.full: You propose working together on the antidote.

G3Istituto.8.full: The rector signs the cheque without haggling. A week later a poster appears in the Institute's windows: *The Salt of the Estate: Science in the Service of the People*. It does not say which people.
G3Istituto.8.easy: The rector signs the cheque without arguing. A week later, in the Institute's windows, there is a poster: *The estate's salt: science in the service of the people*. It does not say which people.
G3Istituto.8.short: You sell. The Institute announces *The estate's salt: science in the service of the people*. It does not say which.

G3Istituto.10.full: The rector thinks it over for a long time, then introduces you to two young assistants, bright, with yellow-stained fingers. They work with you for three nights. They do not find the impurity, but they teach you a method for looking for it.
G3Istituto.10.easy: The rector thinks it over for a long time, then introduces you to two young, sharp assistants with yellow-stained fingers. They work with you for three nights. They do not find the impurity, but they teach you a method for looking for it.
G3Istituto.10.short: Two assistants work with you for three nights. They do not find the impurity, but teach you how to look.

G3Istituto.12.full: You refuse politely, and the rector sees you to the door just as politely. In the corridor, through a half-open door, you see a professor pour white salt into a glass of water, and wait. The colour turns red, and stops there.
G3Istituto.12.easy: You politely refuse, and the rector shows you out just as politely. In the corridor, through a half-open door, you see a professor pouring white salt into a glass of water, and waiting. The colour turns red, and stops there.
G3Istituto.12.short: You refuse. In the corridor a professor tests the salt: the colour turns red, and stops.

G3Prigioniero.2.full: The relative accused of being Umber, so many years ago, is still in their cell, because no one has ever had the courage to reopen the case. They have grown old within those walls: thin, stooped, with the pale eyes of someone who has been looking out of a window for twenty years. The window looks onto the alley.
G3Prigioniero.2.easy: The relative accused of being Umber, years ago, is still in a cell, because no one has ever dared reopen the case. They have grown old within those walls: thin, bent, with the pale eyes of someone who has looked out of a window for twenty years. The window looks onto the alley.
G3Prigioniero.2.short: The relative accused years ago is still in a cell, old and bent. The window looks onto the alley.

G3Prigioniero.3.full: "I see him go by, you know," he tells you. "Nearly every night. Umber. He's not what he used to be: he's grown old too."
G3Prigioniero.3.easy: "I see him go by, you know," they tell you. "Nearly every night. Umber. He's not what he was: he's grown old too."
G3Prigioniero.3.short: "I see him go by nearly every night. He has grown old too."

G3Prigioniero.5.full: You listen to him to the end.

G3Prigioniero.6.full: You pay the warder $3 to let them out.

G3Prigioniero.7.full: "He walks with a new stick, ebony," he says. "And he carries a leather bag, the kind with a brass clasp, like doctors have. Or notaries. Sometimes he stops under my window and raises his hat. He knows me. I think he's sorry."
G3Prigioniero.7.easy: "He walks with a new ebony stick," they say. "And he carries a leather bag, the kind with a brass clasp, like doctors. Or notaries. Sometimes he stops under my window and raises his hat. He knows me. I think he's sorry."
G3Prigioniero.7.short: "He has an ebony stick and a leather bag, like a doctor's. Or a notary's. Sometimes he raises his hat. I think he's sorry."

G3Prigioniero.9.full: The warder counts the money, scratches his head and leaves the cell door open one night, forgetting to lock it. Your relative comes home to the estate at dawn, on foot, shoes muddy from the alley. They plant roses in the garden all spring, and never speak of what they saw from the window.
G3Prigioniero.9.easy: The warder counts the money, scratches his head and one night "forgets" to lock the cell door. The relative comes back to the estate at dawn, on foot, their shoes dirty with mud from the alley. All spring they plant roses in the garden, and never speak of what they saw from the window.
G3Prigioniero.9.short: You pay the warder, and one night the cell is left open. The relative comes home and plants roses. They never speak of what they saw.

G3Banca.2.full: Your great-grandfather's account is still open: fifty years, now. The manager of the Bank has changed three times, but the ledger is the same, and he keeps it under lock and key like a relic. The last withdrawal was yesterday. The signature slants backwards, and trembles.
G3Banca.2.easy: Your great-grandfather's account is still open, after fifty years. The Bank's manager has changed three times, but the ledger is the same, kept under lock and key like a relic. The last withdrawal was yesterday. The signature slants backwards, and shakes.
G3Banca.2.short: Your great-grandfather's account has been open fifty years. The last withdrawal was yesterday, with a shaky, backward-slanting signature.

G3Banca.3.full: The deposits, says the manager, are still brought by the clerk from Pell's practice. He is an elderly man now, and no longer smiles.
G3Banca.3.easy: The manager says the deposits are still brought by the clerk from the Pell's notary practice. He is an old man now, and no longer smiles.
G3Banca.3.short: The deposits still come with Pell's clerk, now old.

G3Banca.5.full: You pay $2 to see the last cheque.

G3Banca.6.full: You ask the court to freeze the account.

G3Banca.7.full: The manager shows it to you under the lamp. The handwriting is the usual one, small, backwards. The ink is not: it is violet, that acid violet you cannot buy at any stationer's and that only notaries' offices use, for deeds that must not be forged.
G3Banca.7.easy: The manager shows it to you under the lamp. The handwriting is the usual one, small, backwards. The ink is not: it is violet, that sharp violet you cannot buy in stationers' shops and that only notaries' offices use, for deeds that cannot be forged.
G3Banca.7.short: The handwriting is the usual. The ink is violet: the kind only notaries' offices use.

G3Banca.9.full: The court takes a month, and in the end finds for the family: the account is frozen until the final reading of the will. The day after the ruling, on the estate's doorstep, there is a cheque torn into eight pieces.
G3Banca.9.easy: The court takes a month, and in the end finds for the family: the account is frozen until the final reading of the will. The day after the ruling, on the estate doorstep, there is a cheque torn into eight pieces.
G3Banca.9.short: The court freezes the account. The next day, on your doorstep, lies a cheque torn into eight pieces.

G3Nell.2.full: They bury Inspector Nell Haskett on a sunny day, at eighty-six, with the police band and two speeches that go on too long. Ada is in the front row, in her old inspector's coat, her aunt's black notebook clutched in her hand. Ezra Pell the notary is at the cemetery too, at the back, by the gate. He leaves before the blessing.
G3Nell.2.easy: Inspector Nell Haskett is buried on a sunny day, at eighty-six, with the police band and two speeches that go on too long. Ada is in the front row, in her old inspector's coat, holding her aunt's black notebook tight. Ezra Pell the notary is at the cemetery too, at the back, by the gate. He leaves before the blessing.
G3Nell.2.short: Nell Haskett is buried at eighty-six. Ada clutches her aunt's black notebook. Ezra Pell, at the back, leaves before the blessing.

G3Nell.4.full: You ask Ada if you may read her aunt's notebook.

G3Nell.5.full: You lay a flower on the grave, and go.

G3Nell.6.full: Ada hesitates, then hands it to you. "My aunt used to say you could be trusted," she says. "One of you, at least." The pages are fifty years of notes in block capitals. The last entry about Umber is from 1895: *The cheques are changing. Same hand, but heavier. This is the winter the young Pell stops sleeping.*
G3Nell.6.easy: Ada hesitates, then hands it to you. "My aunt said you could be trusted," she says. "One of you, at least." The pages hold fifty years of notes in block capitals. The last entry on Umber is from 1895: *The cheques change. Same hand, but heavier. It begins the winter young Pell stops sleeping.*
G3Nell.6.short: Ada hands you the notebook. The last entry on Umber, from 1895: *The cheques change. Same hand, but heavier. It begins the winter young Pell stops sleeping.*

G3Nell.8.full: Ada clutches the notebook to her chest. "My aunt left it to me," she says. "And you never trusted her. Why should I trust you?" She turns away, and goes back to her aunt.
G3Nell.8.easy: Ada holds the notebook to her chest. "My aunt left it to me," she says. "And you never trusted her. Why should I trust you?" She turns away, back to her aunt.
G3Nell.8.short: "You never trusted her. Why should I trust you?" Ada keeps the notebook.

G3Nell.10.full: You lay a flower on the grave and stand there a moment. Next to it, on Silas Pell's headstone, there is a posy of fresh violets, tied with string. The keeper says the notary brings them, every morning, at dawn.
G3Nell.10.easy: You leave a flower on the grave and stand there a moment. Nearby, on Silas Pell's headstone, is a little bunch of fresh violets, tied with string. The keeper says the notary brings them every morning, at dawn.
G3Nell.10.short: On Silas Pell's headstone are fresh violets. The keeper says the notary brings them every morning at dawn.

G3Municipio.2.full: At the land registry, in the town hall, you meet Ezra Pell the notary. He has come to file a deed, and is waiting his turn on a bench, his hat on his knees. He is very thin, he coughs, and he wears gloves even indoors.
G3Municipio.2.easy: At the land registry, in the town hall, you meet Ezra Pell the notary. He has come to file a deed, and is waiting his turn on a bench, hat on his knees. He is very thin, he coughs, and he wears gloves even indoors.
G3Municipio.2.short: At the land registry you meet Ezra Pell: very thin, coughing, gloved even indoors.

G3Municipio.3.full: Under his arm is a book you recognise: *An Essay on the Dual Nature of Man*, with the library's lending slip sticking out from between the pages.
G3Municipio.3.easy: Under his arm is a book you recognise: the *Essay on the Dual Nature of Man*, with the library card sticking out of its pages.
G3Municipio.3.short: Under his arm is the *Essay on the Dual Nature of Man*.

G3Municipio.4.full: He asks you, with an interest he cannot hide, how your antidote is coming along.
G3Municipio.4.easy: He asks you how your antidote is coming along, with an interest he cannot hide.
G3Municipio.4.short: He asks, too keenly, about the antidote.

G3Municipio.6.full: You tell him how far you have got.

G3Municipio.7.full: You ask him to sign you a receipt.

G3Municipio.9.full: Ezra listens, nods, asks two precise questions about temperature and timing. Then he opens his wallet and gives you some money "for laboratory expenses, in memory of my father". When you thank him, he looks at you the way one looks at someone about to leave on a journey.
G3Municipio.9.easy: Ezra listens, nods, asks two precise questions about temperature and timing. Then he opens his wallet and gives you money "for laboratory expenses, in memory of my father". When you thank him, he looks at you the way one looks at someone about to leave.
G3Municipio.9.short: Ezra listens, asks two precise questions and gives you money for the laboratory. He looks at you like someone about to leave.

G3Municipio.11.full: Ezra takes off a glove, slowly. His fingers are stained with violet ink. He takes the pen in his right hand and begins to write: an upright, orderly hand, a notary's hand. Halfway through his name his hand stiffens, and the last letters bend backwards. Ezra looks at the sheet, crumples it, puts it in his pocket and leaves without waiting his turn.
G3Municipio.11.easy: Ezra slowly takes off a glove. His fingers are stained with violet ink. He takes the pen in his right hand and starts to write, in an upright, tidy, notary's hand. Halfway through his name the hand stiffens, and the last letters bend backwards. Ezra looks at the sheet, crumples it, puts it in his pocket and leaves without waiting his turn.
G3Municipio.11.short: Ezra removes a glove: violet fingers. He writes his name upright, but the last letters bend backwards. He crumples the sheet and leaves.

G3Municipio.13.full: You say goodbye and leave. On the threshold you turn: Ezra Pell is still on the bench, staring into space, his gloved hands clasped around his hat. In the glass of the door his reflection is smaller than he is.
G3Municipio.13.easy: You say goodbye and leave. In the doorway you turn round: Ezra Pell is still on the bench, staring into space, his gloved hands clutching his hat. In the glass of the door his reflection is smaller than he is.
G3Municipio.13.short: You leave. In the door's glass, Ezra's reflection is smaller than he is.

G3Emporio.2.full: Lomax's heirs are selling off everything from the old pharmacy: boxes, jars, little scales, yellowed prescriptions, whole drawers of unlabelled powders. It is all piled on a table at the back of the General Store, and people rummage through it as at a flea market.
G3Emporio.2.easy: Lomax's heirs are selling off everything from the old pharmacy: boxes, jars, little scales, yellowed prescriptions, whole drawers of unlabelled powders. It is all heaped on a table at the back of the General Store, and people rummage through it as at a flea market.
G3Emporio.2.short: Lomax's heirs sell off the old pharmacy: jars, prescriptions, drawers of unlabelled powders.

G3Emporio.4.full: You buy the whole drawer of powders, for $3.

G3Emporio.5.full: You buy the pharmacy ledgers, for $2.

G3Emporio.6.full: At the bottom of the drawer, inside a carefully folded paper twist, there is a pinch of grey powder. It tastes of nothing. In the laboratory, dissolved with the new salt, it takes the colour from violet to green, for an instant, before it turns back. There is very little. But it is the one.
G3Emporio.6.easy: At the bottom of the drawer, in a carefully folded paper packet, is a pinch of grey powder. It tastes of nothing. In the laboratory, dissolved with the new salt, it takes the colour from violet to green, for an instant, before it turns back. There is little of it. But it is the one.
G3Emporio.6.short: At the bottom of the drawer is a pinch of grey powder. With the new salt the colour reaches green, for a moment. There is little, but it is the one.

G3Emporio.7.full: Pay $3. The antidote takes a step forward: return one of the Collaborative Experiments not yet completed to the box.

G3Emporio.9.full: The drawer holds powders of every colour: white, yellow, pink, even a blue one. No grey. You take them home all the same. Some of them, at least, will be useful.
G3Emporio.9.easy: In the drawer there are powders of every colour: white, yellow, pink, even a blue one. No grey ones. You take them home anyway. Some of them, at least, are useful.
G3Emporio.9.short: Powders of every colour, but no grey. You take them anyway.

G3Emporio.11.full: There are twelve cloth-bound volumes, damp from the cellar. In the fourth, under the date 9 November 1859, is the crossed-out line you know, or have heard of. With a magnifying glass and a candle behind the page, the ink beneath the crossing-out can still be read: *grey powder, from S. P.'s cupboard.*
G3Emporio.11.easy: There are twelve cloth-bound volumes, damp from the cellar. In the fourth, under the date 9 November 1859, is the crossed-out line you know, or have heard of. With a magnifying glass and a candle behind the page, the ink under the crossing-out can still be read: *grey powder, from S. P.'s cupboard.*
G3Emporio.11.short: In the 1859 ledger, under the crossed-out line, you can still read: *grey powder, from S. P.'s cupboard.*

G3Lomax.2.full: **Deathbed statement of Lomax, chemist – taken down by Ezra Pell, notary, *1912.***

G3Lomax.3.full: The salt in that first batch was mine, but it was not pure. The old man from the estate came to the pharmacy one winter evening with a phial of grey powder, and asked me to mix it into the salt: a teaspoon to each phial, and not to write it in the ledger. He paid me not to write it: enough to buy the pharmacy twice over, and my silence for more than fifty years.
G3Lomax.3.easy: The salt of that first batch was mine, but it was not pure. One winter evening the old man from the estate came to the pharmacy with a phial of grey powder. He asked me to mix it into the salt, a teaspoon per phial, and not to write it in the ledger. He paid me not to write it: enough to buy the pharmacy twice over, and my silence for more than fifty years.
G3Lomax.3.short: The first batch was not pure. The old man had me mix in a grey powder, a teaspoon per phial, and paid me to keep quiet for fifty years.

G3Lomax.4.full: I asked him where the powder came from. He told me he had taken it from a friend's cupboard, a man of law who had studied to be an apothecary in his youth and kept his powders under lock and key; and that the friend was not to know. The notary. Your father, Mr. Pell. The good salt was never the old man's discovery: it was a theft.
G3Lomax.4.easy: I asked him where the powder came from. He said he had taken it from a friend's cupboard, a man of law who had trained as an apothecary when young and kept his powders under lock and key. And that the friend must not know. The notary. Your father, Mr. Pell. The good salt was never the old man's discovery: it was a theft.
G3Lomax.4.short: The powder came from the notary's cupboard, your father's, Mr. Pell, without his knowing. The good salt was not a discovery: it was a theft.

G3Lomax.5.full: I kept one phial of that batch. Just one, for fifty years, at the back of the drawer. I never opened it. Take it, and do with it what you will: I want nothing more to do with it.
G3Lomax.5.easy: I kept one phial of that batch myself. Just one, for fifty years, at the bottom of a drawer. I never opened it. Take it, and do what you like with it: I want nothing more to do with it.
G3Lomax.5.short: I kept one phial of that batch, never opened. Take it.

G3Lomax.7.full: I took down these words with a steady hand. It was the last time.
G3Lomax.7.easy: I wrote these words with a steady hand. It was the last time.
G3Lomax.7.short: I wrote this with a steady hand. For the last time.

G3DoseOfferta.2.full: Each player secretly takes in hand as much money as they wish to offer for the last dose of the impure salt, even nothing. When everyone is ready, reveal your offers together.

G3DoseEsito.2.full: Who offered the most *(in case of a tie, the Start Player decides; if no one offered anything, no one)*?

G3DosePresa.2.full: Lomax dies that same night, his hands folded. The phial passes to {0}, who wraps it in a handkerchief and puts it in the inside pocket of their jacket, over the heart. It weighs more than it should.
G3DosePresa.2.easy: Lomax dies that same night, hands folded. The phial passes to {0}, who wraps it in a handkerchief and puts it in their inside jacket pocket, over the heart. It weighs more than it should.
G3DosePresa.2.short: Lomax dies that night. The phial passes to {0}, who keeps it over the heart. It weighs more than it should.

G3DosePresa.3.full: **{0}** pays their offer and takes the **Rehabilitation token** {icon:S2_RehabilitationToken} from the **Fear of the Unknown** Scenario Box: it is the last pure dose. The others take back their offers.

G3DosePresa.4.full: No one wants it. Lomax dies that same night, the phial clutched in his hand; when the nurse tries to take it from him, his fingers will not open. They bury him like that. The next day, on his grave, someone has left a flower and a cheque.
G3DosePresa.4.easy: No one wants it. Lomax dies that same night, the phial clutched in his hand. When the nurse tries to take it from him, his fingers will not open. They bury him like that. The next day, on his grave, someone has left a flower and a cheque.
G3DosePresa.4.short: No one wants it. Lomax dies holding the phial, and is buried with it. On his grave, a flower and a cheque.

G3DosePresa.5.full: The offers go back to the players.

G3Cronaca1.3.full: The liberal paper and the conservative one, for once, come out with the same news on the front page: Lomax the chemist, the salt man, is dead. The two versions, naturally, do not agree. For the liberal paper he was a small tradesman crushed by the powerful; for the conservative one, a poisoner pardoned by old age.
G3Cronaca1.3.easy: For once the liberal paper and the conservative one come out with the same front-page news: Lomax the chemist, the salt man, is dead. Naturally the two versions differ. For the liberal paper he was a small shopkeeper crushed by the powerful. For the conservative one, a poisoner saved by old age.
G3Cronaca1.3.short: Lomax is dead. For one paper he was a victim of the powerful, for the other a poisoner saved by old age.

G3Cronaca1.4.full: Both recall, in their articles, the "surprising interview" given months ago by an heir of the estate, who told the story of the salt to both papers and was paid twice. Both call it "illuminating".
G3Cronaca1.4.easy: In the article both recall the "surprising interview" given months ago by an heir of the estate, who told the story of the salt to both papers and got paid twice. Both call it "illuminating".
G3Cronaca1.4.short: Both recall your interview, paid twice. They call it "illuminating".

G3Cronaca1.5.full: The liberal paper recalls that it always maintained Umber was a bored rich man. The conservative paper recalls that it always maintained the liberal paper was in the pay of the estate.
G3Cronaca1.5.easy: The liberal paper recalls that it always said Umber was a bored rich man. The conservative paper recalls that it always said the liberal paper was paid by the estate.
G3Cronaca1.5.short: Each paper recalls that it was always right.

G3Cronaca1.6.full: The conservative paper proudly recalls the raids on the lodging houses by the station, which "restored order". The liberal paper recalls that none of those arrested was Umber.
G3Cronaca1.6.easy: The conservative paper proudly recalls the raids on the station lodging houses, which "restored order". The liberal paper recalls that none of those arrested was Umber.
G3Cronaca1.6.short: One recalls the raids proudly. The other recalls that none of those arrested was Umber.

G3Cronaca1.7.full: On page two, a letter to the editor from a mother whose son is a patient in the gentlefolk's ward: she thanks "a family of this town" who promised her a cure. The letter is signed only with initials.
G3Cronaca1.7.easy: On page two is a letter to the editor from a mother whose son is in the gentlefolk's ward. She thanks "a family in town" that has promised her a cure. The letter is signed only with initials.
G3Cronaca1.7.short: A mother thanks "a family in town" that promised her son a cure.

G3Cronaca1.8.full: The Library announces with satisfaction that it has catalogued the archive of the late Silas Pell, notary, donated by his son. The catalogue is open to the public. The year 1861, it is specified, is missing.
G3Cronaca1.8.easy: The Library is pleased to announce that it has catalogued the archive of the late Silas Pell, notary, donated by his son. The catalogue is open to the public. The year 1861, it notes, is missing.
G3Cronaca1.8.short: The Library has catalogued Silas Pell's archive. The year 1861 is missing.

G3Cronaca1.9.full: In the local news, a short item: the town's old blacksmith has shut up shop and gone to live with his daughter. He says that lately too many people were asking him about a key "very old and very strange".
G3Cronaca1.9.easy: In the local news, a short item: the town's old blacksmith has shut up shop and gone to live with his daughter. He says that lately too many people were asking him about a key "very old and very strange".
G3Cronaca1.9.short: The old blacksmith has shut up shop: too many asked about a key "very old and very strange".

G3R2.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 8**: the innocent one is still in the Jail.

G3R2.3.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 20**.

G3R2.5.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Jail, to visit the relative still in their cell,

G3R2.8.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Memorial Institute,

G3R2.26.full: The Institute of science on the hill has changed its mind: now it offers a fortune for the formula of the salt, and a chair to whoever brings it. The professors come to the estate by motor car, wearing gloves.
G3R2.26.easy: The Institute of Science on the hill has changed its mind: now it offers a fortune for the salt's formula, and a chair to whoever brings it. The professors come to the estate by motor car, wearing gloves.
G3R2.26.short: The Institute now offers a fortune for the salt's formula. The professors arrive by motor car.

round.G3R2.end.full: The Middle Years of the Third Generation have ended.

G3Cronaca2.2.full: **Letter from Ada Haskett, retired inspector, to the family at the estate – *1913.***

G3Cronaca2.3.full: Dear friends, for I think I may call you that now: I write because I need to tell someone, and my aunt is gone.
G3Cronaca2.3.easy: Dear friends, for I may call you that now: I am writing because I need to tell someone, and my aunt is gone.
G3Cronaca2.3.short: Dear friends, I write because I must tell someone, and my aunt is gone.

G3Cronaca2.4.full: Ladies and gentlemen, we have never been friends, and I shall not pretend to be now. I write because I have no one else to write to, and because what I have to say concerns you more than anyone.
G3Cronaca2.4.easy: Ladies and gentlemen, we have never been friends, and I shall not pretend to be now. I am writing because I have no one else to write to, and because what I have to say concerns you more than anyone.
G3Cronaca2.4.short: We have never been friends. But what I have to say concerns you more than anyone.

G3Cronaca2.5.full: For fifty-two years my family has been hunting Mr. Umber. My aunt began when she was younger than I am now; I carried on when she could no longer manage. We have stopped forty short men and a few innocents, and closed more than one file out of weariness. We never caught him.
G3Cronaca2.5.easy: For fifty-two years my family has hunted Mr. Umber. My aunt started when she was younger than I am now. I carried on when she could no longer manage. We stopped forty short men and a few innocents, and closed more than one file out of weariness. We never caught him.
G3Cronaca2.5.short: For fifty-two years my family has hunted Umber. We stopped many innocents. Never him.

G3Cronaca2.6.full: Have you seen the old man's statue, in the square? Everyone says it is a good likeness. I never saw the old man. But walking past it at night, I had the impression the statue looked like someone else.
G3Cronaca2.6.easy: Have you seen the old man's statue in the square? Everyone says it looks like him. I never saw the old man. But walking past it at night, I had the feeling the statue looked like someone else.
G3Cronaca2.6.short: Everyone says the statue looks like the old man. At night, to me it looks like someone else.

G3Cronaca2.7.full: My aunt's notebook, which I let you read at the cemetery, I have read again myself, all of it, at night. I read the last page about Umber three times. I believe she understood, in the end, and did not have the courage to write it out in full.
G3Cronaca2.7.easy: My aunt's notebook, which I let you read at the cemetery, I have read again myself, all of it, at night. I read the last page on Umber three times. I think in the end she had understood, and did not have the courage to write it all down.
G3Cronaca2.7.short: I reread my aunt's notebook. I think in the end she understood, but lacked the courage to write it.

G3Cronaca2.8.full: I know one of you went to the Bank to see the last cheque on the old account. Violet ink, wasn't it? I have seen it too. There are few places in this town where that ink is used.
G3Cronaca2.8.easy: I know one of you went to the Bank to see the last cheque from the old account. Violet ink, wasn't it? I saw it too. There are few places in this town where that ink is used.
G3Cronaca2.8.short: I know about the last cheque. Violet ink, wasn't it? Few places in town use it.

G3Cronaca2.9.full: I also know you went to visit your relative in the cell, and that they told you about the elderly gentleman with the leather bag. They never told me. Perhaps I never asked the right way.
G3Cronaca2.9.easy: I also know you visited your relative in the cell, and that they told you about the old gentleman with the leather bag. They never told me. Perhaps I never asked the right way.
G3Cronaca2.9.short: I know about the old gentleman with the leather bag too. Your relative never told me.

G3Cronaca2.10.full: I no longer have the badge, and I am no longer young. But if one day you should need someone who knows how to listen, you know where I live. Ada Haskett.
G3Cronaca2.10.easy: I no longer have the badge, nor the age for it. But if one day you need someone who knows how to listen, you know where I live. Ada Haskett.
G3Cronaca2.10.short: If you need someone to listen, you know where I live. Ada Haskett.

G3Notte.2.full: The newspapers, for once in agreement, forecast the worst storm in fifty years. That afternoon a note arrives at the estate from Ezra Pell the notary, in handwriting so shaky it can hardly be read: he asks to see the whole family, on the evening of the storm, in the study with two doors. He will bring the will.
G3Notte.2.easy: For once the papers agree: the worst storm in fifty years is coming. That afternoon a note arrives at the estate from Ezra Pell the notary, in a hand so shaky it is hard to read. He wants to see the whole family on the night of the storm, in the room with two doors. He will bring the will.
G3Notte.2.short: The worst storm in fifty years is coming. Pell the notary writes: that night he will bring the will, to the room with two doors.

G3Notte.4.full: You accept, and wait for him at the estate.

G3Notte.5.full: You ask Ada Haskett to be present.

G3Notte.6.full: Before answering, you call at his office.

G3Notte.7.full: You reply with a two-line note: the family will expect him. The clerk from the practice collects it at the door and leaves without waiting for a tip.
G3Notte.7.easy: You reply with a two-line note: the family will expect him. The office clerk collects it at the door and leaves without waiting for a tip.
G3Notte.7.short: You reply that you will expect him.

G3Notte.9.full: Ada Haskett, retired now, accepts at once. "My aunt always said she never liked that notary," she says. "She couldn't say why. I'll be there."
G3Notte.9.easy: Ada Haskett, retired now, accepts at once. "My aunt said she never liked that notary," she says. "She couldn't say why. I'll be there."
G3Notte.9.short: Ada Haskett accepts at once: "My aunt never liked that notary. I'll be there."

G3Notte.10.full: Ada Haskett will be present on the last night.

G3Notte.11.full: Ada Haskett has her housekeeper answer for her: she is retired, and your family was never kind to hers. On the evening of the storm she will stay at home.
G3Notte.11.easy: Ada Haskett has her housekeeper reply: she is retired, and your family has never been kind to hers. On the night of the storm she will stay at home.
G3Notte.11.short: Ada Haskett refuses: your family was never kind to hers.

G3Notte.13.full: You call at Pell's practice in the afternoon, on a pretext. The notary is out; the clerk has you wait in the file room. In one corner stands an old walnut cupboard, its doors open. There is nothing inside, except a bitter smell and a grey film on the shelves.
G3Notte.13.easy: In the afternoon you call at the Pell office, on some pretext. The notary is out, and the clerk has you wait in the files room. In a corner stands an old walnut cupboard, its doors open. There is nothing inside, only a bitter smell and a grey film on the shelves.
G3Notte.13.short: At the Pell office you see the old cupboard, open. It is empty: only a bitter smell and a grey film.

G3R3.3.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 21**: the night.

G3R3.8.full: The first player to send one of their pieces to the Traveling Caravan,

G3R3.14.full: Lomax's heirs are selling off the pharmacy's stock. The first player to send one of their pieces to the General Store,

G3R3.20.full: The sky over the town is low and yellow. In every house the shutters are closing. Tonight the notary will read the will for the last time.
G3R3.20.easy: The sky over the town is low and yellow. In every house the shutters are closing. Tonight the notary will read the will for the last time.
G3R3.20.short: The sky is yellow. Tonight the will is read for the last time.

round.G3R3.end.full: The Late Years of the Third Generation have ended.

G3Dose.3.full: Before the notary arrives you shut yourself in the bathroom with Lomax's phial and a glass of water. You break the seal. The salt is white, fine as sugar, with a yellowish sheen when you hold it to the light. A sentence comes back to you, who knows from where, a sentence you have never read: *a single sip. Then the door.*
G3Dose.3.easy: Before the notary arrives you lock yourself in the bathroom with Lomax's phial and a glass of water. You break the seal. The salt is white, fine as sugar, with a yellowish sheen when you hold it to the light. A sentence you have never read comes back to you, who knows from where: *a single sip. Then the door.*
G3Dose.3.short: Before the notary arrives you lock yourself in with Lomax's phial. A sentence you never read comes back to you: *a single sip. Then the door.*

G3Dose.4.full: No one will know what you chose, until it is too late to change it.
G3Dose.4.easy: No one will know what you chose until it is too late to change it.
G3Dose.4.short: No one will know what you chose until it is too late.

G3UltimaNotte.2.full: The storm arrives at sunset. The family is gathered in the study with two doors, among the old man's mirrors, and the electric light comes and goes. Ezra Pell the notary stands by the fireplace, his coat wet and the will in his hand. He has aged all at once, like someone who has not slept for years.
G3UltimaNotte.2.easy: The storm breaks at sunset. The family is gathered in the room with two doors, among the old man's mirrors, and the electric light flickers on and off. Ezra Pell the notary stands by the fireplace, in a wet coat, the will in his hand. He has grown old all at once, like someone who has not slept for years.
G3UltimaNotte.2.short: At sunset, in the study of mirrors, Ezra Pell waits with the will in his hand. He looks as if he has not slept for years.

G3UltimaNotte.3.full: "The circumstances have been doubtful for fifty years," he says. "The will obliges me to hand everything over to Mr. Umber. Before I do, I want to know from you what I should do." Outside a clap of thunder rattles the windows, and for a moment, in all the mirrors, the notary seems smaller.
G3UltimaNotte.3.easy: "The circumstances have been doubtful for fifty years," he says. "The will obliges me to hand everything to Mr. Umber. Before I do, I want you to tell me what I must do." Outside, thunder rattles the windows, and for a moment, in every mirror, the notary looks smaller.
G3UltimaNotte.3.short: "The will obliges me to give everything to Mr. Umber. Tell me what I must do." For a moment, in the mirrors, the notary looks smaller.

G3UltimaNotte.4.full: The black coat hangs on the hall coat stand, where you put it. The notary, coming in, hangs his hat on it without thinking, as one does at home.
G3UltimaNotte.4.easy: The black coat hangs on the hall coat stand, where you put it. Coming in, the notary hangs his hat on it without thinking, as one does at home.
G3UltimaNotte.4.short: Coming in, the notary hangs his hat on the black coat, as if at home.

G3UltimaNotte.5.full: In a corner, seated, is Ada Haskett, retired but with her aunt's notebook on her knees. The notary greets her with a bow, and from that moment never turns his back on her.
G3UltimaNotte.5.easy: In a corner sits Ada Haskett: retired, but with her aunt's notebook on her knees. The notary greets her with a bow, and from then on never turns his back on her.
G3UltimaNotte.5.short: In the corner sits Ada Haskett, with her aunt's notebook. The notary never turns his back on her.

G3UltimaNotte.6.full: None of you says it aloud. But while the notary speaks, you all watch his hands, and the gloves he never takes off. Each of you, over these years, has seen something: a signature, an ink, a name on a slip, an open door. Taken one by one, they mean nothing. Put together, they make a single person. And in the mirrors, for a moment, you all see the same thing.
G3UltimaNotte.6.easy: None of you says it aloud. But while the notary speaks, you all watch his hands, and the gloves he never takes off. Over these years each of you has seen something: a signature, an ink, a name on a card, an open door. On their own, they mean nothing. Put together, they make a single person. And in the mirrors, for a moment, you all see the same thing.
G3UltimaNotte.6.short: While the notary speaks, you all watch his gloves. Each of you has seen something. Together, those things make one person. And in the mirrors you all see the same thing.

G3UltimaNotte.7.full: One of you, for some reason, cannot stop looking at the notary's hands.
G3UltimaNotte.7.easy: One of you, who knows why, cannot stop looking at the notary's hands.
G3UltimaNotte.7.short: One of you cannot stop looking at the notary's hands.

G3VotoAntidoto.2.full: On the table is the antidote, a glass for each of you. The notary looks at it the way one looks at a weapon.
G3VotoAntidoto.2.easy: On the table is the antidote, one glass each. The notary looks at it as one looks at a weapon.
G3VotoAntidoto.2.short: On the table is the antidote. The notary eyes it like a weapon.

G3VotoAntidoto.4.full: YAY: you all drink the antidote, and Umber disappears for ever.

G3VotoAntidoto.5.full: NAY: you recognise Umber as heir, as the will requires.

G3VotoAntidoto.6.full: *The vote of the Heir in the Shadow, who revealed themselves at the start of the Generation, counts double.*

G3VotoConfessione.2.full: The reporters from both papers are waiting outside the gate, in the rain. You would only have to open the door and tell everything.
G3VotoConfessione.2.easy: The reporters from both papers wait outside the gate, in the rain. You would only have to open the door and tell everything.
G3VotoConfessione.2.short: Outside, in the rain, the reporters wait.

G3VotoConfessione.3.full: Half the story, after all, they know already: you sold it to them.

G3VotoConfessione.5.full: YAY: the family confesses everything, in public.

G3VotoConfessione.6.full: NAY: the family keeps silent, and seals the documents.

G3VotoTestamento.2.full: The notary opens the will on the table, at the page with the clause. His hand shakes so much he has to steady it with the other.
G3VotoTestamento.2.easy: The notary opens the will on the table, at the page with the clause. His hand shakes so much that he has to steady it with the other.
G3VotoTestamento.2.short: The notary opens the will at the clause. His hand shakes.

G3VotoTestamento.4.full: YAY: the notary carries out the clause: everything to Mr. Umber.

G3VotoTestamento.5.full: NAY: the will is contested, and the documents sealed.

Epilogo.2.full: Ada Haskett lived another twenty years, in her aunt's little house by the station, with the cat and the black notebook. Every Christmas she received from the estate a box of apples and a card, and every Christmas she replied with two lines: *Still nothing. I'm keeping an eye on you.*
Epilogo.2.easy: Ada Haskett lived another twenty years, in her aunt's little house near the station, with the cat and the black notebook. Every Christmas she received a box of apples and a note from the estate, and every Christmas she replied with two lines: *Nothing yet. I'm keeping an eye on you.*
Epilogo.2.short: Ada Haskett lived another twenty years. Every Christmas she answered your apples: *Nothing yet. I'm keeping an eye on you.*

Epilogo.3.full: Ada Haskett left the town the following year, without saying goodbye to anyone, and went to live in a seaside town where no one had ever heard of Umber. They say she was happy there. They also say that at night she checked the lock twice.
Epilogo.3.easy: Ada Haskett left town the following year without saying goodbye to anyone, and went to live in a seaside town where no one had ever heard of Umber. They say she was happy there. They also say that at night she checked the lock twice.
Epilogo.3.short: Ada Haskett moved to the sea, where no one knew Umber. They say she was happy, and checked the lock twice.

Epilogo.4.full: The study on the alley, the one with the mirrors, the one **{0}** had found so many years before by following the footprints in the mud, stayed as it was. The door with no handle never opened again from the alley. From the inside, now and then, it did.
Epilogo.4.easy: The room on the alley, the study of mirrors, which **{0}** had found years before by following the footprints in the mud, stayed as it was. The door with no handle never opened again from the alley. From inside, sometimes, it did.
Epilogo.4.short: The study of mirrors, found by **{0}**, stayed as it was. From the alley the door never opened again. From inside, sometimes, it did.

Epilogo.5.full: The asylum archive on the hill still keeps the file of the first patient of quality in the gentlefolk's ward, an heir of the estate, with the diagnosis written by Lady Carew herself: *interesting case*.
Epilogo.5.easy: In the archive of the asylum on the hill there is still the file of the gentlefolk's ward's first important patient, an heir of the estate, with the diagnosis written by Lady Carew herself: *interesting case*.
Epilogo.5.short: The asylum still keeps the committed heir's file: *interesting case*.

Epilogo.6.full: The cell in the Jail with the window onto the alley, where an innocent member of the family spent so many years, has been closed and turned into a records room. The constables do not like going in at night. They say you can see someone pass by the window.
Epilogo.6.easy: The Jail cell with the window on the alley, where an innocent member of the family spent so many years, has been closed and turned into a records room. At night the constables do not like going in. They say you can see someone go by from the window.
Epilogo.6.short: The cell on the alley is a records room now. The constables say that at night someone can be seen passing the window.

Epilogo.7.full: The trial of the Heir in the Shadow, the only time the town ever laid hands on Umber, is still studied in law schools, as an example of a culprit who did not remember the crime. The professors agree on nothing. The students enjoy it enormously.
Epilogo.7.easy: The trial of the Heir in the Shadow, the only time the town managed to lay hands on Umber, is still studied in law schools, as the case of a culprit who did not remember his crime. The professors agree on nothing. The students enjoy it enormously.
Epilogo.7.short: The Heir in the Shadow's trial is still studied in law schools. The professors argue, the students enjoy it.

Epilogo.8.full: On the old man's grave, beneath the name, the three words the family had engraved can still be read: *Come back soon*. Someone recuts them with a chisel every few years, so the moss will not cover them.
Epilogo.8.easy: On the old man's grave, under the name, you can still read the words the family had carved: *Come back soon*. Every few years someone goes over them with a chisel, so the moss does not cover them.
Epilogo.8.short: On the old man's grave *Come back soon* can still be read: someone recuts it every few years.

Epilogo.9.full: The old man's grave, nameless, is the most visited in the cemetery. People bring their children, to frighten them. They bring flowers, for luck. The violets, every morning, are always there.
Epilogo.9.easy: The old man's nameless grave is the most visited in the cemetery. People bring children there, to frighten them. They bring flowers, for luck. And every morning the violets are always there.
Epilogo.9.short: The old man's nameless grave is the most visited. Every morning the violets are there.

Epilogo.10.full: Ezra Pell the notary is buried in the new cemetery, by the boundary wall, under a lime tree, in a grave paid for twenty-five years earlier with a cheque. The headstone reads only: *Here lies the one who kept the key*.
Epilogo.10.easy: Ezra Pell the notary is buried in the new cemetery, by the wall, under a lime tree, in a grave paid for twenty-five years earlier with a cheque. The headstone says only: *Here lies the one who kept the key*.
Epilogo.10.short: Ezra Pell lies under the lime tree, in the grave Umber paid for: *Here lies the one who kept the key*.

Epilogo.11.full: The old man's bronze statue still stands in the square, the Journal under its arm. The pigeons prefer it to all the others. Lovers arrange to meet beneath it in the evening, and no one can explain why, at a certain hour, the statue's shadow is much shorter than the statue.
Epilogo.11.easy: The old man's bronze statue is still in the square, the Journal under its arm. The pigeons prefer it to all the others. In the evening lovers meet beneath it. And no one can explain why, at a certain hour, the statue's shadow is much shorter than the statue.
Epilogo.11.short: The old man's statue still stands in the square. At a certain hour its shadow is much shorter than it is.

Epilogo.12.full: The old man's black coat ended up, after the company disbanded, in a junk dealer's storeroom. Every so often someone buys it. Every time, after a few weeks, the dealer finds it hanging on his door, carefully folded.
Epilogo.12.easy: When the company broke up, the old man's black coat ended up in a junk dealer's storeroom. Every so often someone buys it. And every time, after a few weeks, the dealer finds it hanging on his door again, carefully folded.
Epilogo.12.short: The black coat is at a junk dealer's. Whoever buys it, within weeks it is back on his door.

Epilogo.13.full: The Pell file, or what remains of it, is what you have just finished reading. If you read it in order, skipping nothing, you already know who closed it. If you think you recognise the handwriting of the last pages, do not stop to think about it. Close it, and go to bed. With the light on, perhaps.
Epilogo.13.easy: The Pell file, or what is left of it, is what you have just finished reading. If you read it in order, skipping nothing, you already know who closed it. If you think you recognise the handwriting of the last pages, do not stop to think about it. Close it and go to bed. With the light on, perhaps.
Epilogo.13.short: This is the Pell file. If you recognise the handwriting of the last pages, don't think about it. Go to bed. With the light on.

FinaleForca.3.full: To whoever opens the file, after me.

FinaleForca.4.full: The town had caught Umber once before, and had enjoyed it. When the sightings began again, no one cared to wait for another expert's report. One night in March they came to the estate with torches, and left with one of us: the one who wrote fastest, and whose hand, when writing fast, slanted backwards. The trial lasted an afternoon. They put up the gallows in the square, in front of the Jail, where the market used to be.
FinaleForca.4.easy: The town had caught Umber once before, and had liked it. When the sightings began again, no one wanted to wait for another expert's report. One night in March they came to the estate with torches, and left with one of us: the one who wrote fastest, and whose hand, when writing fast, slanted backwards. The trial lasted an afternoon. They put up the gallows in the square, in front of the Jail, where the market used to be.
FinaleForca.4.short: When Umber returned, the town did not wait. They came with torches and took one of us, the one whose hand slanted backwards. The trial lasted an afternoon. They put the gallows up in the square.

FinaleForca.5.full: It was not them. I know because on the night after the hanging, at the far end of the cemetery, by the gate, someone laughed for a whole hour. Everyone heard it, and no one went out to look.
FinaleForca.5.easy: It was not him. I know because the night after the hanging, at the far end of the cemetery, by the gate, someone laughed for a whole hour. Everyone heard it, and no one went out to look.
FinaleForca.5.short: It was not him. The next night, in the cemetery, someone laughed for an hour.

FinaleForca.6.full: Ezra Pell the notary watched the execution from the front row, hat in hand, and died a month later. When we opened his file, the last pages were written in a small, quick hand that slanted backwards. The last line said only: *I am sorry. It was not them. It was me.*
FinaleForca.6.easy: Ezra Pell the notary watched the execution from the front row, hat in hand, and died a month later. When we opened his file, the last pages were written in a small, quick hand that slanted backwards. The last line said only: *I am sorry. It was not him. It was me.*
FinaleForca.6.short: Ezra Pell died a month later. The last line of his file, slanting backwards: *I am sorry. It was not him. It was me.*

FinaleForca.7.full: They took the gallows down the next day, and the timber was sold at auction: the caravan theatre bought it for next to nothing and built a new stage with it. Since then, every time I go to the theatre, I sit in the back row, by the door.
FinaleForca.7.easy: They took the gallows down the next day, and the wood was sold at auction. The travelling players' theatre bought it for next to nothing and built a new stage with it. Since then, whenever I go to the theatre, I sit in the back row, near the door.
FinaleForca.7.short: The gallows wood became the theatre's stage. Since then I sit near the door.

FinaleForca.8.full: Ada Haskett, who was with us in the study that night, refused to testify at the trial. She returned her aunt's black notebook to the police, with a two-line letter, and left the town.
FinaleForca.8.easy: Ada Haskett, who was with us in the room that night, refused to testify at the trial. She returned her aunt's black notebook to the police, with a two-line letter, and left town.
FinaleForca.8.short: Ada Haskett refused to testify. She returned her aunt's notebook and left town.

FinaleForca.9.full: The two papers printed our story in full on the day of the hanging, under the same headline as a year before. This time, beneath it, there was a photograph.
FinaleForca.9.easy: On the day of the hanging both papers printed our whole story, under the same headline as a year before. This time there was a photograph beneath it.
FinaleForca.9.short: The papers printed our story under the same headline as before. This time with a photograph.

FinaleSpecchio.3.full: I write with the other hand, because this one is mine now. The heir who used it before me drank the new salt one evening, to see whether they could go back. They could not. They had been halfway to the other side since birth, and the new salt only closed the door.
FinaleSpecchio.3.easy: I write with the other hand, because it is mine now. The heir who used it before me drank the new salt one evening, to see if they could go back. They could not. They had been halfway across since birth, and the new salt only shut the door.
FinaleSpecchio.3.short: I write with the other hand: it is mine now. The heir before me drank the new salt to go back. It only shut the door.

FinaleSpecchio.4.full: I do not regret it. They were a dull person: slept at night, paid their debts, apologised. Not I. I broke every mirror in the study, so that neither of us would ever need to look at the other again, and I have felt splendid ever since.
FinaleSpecchio.4.easy: I do not regret it. They were a dull person: slept at night, paid their debts, apologised. I do not. I broke every mirror in the room, so that neither of us would need to look at the other again, and I have been very well ever since.
FinaleSpecchio.4.short: I do not regret it: they were dull. I broke every mirror, and I have been very well since.

FinaleSpecchio.5.full: One thing only, before I close this notebook, so that the family cannot say Umber does not pay his debts. The cheques of the last twenty years were not all signed by me. On the night of the storm, in the study, there was another of us: standing by the fireplace, his coat wet and the will in his hand. I saw him in the mirrors, before I broke them. He was laughing with my own mouth.
FinaleSpecchio.5.easy: One thing only, before I close this notebook, so the family cannot say Umber does not pay his debts. I did not sign all the cheques of the last twenty years. On the night of the storm, in the room, there was another of us: standing by the fireplace, in a wet coat, the will in his hand. I saw him in the mirrors, before I broke them. He was laughing with my own mouth.
FinaleSpecchio.5.short: One more thing: I did not sign all the last twenty years' cheques. On the night of the storm, by the fireplace, stood another of us, the will in his hand. He laughed with my mouth.

FinaleSpecchio.6.full: Ask the notary what was in his father's cupboard. Ask him soon: he has not much time left.
FinaleSpecchio.6.easy: Ask the notary what was in his father's cupboard. Ask him soon: he has not got long.
FinaleSpecchio.6.short: Ask the notary what was in the cupboard. Soon.

FinaleSpecchio.7.full: The family treats me kindly, the way one treats a sick relative. They leave me the laboratory at night, and the door onto the alley. In the morning they find the glasses washed and the Journal brought up to date, in a hand that slants backwards and that is, I must say, far more legible than yours.
FinaleSpecchio.7.easy: The family treats me kindly, the way one treats a sick relative. At night they leave me the laboratory and the door onto the alley. In the morning they find the glasses washed and the Journal up to date, in a backward-slanting hand that is, I must say, far easier to read than yours.
FinaleSpecchio.7.short: The family treats me like a sick relative. At night I use the laboratory. My handwriting is easier to read than yours.

FinaleSpecchio.8.full: The black coat in the hall is mine now. It fits me perfectly.

FinaleSpecchio.9.full: You burned my coat. No matter: I bought another, just the same, with your money.
FinaleSpecchio.9.easy: You burned my coat. It does not matter: I bought another just like it, with your money.
FinaleSpecchio.9.short: You burned my coat. I bought another, with your money.

FinaleCitta.4.full: Lomax's new salt has never stopped. Students buy it for a bet, ladies out of boredom, bankers for courage. Lomax sold more than he could prepare, and after his death the Institute of science bought the recipe, and sells it with a more elegant label and a higher price.
FinaleCitta.4.easy: Lomax's new salt never stopped. Students buy it for a bet, ladies out of boredom, bankers for courage. Lomax sold more than he could make, and after his death the Institute of Science bought the recipe, and sells it with a smarter label and a higher price.
FinaleCitta.4.short: Everyone buys the new salt. After Lomax died, the Institute bought the recipe and sells it dear.

FinaleCitta.5.full: Our family, in all this, no longer counts for anything. We are the old man's relatives, the ones who started it, and people greet us in the street with absent-minded respect, the way one greets an inventor's descendants. Some of us, in the evening, go out with the others. No one asks who.
FinaleCitta.5.easy: Our family no longer counts for anything in all this. We are the old man's relatives, the ones who started it, and people greet us in the street with absent-minded respect, the way one greets an inventor's descendants. In the evening some of us go out with the others. No one asks who.
FinaleCitta.5.short: Our family no longer counts: we are just the relatives of those who started it. At night some of us go out with the others. No one asks who.

Nothing spectacular happened: a little nausea, a great drowsiness, and in the morning a strange sense of silence, like when the rain stops. Since that night no one has seen Umber again.
